Question: How much Assembly language do you think I will need to write for a console for an 80486 x86 processor with the firmware and OS only reaching a single digit KB, so most of the 20MB of RAM can go to user applications?
Answer: What you're describing is essentially a bootloader. Limiting it to 9.999kB is also a false economy. Actually, it's multiple false economies. False Economy #1 Firmware usually resides in read-only memory. In the 486 era, that was quite possibly still EPROM, as it is on this 486 motherboard: That chip I circled holds the BIOS. It’s most likely an EPROM although there's a chance it's a mask ROM. Either way, I will refer to it as “the ROM,” as it is read-only when your system is active. The CPU can execute directly from the ROM. You don't need to copy it to RAM—although you could. That’s known as BIOS shadowing. DRAM of that era was typically faster than ROM for a variety of reasons. Caches, however, can hide the difference.The Intel® i486s have 8KiB to 16KiB of L1 cache, and many 486 motherboards had L2 cache. ln the picture above, the long, skinny chips in the top right corner are the L2 cache. Thus, your program won't take up any RAM for the program image. Its size won't matter. All that will matter is the space you take in RAM for variables. False Economy #2 You said user applications, plural. Your original goal was to stick to a single digit kilobyte total size. I called that a bootloader, because you're not fitting much more in there—maybe some really basic support for a specific set of hard drives and floppies, and something to talk to the keyboard controller. (Note: the keyboard controller itself is a microcontroller running its own firmware. That's probably another 4KiB - 8KiB. It does a little more than just reading the keyboard—look up A20 Gate for an example—but not tons more.) The point is, you're not going to fit a lot of services in there. To put it in perspective, MS-DOS 2.0 was about 16KiB just for MSDOS.SYS. That still required the BIOS to be present so that MS-DOS could actually access disks. You proposed replacing all that with something less than half the size. So now you want to have multiple applications on this platform, and the only common services they have access to—filesystems, I/O, etc—are whatever you’ve crammed into your firmware. All that space you saved for the applications? They're going to spend it reimplementing what you didn't provide. Chances are good that each application will implement those differently, and possibly incompatibly. I’ve lived through that era. I remember when the Apple ][ had multiple incompatible DOSes, as well as a completely different OS on its Pascal disks, and different disk formats for many individual software packages. It's not a good tradeoff if you have the resources to avoid it. You're doing this on a machine with over 400 times as much RAM and plenty of address space for ROM. There's absolutely zero reason to make this tradeoff. Most sane programmers writing PC-style applications will just use your bootloader firmware to load a more traditional operating environment and will completely ignore your bootloader thereafter. The only folks that might find your setup vaguely interesting are embedded folks that didn't feel like writing a bootloader for their embedded systems project. Those sorts of systems tend to run only one, maybe two programs. (The other program, if it exists, is probably a manufacturing test + diagnostics package.) False Economy #3 You want to write this in assembly language. Since you said firmware, my presumption is that you're replacing the BIOS. You will need some amount of assembly language to set up the CPU and chipset. After that, you can do the rest in C code easily enough. It might be a bit larger and maybe even a bit slower, but who cares? You’ve already committed to not providing much meaningful capability to outside software. Once your bootloader has finished loading the second stage bootloader* that came with the application, exactly 0.00‰ of your code will be performance or size critical until the next reboot. It's just going to sit in ROM, ignored. Why? Your bootloader doesn't offer enough services to be worth calling, most likely. The application will probably bring a second stage bootloader/resident firmware with actual services. Your code will largely be ignored from then on. None of this is hypothetical, by the way. That's pretty much how I have seen other, similar systems play out. I’ve even written a first stage bootloader that's about that size. That was large enough to contain a serial port driver, optimized SPI flash driver, and some basic hash computation for boot integrity purposes. And then it jumped to a stage 2 bootloader, which set up specialized resident firmware and initialized the PCIe and DRAM controllers. That loaded the stage 3 bootloader that then loaded Linux. BTW, I am not making up that bootloader sequence. What might blow your mind is that that was on a network card. Also, fun fact: The firmware we loaded into the DRAM controllers was several times larger than your proposed firmware. It gets loaded into RAM embedded inside the DRAM controller, where a little 32-bit CPU runs it to manage a couple DRAM channels (out of several). There's a similar situation on the PCIe links. If you really want to fiddle around with low level stuff on a 486, why not check out an existing project such as FreeDOS? It just turned 30 two months ago. Update I see Jerry Coffin mentioned FreeRTOS, and the fact it can compile to a tiny runtime—on the order of 4KiB for a minimal configuration. That might be an interesting substrate for you to experiment with as well. IMHO, it's more interesting as a substrate for the actual application itself, rather than the boot code. However, I anticipate you're still going to need other code to get the system to a functional state, unless you retain the BIOS that came with the system. I’m sure Jerry will correct me if I am off base here. I haven't played with x86 ports of FreeRTOS. Update 2 Someone is likely to point out early UNIX™ crammed into sub-64KiB machines way back when. It certainly did. And yes, they crammed a lot into a few kilobytes. You can browse around The UNIX™ Heritage Society archives to judge just how much “there” was there in those earliest iterations. Version 6 is probably the first version that truly resembles UNIX™ as we know it. Link: https://www.tuhs.org/cgi-bin/utree.pl C was invented precisely so they didn't have to write everything in assembly language. The archives include the source for compilers for those early dialects of C. (Which, of course, are written in roughly those same dialects of C.)

Question: Is it still true that I can outperform a C++ compiler using Assembler?
Answer: First, some clarifying questions: For short stretches of code, a sufficiently skilled developer can often outdo the compiler, even today. That bar is pretty high, and continues to go higher. Now repeat after me: Assembly Language Isn’t Magic™. Mainstream Computing There can be good reasons to invest the time in hand tuned assembly—for example, key loop kernels in a broadly used performance critical library. Most often it's not the best use of your time. That's particularly true in mainstream computing, with beefy processors and a continually evolving landscape. (For embedded systems, see below.) Around 30 years ago, I could routinely beat the C compiler by a factor of 2 with hand written assembly code on my 32-bit 486 system. That was with GCC running under Linux. Michael Abrash demonstrated an even bigger spread—more like 3×—for 16-bit code running on MS-DOS. That was published under the heading Their Ain’t No Such Thing As The Fastest Code. That material originated in PC Techniques magazine, and then found its way into a couple different books (The Zen of Code Optimization, and Abrash's Graphics Programming Black Book and perhaps others). All of that is ancient history now. Case in point: I took the C and assembly Abrash published above and compiled it on a modern machine. The 3× advantage for assembly was replaced with a 4× advantage for the C compiler. The assembly wasn't optimized for modern hardware. You could probably beat the C compiler again by reoptimizing the code, but “y tho?” Realistically, for most software developers, the compiler will generate far better assembly code than they will. The human might beat the compiler from time to time, but most often the compiler will win overall. The more crunched for time you are, the more often that's true. A compiler upgrade and recompile will potentially net you instant performance gains on the next generation of cores, for almost no effort—but not on your assembly code. Only the compiled code benefits. Furthermore, a compiler will aggressively transform your code while performing its optimizations. If you performed those same transformations and optimizations, either at the C++ or assembly level, you’ll likely end up with unmaintainable spaghetti. Thus, in real world code that needs to remain maintainable, the compiler has some inherent advantages. Take the time you would have spent shining up some soon-to-be-obsolete assembly language, and spend that on tuning the algorithms, data structures, and higher level data flow. That can pay off much better in the long run. I personally have not bothered to hand optimize any meaningful amount of x86 code in about 25 years. The potential gains were too small, the ISA continued to change every couple years, and I had far bigger fish to fry. Embedded Systems Tightly focused embedded systems are another story. Replace “vinyl” with “embedded software optimization” in the comic below, and that's where certain quirky folks like myself sometimes are. 😉 Embedded systems have some interesting characteristics that differ from mainstream computing: In that environment, low level optimizations and hand written assembly might provide a reasonable return on investment. It's not an absolute guarantee, but it is worth acknowledging the different dynamic. For the record, I have spent considerable time micro-optimizing C, C++, and assembly language code on embedded systems the last 25 years. I still keep as much as I can in C or C++. But for the most constrained systems, such as a 40MHz 16-bit PIC24, I still wrote considerable amounts of assembly. Additional Reading Your particular question is evergreen. I have answered many variations of it. Rather than repeat everything I said before, I will point you this answer that links to several others: And this one in particular pokes on the idea that the compiler will perform optimizations that you're not likely to, for maintenance or other reasons:

Question: What is the highest positive value which can be represented by the 8-bit floating point notation?
Answer: You say “the 8-bit floating point” format, as if there's only one. I’m aware of a few, and I am certain there are more. For example, I have seen variations known as 1.5.2 and 1.4.3. The digits specify the number of sign, exponent, and significand bits the format uses. I’ve also seen an unsigned 0.3.5 that didn't use a hidden 1 in the significand. That last one was used in an ancient voice synthesis device. Once you squeeze down to 8 bits, you often need to tweak the format to the application’s needs. You might adjust the exponent bias, for example, or shift bits between exponent and significand. I vaguely recall one person mentioning one variant that only had exponent and sign, and an implicit 1 for the significand; however, I can't guarantee I didn't dream it. In any case, if the format follows IEEE 754 principles—and there's no guarantee it does—then the simple answer is + ∞ . Otherwise, you're going to have to look at the specifics of the format you're using.

Question: Is C, Assembler or C++ better for performance critical code and why is assembly and C++ a hard language for me? Am I just an idiot?
Answer: There's a lot to unpack here. I’ll take this in a few steps. C++ isn't a beginner language, IMHO. At least, I didn't truly understand it or appreciate it until I had a lot more experience under my belt. It wasn't the syntax necessarily, or even the semantics most of the time. I simply did not understand how to use all of the complex functionality effectively. The Effective C++ book series along with a few other books, really helped. (See the list in the pinned answer on my profile.) It could be that you're simply not sufficiently experienced as a programmer. Or, it's possible you haven't found the right resources to guide you through the language and material. At the other extreme is assembly language. Assembly language is barely a language. Worse, every processor architecture has its own assembly language, and often multiple dialects. Assembly is mostly a human readable syntax for the instructions the CPU executes natively. In its most basic form, it has no structure of its own, beyond whatever restrictions the instruction set imposes. Structured programming constructs such as if statements, loops, and functions don't exist in the form you're accustomed to. Some instruction sets have instructions that are named after those things, but they aren't those things. They're all just building blocks. For example, the LOOP instruction on x86 isn't a loop. It decrements a register and jumps if the register is non-zero. That's useful for making a common kind of loop. The instruction doesn't automatically give you a loop. You can use it for non-loop things. Many architectures have a CALL instruction can be used to make function calls. On one architecture I used, it was just an alias for an unconditional branch, though. It didn't even have the courtesy to set up a return address. On another, CALL was often abused to initialize a pointer to some data: And finally, modern instruction sets have sprouted all sorts of complex functionality in SIMD and vector extensions. Those can do some crazy fast computations; however, there's a lot of work involved in learning how to leverage them. What both of these have in common is that they provide a potentially bewildering array of sharp, powerful, and sometimes oddly shaped primitives, but not a lot of guidance on how to use them. Neither provides much in the way of guard rails either. C++ adds towers of interesting abstractions, modeled after similar abstractions in other languages. When used correctly, they're quite useful. However, C++ tends to err more on the side of exposing low level details than on buttoning up abstractions to make them air tight. Consider iterator invalidation rules, for instance. Which is best for performance? Whichever one you're able to develop with most effectively to solve the types of problems you're trying to solve. You're unlikely to write good code—let alone performant code—in a language you don't know how to program effectively. The right answer for you might not even be on the list you gave. The right answer also might change over time, particularly if you continue to grow as a developer. It might also change based on the specifics of the problem you're solving. You need to learn how to break down the problems you're trying to solve in a way that allows you to map the pieces to good solutions. That might expose places where different languages or libraries might help you. You need to learn how to determine why your programs perform the way they do. That includes learning how to measure and test, as well as how to analyze the behavior of the algorithms you chose. In general: get really good at programming in one or two languages. Program in languages you understand, so you get practice under your belt. You can pick up more languages over time. Tackle progressively bigger challenges, and occasionally dip your toes into something new.

Question: Why don't decimal floating points have hardware implementation in usual computers for execution speed like FPU for float point numbers, if even decimal floating point are in IEEE 754-2008 standard?
Answer: tl;dr: Economics 101: Supply and demand. There's insufficient market demand to justify developing it and supplying it to the broad market. Even if the price went way down, I doubt you would see much increase in demand currently. Meanwhile, the current set of hardware manufacturers that provide hardware decimal float only provide it in high end gear meant for big business workloads. The supply curve looks closer to the monopolistic competition model: nearly horizontal. If the demand curve were less vertical, then you would see more interest in supplying the market, and the supply curve would move to something less horizontal as more producers come online and compete with each other. The equilibrium point would shift, similar to the arc traced by the green line here: Don't get too hung up on the diagrams, BTW. I just threw them together to illustrate the general dynamic at play here. So why is demand so anemic? Let's compare the options and see. Advantages of Binary vs. Decimal Floating Point Advantages for binary floating point: Advantages for decimal floating point: That's a pretty lopsided comparison! I dig into more detail in these answers: FWIW, decimal floating point hardware isn't vastly more expensive than binary floating point hardware. Companies such as IBM have spent considerable amounts of engineering effort optimizing it. John Gustafson's answer suggests it's around half the speed at twice the area and power. That's about 4× more costly, but still within an order of magnitude. It's likely one or two orders of magnitude faster than software. Not awesome, but not terrible, if you have a use for it. It's obviously not free. It is more expensive, and it is not particularly in demand. Why Decimal, Then? Financial calculations were historically done by hand, and then accelerated by decimal adding machines. That's one space that wants decimal rounding; however, decimal fixed point is often a better choice if you need to control precision to that degree. There is some programming language support for decimal floating point, including recently added support in C23. Otherwise, there aren't many programs that even try to make use of it. Whether the programming language directly supports decimal floating point or not, software libraries are available for those who want to use it. Decimal rounding is mainly useful for providing “human friendly” rounding. It's not better numerically, as the links I gave above explored. For a given number of bits, it's actually slightly worse. The vast majority of the arithmetic performed by personal computers is never looked at by humans in a form where decimal rounding matters. “B-b-bu-but what about spreadsheets?” What about them? With modern graphics cards and compositor based GUI rendering pipelines, there are probably several orders of magnitude more floating point computations involved in drawing any numbers you read on the screen than went into calculating most of those numbers… and those compositor computations happen every screen refresh.* That's not universally true, of course. But for most computations on personal computers for which decimal rounding adds value, I believe it's true waaaaaay more often than not. You can get perfectly adequate performance for personal computing needs with a software library. It's the large institutions cranking gazillions of transactions a second that see benefit. Stages of Grief I’ve seen questions related to decimal vs. binary rounding differences for years. I have also seen a wide range of reactions to these differences. They vaguely resemble the five stages of grief. Some folks remain in denial, or somewhere between denial and anger. They insist decimal is superior to binary. It isn't, other than at rounding at decimal digit boundaries, but I have encountered some truly insistent individuals. It doesn't help when big names like IBM make inaccurate statements that can be misread in support of that denial: I think IBM’s really talking about decimal fixed point there, under a very particular set of unstated assumptions about the target application space. I don't think you'll find many mathematicians that would agree with the phrasing above in isolation, though. (Cue discussions about “infinite digits of π ”…) Your question seems to sit right in the bargaining stage. “Why can't we just build hardware that does this?” The answer, of course, is that software decimal floating point is sufficiently fast for the very few applications it adds value to on consumer gear. If it weren't, there would be more demand for hardware acceleration. Once you get to acceptance, you can focus your energy on programming topics that matter far more, such as: Obviously that last part is tongue-in-cheek, but there's a shade of truth to it if you look at how much time people actually spend time talking about those things. Field of Decimal Dreams? I mentioned at the top that there's no demand, thus there's no supply. Part of the reason there's no demand is that there's not much supply. Developers assume nobody will have hardware acceleration for decimal float, so they design it out or never consider designing it in. Demand doesn't always lead supply. Sometimes, supply leads demand. Supply increases, and latent demand eventually surfaces as habits change. Economists call this induced demand. If you build it, will they come? If a major vendor put hardware support for fast decimal floating point in mainstream desktop computers, you might see an uptick in its use. I am skeptical, however, that it would see much serious use. I have a feeling it would just turn into another piece of baggage anyone wanting to make an x86 compatible PC needs to carry. It would become another barrier to entry in that space. I doubt you’d see a big shift towards using it, though. Addendum I answered a related question several years ago. My position hasn't changed. Addendum 2 I quantified the differences between decimal and binary floating point for IEEE 754 decimal32 vs. binary32 and decimal64 vs. binary64 in a comment below. For everyone’s benefit, I’m copying that up here. … Let’s compare IEEE 754 decimal32 to binary32. First, there’s dynamic range. binary32 has a smaller dynamic range of representable values than decimal32. Dynamic range is over twice as large, so that’s a clear win for decimal32. Next, there’s relative error. At 1.000 000 , +1 ulp* for binary32 is 1 × 2 − 23 ≈ 1.192 × 10 − 7 . +1 ulp for decimal32 is 1 × 10 − 6 . That’s more than a factor of 8 larger relative error. (* 1 ulp is one unit in the last place.) Now, at 9.999 999 , -1 ulp for decimal32 is still 1 × 10 − 6 , so the relative error at that end of the range is about a factor of 10 smaller than at 1.000 000. The nearest binary32 value to 9.999 999 is roughly 9.999 999 046. -1 ulp for binary32 here is 2 − 20 ≈ 0.954 × 10 − 6 . That’s again slightly smaller relative error than for decimal32. In the interval [ 1.0 , 2.0 ) , binary32 has 2 23 = 8 388 608 representable values. Meanwhile, decimal32 has 10 6 = 1 000 000 representable values. That’s over a factor of 8 greater resolution. If you’re dealing with scale-invariant values—i.e. values that are evenly spread on a logarithmic scale—Benford’s Law says about 30% of your numbers will have a leading digit of 1 when expressed in decimal. But, let’s suppose Benford’s Law isn’t a concern. Let’s consider the other end of the range for the same decimal exponent, [ 9.0 , 10.0 ) . Over that interval, binary32 has 1 048 576 representable values, while decimal32 has 1 000 000 representable values. Again, binary32 has a slight edge. And if we consider the full span [ 1.0 , 10.0 ) , binary32 has 27 262 976 representable values to decimal32’s 10 000 000 representable values. Let’s repeat the exercise for IEEE 754 decimal64 and binary64. Dynamic range is a little closer: How about relative error? For brevity, I’ll just look at the number of representable values in three intervals I used above: [ 1.0 , 2.0 ) , [ 9.0 , 10.0 ) , and [ 1.0 , 10.0 ) . In the interval [ 1.0 , 2.0 ) , binary64 has over 4 times as many representable values: In the interval [ 9.0 , 10.0 ) , decimal64 has nearly twice as many representable values: In the full interval at a single decimal exponent, [ 1.0 , 10.0 ) : Overall, binary64 has a slight edge over that full range. It just loses out a little at the top end of the range. It has slightly less on the range [ 8.0 , 10.0 ) and more on [ 1.0 , 8.0 ) . If you take Benford’s Law into account—i.e. you’re working with a collection of scale-invariant numbers—that tilts the scales further in binary64’s favor. You spend more time at the lower end of the interval [ 1.0 , 10.0 ) when working with scale invariant numbers in decimal. That’s the range where binary has the biggest edge. * I purposefully left it ambiguous whether I mean monitor refresh or more targeted display redraw that's independent of monitor refresh, as that detail doesn't actually matter.

Question: The assembly language is different as per processors. Are there any categories of processors that use the same assembly?
Answer: Assembly languages are tied to instruction set architectures (ISAs), not individual processors. Informally, processors that support the same ISA are often considered part of a processor family; however, “family” also gets applied in different ways, so that's not a hard and fast rule. If we replace assembly language with machine code, your question has an easier answer: Two different processors that implement compatible subsets of the same machine language can both run the code that sticks to the common subset. Two different processors that support the same ISA—i.e. are part of the same family—theoretically also support the same assembly languages. I pluralized assembly languages, because two different assemblers for the same instruction set may differ in the details of the input syntax they expect. That is, each assembler might support a different dialect of the language. For instance, some assemblers want a % symbol on register names, while others don't. Some use the mnemonics exactly as they appear in the vendor documentation, while others make small tweaks. In a handful of cases, the vendor itself offers multiple mnemonic sets or syntaxes. And of course, some assemblers support multiple dialects and possibly multiple instruction sets. GNU’s assembler both Intel and AT&T syntax for x86. And, GNU’s assembler supports many, many instruction sets. Assembly language isn't a single, standardized language, even if you restrict yourself to a single version of a single ISA. Long-lived instruction set architectures usually evolve over time, adding new instructions and features. The x86 ISA has undergone two major revisions (16-bit→32-bit, 32-bit→64-bit), each with significant enhancements within each major version (16, 32, and 64 bit). Every x86-family processor supports some subset of everything defined for x86. I provide some additional detail about assembly languages in these other Quora answers: … Ultimately, I wouldn't get too hung up on the number and kinds of assembly language. Pay attention to instruction set architectures instead, if you're interested in what processors might be able to run the same machine code.

Question: In MIPS assembly, you can only offset an address by 2^16 signed bytes. How do you offset an address by more than that?
Answer: Think about what offset addressing does: It adds an offset to an address in a register. We can assume your address is already in a register. Can you think of any other ways to add a value to another value that’s already in a register? Hints: Good luck on your homework! Addendum This turned out not to be a homework question. I wrote the additional detail below in a comment, and I may as well move it up here. I’ve fixed a couple typos, added a couple minor clarifications, and added some more detail at the end in the process. … It takes more than one instruction, because immediate operands top out at 16 bits. MIPS has some standard pseudo-instructions,* LI and LA , that expand out to multiple instructions and take this into account. (* I’ve seen some documentation that refers to these as synthetic instructions. Also, some documentation—not necessarily the same documentation—uses the term pseudo-op to refer to what I normally call an assembler directive.) The LUI (Load Upper Immediate) instruction loads the 16 bit immediate into the upper 32 bits of a register, zeroing the lower 16 bits. You can use this to generate the upper 16 bits of a 32-bit immediate. A subsequent ADDIU or ORI can establish the lower 16 bits, if necessary. Example: …might map to LUI + ADDIU… Alternatively, it might map to LUI + ORI: I’ve seen both expansions listed for LI in different toolsets. Gerry Kane’s MIPS book lists the ORI variant: Because ADDIU’s 16-bit immediate is signed, you need to adjust the upper half based on bit 15 of the value, but that's not a big deal. For the ORI variant, the 16-bit immediate is zero extended, and so you don't need to compensate the upper half. Usually, the assembler handles that. The difference between LI and LA is that the latter is explicitly intended for addresses. IIRC, it will emit different relocation entries, and possibly slightly different code sequences for purposes such as position independent code generation. Once you can generate a large immediate, you can add that to your base address to get a large offset: You can also combine LUI with a load or store to access a 32-bit direct address. Here, you need to provide the same compensation based on bit 15 as the ADDIU version of the pattern for LI. As I understand it, MIPS assemblers typically will handle this for you if you give a label in the address field of a load or store: Gerry Kane’s book covers the bit 15 adjustment as well: I currently happen to work for MIPS. Ironically, I haven't spent nearly as much time coding in the MIPS ISA as I have in other instruction sets. I joined after they pivoted to RISC-V for their base instruction set. There's a chance I missed a minor detail above. Speaking of RISC-V: RISC-V uses a similar approach to MIPS, but with a 20/12 split between upper and lower halves. RISC-V defaults to LUI / ADDI for absolute 32-bit constants, and AUIPC/ADDI for PC-relative 32-bit constants. And of course, LUI and AUIPC can be used with loads, stores, and jumps to provide 32-bit absolute or PC-relative addresses there as well. The RISC-V ISA defines some preferred instructions patterns for compilers, to enable RISC-V implementations to easily fuse these into single larger instructions. Because RISC-V always sign extends 12-bit immediate operands—even for ORI—you would need to pick between ANDI and ORI based on bit 11 of the immediate if you didn't use the default ADDI on RISC-V. Most software and documentation I’ve seen sticks to using ADDI. This general pattern—two instructions providing the two halves of a 32-bit constant—was used in other RISC and RISC-like ISAs as well. Examples: You might notice that MIPS, SPARC, and RISC-V use different splits between upper and lower halves. This represents different tradeoffs on the amount of opcode space devoted to immediate operands for general arithmetic and addressing vs. the amount of opcode space devoted to setting the upper bits. In case you’re wondering, ARM went a different direction for generating 32-bit constants. It provides a way to generate 8-bit immediate values, and a handful of modifiers to replicate or position those within a 32-bit word. For other 32-bit immediate values, they use the 8-bit immediate to index constant pools with PC-relative addressing on LDR. The last DSP I contributed to, the C7x VLIW DSP, goes slightly different direction from all of the above, taking advantage of VLIW’s explicit parallel execution packets. The immediate operand field on relevant instructions—mostly arithmetic and some load/store—provides both a signed 5-bit value and a constant extension flag. A separate constant extension opcode can be scheduled into the same parallel execute packet to provide 27 additional immediate bits to instructions that request it. A parallel execution packet can have up to two 27-bit constant extension opcodes. Each targets a different set of functional units. The same constant extension can be used by multiple units in the same packet. The MVK64 instruction gangs both 27-bit constant extensions together with a 10-bit immediate to produce 64-bit constants in one cycle. IIRC, the constant extension can also extend the displacement field on relative branches and calls. As an added bonus, the constant extension works equally well with vector instructions and scalar instructions. There are some other details that I am not certain are disclosed publicly, so I’ll leave it at that. Full disclosure: The C7x constant extension scheme is covered in part by US Patent 10,620,957. Some of the claims were split out into a still-active patent application, published as US20230325189A1. I’m listed as one of the inventors on both. FWIW, we filed the applications for these over a decade ago.

Question: Can a C++ program be written to run on any CPU, regardless of its architecture?
Answer: I’m going to make the simplifying assumption that you’re compiling this C++ program with a compiler appropriate for each given CPU, and that that C++ compiler magically exists. It may not actually exist, but let’s assume it does. With the qualifier any, I’d the answer is probably no, even without that massive simplifying assumption. I’m pretty certain there are processor architectures too baroque and/or limited to support even a very simple C++ program. I suppose if you limited the program to… …and used a freestanding C++ implementation,* then you have a decent chance the answer is yes. But once you start adding more code, odds start dropping. In its base configuration, the Intel 4004 only has 256 bytes of 4-bit ROM, and a DRAM with four 20-nibble registers. You could probably get a couple small loops in there, but you probably wouldn’t be able to support most of what’s defined for a compliant freestanding implementation. You’d have to eschew most of the standard library. For more reasonable machines, then I’d say yes, although again with the caveat that you may be using a freestanding implementation. * And since someone is likely to point it out: Freestanding implementations can have an implementation-defined entry point that isn’t named main(). Substitute main() for the appropriate entry point on those implementations, and adjust the return statement as needed.

Question: What is the major difference between Program Syntax and Program Semantic?
Answer: These terms apply to languages generally, not just programming languages. Syntax Syntax determines the structure of a language. It defines the components of the language, and how they're put together to form higher level constructs in that language. The syntax of a language is also called its grammar. The English language has a syntax. For example, English has sentences. Sentences are a syntactic construct. English sentences consist of a sequence of words, ending in some terminating punctuation such as a period. If I leave a that termination off of a sentence, the text becomes more confusing to read I bet you found the jump from the previous sentence to this one a bit jarring. English words have different parts of speech, and those parts of speech compose into larger phrases in a particular way. If I had written “Words English speech parts different have, speech parts phrases larger into ways particular compose and,” you would immediately recognize that this is not standard English grammar. Semantics Semantics determine the meaning of those constructs. Not all syntactically valid constructs in a particular language are semantically meaningful. Two syntactically identical constructs may have very different meanings. For example, consider the sentence: I feel as much like I did yesterday as I do today. This is grammatically correct, but pretty meaningless. Now consider these two sentences: I sat in bed. I sat in silence. These two sentences have the same structure: noun, verb, preposition, noun. Their meanings are quite different. A bed is a literal place I can physically sit. Silence is a state I can maintain while sitting pretty much anywhere, in principle at least. There isn't always a bright line between the two. The syntax might be ambiguous, and the semantics of the potential parsings will help you sort it out. Consider this example from Groucho Marx: Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana. These two sentences actually have different structure. The humor arises from the word choice that initially obscures that difference. Programming These concepts apply to programming languages as well. Consider the following expression. It appears to use a syntax that is common to many programming languages: What does it actually mean? You might say “addition!” Right, but what if a and b hold strings? What if one is a string and one is an integer? What if they're both set objects? Even though you might understand the syntax above, you don't actually know what that expression means without additional information. It might even be meaningless, depending on those other details. At a minimum, you need to know what language this comes from. Guess what: It’s an argument to the MS-DOS COPY command, and it tells the COPY command to concatenate two files named a and b: Oh, wait, no… It's a fragment of Forth that applies the + operator to a and whatever was already on the top of stack beforehand. Typically, that would add the value in a to the value on the top of the stack, leaving the sum on the top of the stack. It then pushes b. (That all assumes, of course, that the stack is non-empty and that the values in a and on the top of stack can be operated on by +.) OK, that Forth example isn't quite fair, as it also shifts the syntactic structure from infix to postfix. You need to know both the syntax and the semantics in play to correctly interpret the meaning of a construct in a language. They govern different aspects of that process, however. Syntax is primarily concerned with structure, while semantics is concerned with meaning.

When you write an expression such as a + b * c, you expect that to mean a + (b * c) because multiplication has higher precedence than addition. Meanwhile, you expect x - y + z to mean (x - y) + z, because addition and subtraction have the same precedence, and they associate left-to-right. You lose that implicit meaning if you invoke operator overloads directly. You have to spell out what pairs with what. Weasel Words Now… I ended that last section with some weasel words: “directly calling the overload it maps to.” Given some expression a @ b, where @ is an operator with one or more operator overloads, the compiler generates a set of candidates, and then picks one of the candidates. It might pick the built-in operator @ from the candidate set. In that case, there isn’t an equivalent operator overload function to invoke. There might not be a clear best candidate. Overload resolution will fail due to ambiguity. If you invoked one of the overload functions directly, you may be able to circumvent the ambiguity in some cases. There might not be any viable candidates. In that case, there’s no overload to compare to. Wait, There’s More: Calling Class Objects The function call operator adds its own twist when you try to “call” an object that’s an instance of a class. Question: How do I compute a compile time?
Answer: Did you mean compute a compile time, or compute at compile time? Compute (Measure) A Compile Time To measure how long something takes to compile something, just use a timer. Make sure you tell whatever build environment you’re using to recompile everything of interest for your measurement. If you’re compiling at the command line in a UNIX™-like environment (including Linux or macOS), you can add the word time in front of the command line: Compute At Compile Time This really depends on the programming language. Both C and C++ have mechanisms to force computation at compile time. In C, the only computations guaranteed to occur at compile time involve expressions whose values are required at compile time. That includes enumeration values and array dimensions in most (but not all) contexts. For example, this computes the scale values for the ISO binary prefixes mebi- and gibi- from the scale value for the ISO binary prefix kibi-: In C++, the constexpr, constinit, and consteval specifiers can be used to force evaluation at compile time. The constexpr specifier appeared in C++11, and has been extended considerably in subsequent standards. The constinit and consteval specifiers appeared in C++20. Any variable declared constexpr or constinit must be initialized with a compile-time constant expression. Any function declared consteval is an immediate function, and every potentially-evaluated call must produce a compile time constant expression. You can use these to perform rather elaborate computations at compile time, such as computing a lookup table. The additional () at the end invokes the lambda expression immediately. That causes the compiler to evaluate it at compile time and use the returned array as the initializer. The constexpr specifier works nicely with template variables: Now the expression kBit<3> is the compile time constant 8 as a uint32_t. (N.B.: 1 << 3 == 8) The second, optional template argument lets me pick a different type for the data. kBit<3, std::uint64_t> gives me the same value, but as a uint64_t. They even work with template fold expressions (C++17): Now I can say something like kBits32<1, 3, 5, 7> and get a compile time uint32_t constant with bits 1, 3, 5, and 7 set. Aside: Unfortunately, the syntax doesn’t allow for an optional type parameter as the last argument when using template parameter packs. There are additional template metaprogramming techniques to make that a little cleaner for the end-user. For instance, I could use std::conditional to pick uint32_t or uint64_t based on the bit number in kBit. C++ type promotion rules would make kBits<…> do the right thing, promoting the result to uint64_t if any bit number was greater than 31. And, of course, there are other things I could do to make these more robust library components. That starts to distract from the main point of the example, though. Other languages may have their own facilities for compile-time evaluation. C and C++ are the two I’m most familiar with.

Question: When a thread in user space makes a system call and enters kernel space, what is the same thread executing throughout the process?
Answer: Let’s ignore threads for a moment and consider a single-tasking system. We’ll build up from there. Single Tasking When a program makes a system call, the processor executes the system code associated with the system call, and then returns to the program that made the call. In simpler machines without privilege levels and memory protection, a system call was essentially a fancy function call to a system-defined entry point. It may have even used the same opcode used for function calls, such as JSR on the 6502. On PC-compatible x86 machines running DOS, DOS and the BIOS set up software interrupt vectors as system call entry points, and used the INT opcode to make a system call. You could even do something similar on the 6502 with the BRK opcode, and I believe some environments did. Once you add privilege levels, then you add in a privilege transition. That either requires a special instruction, or extending some existing instructions to effect the privilege transition. And, when you add in memory protection, the memory protection hardware needs to understand which privilege level you’re operating at. Each of those transitions—program counter, privilege level, MMU setup—are part of a context switch. The CPU’s operating context switches from the program’s context to the system’s context and back. The single thread of execution flows through those context switches. In the simpler machines, there may not be much actual hardware or software activity involved with the context switch; rather, the context switch is more conceptual in nature. The program and the system each manage their resources separately, and they communicate through well defined interfaces such as the system call. In more complex machines, the context switch may involve saving some amount of process state—either in hardware, software, or some combination—and reconfiguring that state to operate in the system context. In all of these cases, the system call is synchronous: The execution time of the system call—from the time the program executes the instruction to initiate the call to the time the system resumes execution of the program—exactly overlaps the time the processor spends executing the code associated with the system call. There’s a single thread of execution that starts in the program context, switches to the system context to execute the call, and then switches back to the program context when it’s done. Multitasking: Multiple Single-Thread Processes Now let’s consider a multitasking system. The operating system now manages one or more independent processes. For now, let’s assume each process is single-threaded. The basic system call execution pattern remains the same. There’s a single thread of execution that starts in a process’s context, switches to the system context to execute the call, and then switches back to the process’s context when it’s done. Multitasking environments add some new potential twists, however. For example, suppose Process A makes a system call that involves reading data from disk. That can take quite a long time from the processor’s perspective. The system could wait until the data is available, but the processor is now effectively stalled waiting for the data to transfer, doing nothing useful during that time. Suppose Process B is waiting to run. The system might decide to let Process B run for a bit while the disk fetches the data for Process A, as long as the hardware can move data in the background. It can switch to Process B’s context until the data for Process A is available. Later, after Process A’s data is available, it can return to Process A’s context. In this example, the system call is still synchronous from Process A’s perspective. The entire duration of the system call exactly overlaps the time from the instruction that initiates the call until the system returns to the instruction after that in Process A. From the system’s perspective, the data transfer happens asynchronously in the background while Process B executes. Process A is paused while Process B executes. Until the I/O completes, Process A is sleeping because it’s not ready to run. Next, suppose the system introduces a notion of asynchronous I/O. The goal is to let a process launch I/O but continue executing. What does that look like? System calls still remain synchronous. Process A makes a system call to launch I/O. The thread of execution switches to the system context to launch the I/O, and then returns to Process A. There’s still a context switch, and the system call is still synchronous from Process A’s perspective. The I/O, however, happens asynchronously to Process A. Let’s assume the I/O signals an interrupt when it completes. The interrupt will trigger an asynchronous context switch to the system. At that point the data is ready for Process A. Depending on the design of the asynchronous I/O mechanism, the system could alert Process A with an interrupt-like signal—a context switch into a special interrupt-like handler in Process A’s context—or make the information available through an interface Process A polls. (See POSIX’s select() as a historic example.) That polling interface may involve another system call and associated context switches, or it may just involve the system writing to a variable in Process A’s context. In this picture, I show I/O alerting with an interrupt, and Process A polling for completion. Either way, the communication steps to launch the transfer and learn between Process A and the system remain largely synchronous, and just the I/O occurs asynchronously. There is some asynchrony for the message delivery. Signal handlers (or moral equivalent) get invoked without an explicit instruction in Process A. The polling interfaces are synchronous from Process A’s perspective, but the variable(s) that indicate I/O completion get updated asynchronously to Process A’s code execution. Multitasking: Multiple Processes with Multiple Threads Processes with multiple software threads add another dimension. In some environments, each process may manage its own threads, deciding which thread runs when. To the system, the threads are largely invisible. In other environments, the system may manage the threads in a manner similar to managing multiple processes. And then there are hybrid environments where the system manages some number of system-level threads, and within each system-level thread, software manages which software thread runs. If the system manages all of the threads associated with a process, then each thread of execution looks similar to a distinct process. The software threads share some context, such as their view of memory. However, from a hardware perspective, each has its own CPU registers and program counter and so on that the system must manage similarly to a distinct process. A system call from a system-managed thread looks pretty similar to a system call from an independent process. It may pick other threads in that process to run while one thread is blocked in a system call. If a single process manages multiple software threads, then a system call from any thread blocks all threads in that process. The system only sees the process, not the individual software-managed threads. The system might pick another process to run while one is blocked in a system call. All threads in the blocked process are blocked together. In the hybrid environment, software threads managed by the same system-level thread block when any software thread in that group makes a call. Software threads managed by different system-level threads may get scheduled for execution. Punchline The punchline, however, is that system calls are synchronous from the standpoint of the code making the system call. The thread of execution that makes the system call: The caller doesn’t advance past the point of the system call until the call returns. Other stuff may happen during that second bullet in a multitasking environment. The system could switch to another system-managed thread or process for instance. The caller, however, remains in its current state until the call completes. Nomenclature Coda: Synchronous vs. Asynchronous I/O I’m adding this section at the end, because I’ve received comments in the past that synchronous and asynchronous I/O are named incorrectly. After all, I don’t think they’re misnamed. The confusion I believe comes from what synchronous vs. asynchronous pertains to. From the perspective of the system calls that perform the action, synchronous I/O occurs at the same time as the system call’s execution time, while asynchronous I/O potentially occurs at a different time from the system call’s execution time. Synchronous vs. asynchronous describes the system call behavior with respect to the I/O it triggers. If I make a system call to read data synchronously, the system call remains active during the data transfer from the system to the process. The system call ends once it’s transferred whatever data it will transfer to the process. That may mean waiting for data from disk or the network or a serial port or whatever. The system call may have a timeout or other policy that causes it to terminate before all the requested data is available, but the data transfer between system and process is still synchronous with the call. If I make a system call to read data asynchronously, the system call only remains active long enough to launch the I/O. It returns to the process without waiting for the data to transfer. The data transfer happens asynchronously to the call the launched it. There might* be a shorter synchronous call later to actually learn that the transfer completed and/or perform the final copy into the process; however, the expensive part of the data transfer is not synchronous to the system call that launched it. (* I say might, as it depends on the interface design. There are zero-copy ways to do this directly to user-space.) Question: Playable chess moves aren't the same thing as plausible chess moves, are they?
Answer: I interpret the set of playable moves as the equivalent of the set of legal moves. The set of playable chess moves from any given position often includes a lot of really daft moves. It also likely includes some truly genius moves. And, of course, there's all the moves in between. The same move might fall into multiple categories, as it's the sequence of moves that matters. Plausible, OTOH, means seeming reasonable or probable. There can be moves that look reasonable but fall afoul of some rule. There aren't many such moves AFAIK. Perhaps violations of the “50 move repeat” rule are the largest source of such moves. In any case, I don't think those are particularly interesting. Therefore, let's constrain ourselves to legal move sequences and their plausibility. Now the question in my mind is: What sequences of legal moves would seem plausible or implausible in various contexts? If you're scripting a fictional chess match, the set of moves played by each player ought to correspond roughly to their skill level—give or take a bit by the needs of the plot, of course. A novice player making moves like Magnus Carlsen in implausible. It takes at least a little time to get to that point, even for a wunderkind. Likewise, a player as skilled as Magnus making moves like a third grader playing their first chess game—”How does the horsey move again?”—is similarly implausible. Unless the player underwent some severe trauma that impaired their ability, no one’s going to buy a grandmaster trying to play checkers with chess pieces. OK, let's say you're not writing a fictional chess match. Consider the following two scenarios: Suppose you have a casual player whose moves seem to track with Stockfish or some other engine. That would seem like an implausible coincidence, wouldn't it? It's more plausible that they're cheating, poorly. Now suppose you have a highly skilled player that secretly gets a hint from Stockfish or some other engine for a single, tough move, and otherwise played the entire rest of the match themselves. For most observers, that person’s play would seem completely plausible. And chances are quite good that if someone noticed that single move seemed odd, the skilled player could come up with a plausible explanation for their reasoning behind it. Question: What is the difference between a char and a string in C++?
Answer: tl;dr: It's like the difference between a person and people. Of course, there’s a lot more to it than that. Like people, characters and strings can be messy and complicated. char  vs. characters In C++, char is an integer data type large enough to hold a single character of the basic literal character set. It's at least 8 bits wide, although it can be wider. The widest I’ve personally seen is 32 bits. However wide it is, it defines the width of 1 byte in C++ for that platform. It has two companion types, signed char and unsigned char. All three are distinct types; however, char has the same representation as either signed char or unsigned char. All three—char, signed char, and unsigned char—are each exactly 1 byte in C++, by definition. On most platforms, that’s not wide enough to hold a single character in every character encoding you might want to work with. There are multibyte character encodings such as UTF-8 which require multiple 8-bit units to encode a single Unicode code point. C++11 introduces the explicit width¹ wide character types char16_t and char32_t that are wide enough to absorb other encodings such as UTF-16 and UTF-32. C++20 rounds out the set, adding char8_t. There’s also wchar_t, but because its width isn’t fixed by the standard, you should consider using one of the explicit-width wide character types when you can. Even with wide character types, you may need multiple elements to represent a single code point. Additionally, each grapheme might be represented as a sequence of code points (a grapheme cluster). If you go further down the Unicode rabbit hole, you’ll learn that code points and graphemes are distinct from glyphs. Graphemes may be closer to what you consider as a character most of the time; however, in some circumstances you’ll want to work in terms of glyphs. I’m not a Unicode expert; however, I thought I should at least point out the tip of the iceberg you’ll run into when you start working with something richer than ASCII or EBCDIC. The character data types aren’t specifically tied to characters. As I said above, they’re small integer data types. You can use them for ordinary arithmetic, among other things. The unsigned char data type historically has also been used as a “raw byte” type. Modern C++ has introduced std::byte which has the same size and representation as unsigned char, but is a distinct type which supports a subset of its operations. Link: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/types/byte Strings, Abstractly and Concretely Abstractly, string is short for a string of characters. It’s a linear sequence of characters that’s could be as short as zero characters, or could be arbitrarily long. Strings typically support operations such as: That list isn't complete, but it should give you an idea. Strings are an abstract data type. Link: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_data_type C++ provides multiple concrete string representations. Some come from C and some are specific to C++. In addition to the literal types offered by the core language, the C++ standard library also offers optional string literals for std::string and std::string_view. Each of those representations is a concrete realization of the abstract concept string. The C string representations aren’t distinct data types. They’re defined by convention: a contiguous sequence of elements terminated by a null element. The C++ core language string literal types are only distinct data types in as much as the number of coded units in the string determines the size of the array type. The C++ string classes are truly distinct data types. The std::basic_string<𝘊𝘩𝘢𝘳𝘛> and std::basic_string_view<𝘊𝘩𝘢𝘳𝘛> templates allow you to instantiate concrete implementations for different character types beyond the fundamental character types defined by the standard. Each of C++’s standard string classes guarantees contiguous storage, similar to C’s strings. Custom String Representations C++ lets you define your own string data types as well. C++ provides its own standard realizations, but nothing stops you from creating your own. I’ve had more than one Quoran mention their own preferred string implementations, including string implementations they've developed themselves. I’ve also seen third party string libraries which optimize for different usage patterns. Some go by string-like names such as cord or rope. In fact, the original SGI Standard Template Library included a rope<> class template that represents strings internally as a collection of fragments. That allows for efficient insertion and deletion of substrings within a string. It's available at the Boost website here: https://www.boost.org/sgi/stl/Rope.html Abseil’s absl::Cord is a similar concept: https://github.com/abseil/abseil-cpp/blob/master/absl/strings/cord.h Both SGI’s rope<> and Abseil's absl::Cord relax the contiguous allocation requirement that C++’s standard string representations use. This makes some operations cheaper while making others more expensive. Inserting at the head of a string might get cheaper, while iterating over characters gets more expensive. Depending on your use case and usage pattern, a custom string representation might make sense for one of your applications. ¹ The explicit width wide character types char8_t, char16_t, and char32_t are at least as wide as their names suggest, but may be wider in a particular implementation. char8_t, char16_t, and char32_t are distinct types whose underlying types are unsigned char, std::uint_least16_t, and std::uint_least32_t, respectively. The latter two types are defined in <cstdint>.

Question: Are triple digit birthdays rare? I have one of the most common birthdays in the world. But I know triple digits don't come too easy (EX: 01/01/01). I wonder how rare it actually is to have a birthday like that.
Answer: There are only 12 days per century that fit that pattern, assuming you allow 01/01/01 through 12/12/12. I’m not sure I would call them “triple-digit dates.” However, for consistency with the question, I will use that term to describe a date where month, day, and the last two digits of the year are the same value. And of course, that definition assumes that we really are only looking at the last two digits of the year, rather than specifically years 1 through 12.* So, out of ~36524 days, only a dozen are triples like that. That's only 1 in ~3044 chance that a given date fits that pattern. These 12 dates are relatively evenly spread through the year. I don't expect seasonal variations in birthrate to affect the odds that much. Now if you're looking at birthdays for everyone born, regardless of whether they're still living, we can stop there. Over a long enough period of time, you’ll approach roughly 1 in 3044 people born on a “triple-digit date.” If you're instead interested in what fraction of people alive on a particular day were born on a “triple-digit date,” that gets much trickier. You’ll get a very different answer for December 31, 2000 than you will for January 1, 2013, for example. These dates might be spread relatively evenly within a year, but not so evenly in a century. They're all clumped at the beginning! Thanks to that, along with population growth and human mortality, you’ll see a quick increase at the start of a century, followed by a natural decline in proportion throughout the rest. Of course major events can shift the age distribution of the population even further. Consider the effects of World War I and II on those born in 1901 to 1912, as well as the demographic shift brought by the post-WW2 baby boom. I would expect both of those would mak “triple-digit birthday” folks even less common among the living than if those events hadn't happened, at least up until the next century. If we shifted dates by 50 years—e.g. just artificially add 50 years to the date, without changing anything else—I’d expect “triple-digit birthdays” to be more common than if those events hadn't happened. And finally, the exact proportions will depend on whether you're looking at humanity as a whole, or people within a specific country or region. Different countries and regions have different demographic trends. * If you want to make different assumptions, be my guest and write up your own answer with your own assumptions.

Question: How can modern code be dependent on the instruction set of the CPU (i.e., CISC or RISC)? Why won't a simple change to the compiler of a language be enough to turn every CISC program into a RISC one?
Answer: What exactly do you mean by a CISC program vs. a RISC program? You mentioned using a compiler, so you're starting from a high level language, not assembly language. What makes a given high level language program a CISC program or RISC program? As far as I know, nothing. Is this CISC or RISC?   No. Now, the compiled executable, that's a different story. Once the compiler has generated instructions for a particular instruction set, that executable is tied to that instruction set.¹ It still isn't a CISC program or a RISC program at that point. It's an executable for a specific instruction set with a specific ABI. CISC and RISC are categories of instruction sets, just as station wagons and sedans are categories of cars. In contrast, the Wagon Queen Family Truckster is a specific type of station wagon. The Homer is a specific type of sedan.² Alpha, ARM, AVR, MIPS, POWER, RISC-V, SPARC, SuperH and many others are classified as RISC, but they're all mutually incompatible with each other. Within many of those families, there are multiple variants that aren’t necessarily compatible with each other within the family, such as 32-bit vs. 64-bit. And CISC is, to a first order, anything not claimed by RISC or some other stark architectural style such as VLIW. That's a pretty broad collection there, ranging from the EDVAC to today. Most of those are mutually incompatible as well. And then there's the question of what really defines a RISC processor? These questions are tongue-in-cheek, poking at the ways in which practical architectures differ from some Platonic ideal notion of RISC. None of these are intended as slights toward their respective architectures, either. Personally, I rarely give any thought to whether a given instruction set is RISC or CISC in those terms. I leave that to marketing departments. I care whether it performs well for its intended purpose. RISC is a bit like the instruction set architecture equivalent of vegetarianism or veganism:³ it's historically defined more by what you leave out than anything you add. The reality is that strict adherence to some particular architectural dogma only gets you so far. Practical architectures solve real world problems efficiently, and sometimes that means sidestepping the dogma a bit. They're there to run your programs, not “RISC programs” or “CISC programs,” whatever those might be. Full disclosure: I spent many years working on VLIW DSPs, some of which had very complex instructions and facilities. I also spent several years working with ARM products, and am currently working on RISC-V CPUs and system components. I speak only for myself, however. ¹ There are executable formats that can contain executable code for multiple instruction sets. These go by names such as fat binaries or universal binaries. There are also executable formats that hold CPU independent intermediate code or virtual machine byte code. Those require further translation or interpretation in order to run on a particular CPU. ² At least for the purposes of this answer, we’ll classify it as a sedan. Humor me. The fact that it blurs category lines actually fits well with the overall theme of my answer. ³ This isn't intended as a value judgment on RISC, vegetarianism, or veganism. Substitute low carb, pescatarian, paleo, or something else if it suits you.

Question: Is there an advantage using a struct as the single argument to a function call in C (performance, reliability, etc.)?
Answer: Reliability or Readability? First, a question: Did you mean readability as opposed to reliability? I’m trying to figure out how reliability comes into play here, at least with modern tooling. Decades ago, there were calling conventions that didn't handle passing or returning struct values well. Some had issues with reentrancy and/or signals, IIRC, and others had other issues. I haven't experienced any of these issues in my career so far. With ANSI C, prototypes, and modern compilers, I think you're in much better shape. What should be in a struct ? I would say: if the elements make sense together as a struct, put them in a struct. That is, if the collection of elements forms a meaningful value in its own right, it probably makes sense to group the elements into a struct. [EDIT: See the addendum for reasons to wrap a single element in a struct.] Some examples: … … … Once these elements are grouped together in a struct, instances of the struct act like values in their own right. If your function operates on values of those types, I don't see why you should bust them apart into their constituent pieces unnecessarily. Compare these two: … I personally prefer the first, as it maintains the abstraction in the interface. I find it more readable as it focuses on the values in their natural form, in structures. When to pass struct by value or by pointer In the previous section, you may have wondered: “But what about larger struct arguments?” This is where you potentially start getting into efficiency concerns. Anything up to about one or two long or void* values in size is likely to be passed in registers in most modern calling conventions. Microsoft’s x64 calling convention tops out at 8 bytes (64 bits), while the SysV x86-64 tops out at 16 bytes (128 bits) or 64 bytes (512 bits), depending on the field types. ARM’s AArch64 simply limits register arguments to 8 64-bit registers overall, IIRC. In any case, structures larger than a certain size won’t fit in registers. Modern calling conventions typically handle this a few different ways: In my experience, 16 byte to 32 byte arguments aren’t a problem. I’d say 64 bytes is probably pushing it too far in most ABIs; however, I would measure before I got too concerned. Even if it gets passed on the stack, the copy usually isn't a big deal. It may even be optimized away if the argument is dead in the caller after the call. And besides, if I’m just going to manually create my own copy on the stack and pass a pointer to it, I’m just doing what the compiler might do for me (and might do more efficiently). And finally, it's nearly always a wash if you tend to construct the struct arguments directly in the argument list. You're constructing a temporary value, and compilers can capitalize on that. Return values are similar. Also, the size threshold for when it’s acceptable to return a struct by value tends to be a higher in practice. For instance, Microsoft’s x64 ABI won't pass an __m128 value in registers, but will return an __m128 in registers. If a struct is too large to return in registers, most modern calling conventions provide a hidden argument that tells the callee where to deposit the return value. The callee can deposit the return value directly in its final home as it constructs it, without needing to copy it there. If your function is inline (or static inline), the calling convention doesn't matter at all if the compiler actually expands the function inline.¹ There's no guarantee it will expand it inline, of course, but something small like dist2d() above almost certainly will unless you force inline expansion off. Don't be too cute As I reread the question, I started to wonder what OP meant by “the single argument to a function call.” It can totally make sense to have a function take a single argument. It can also totally make sense for that argument to be a value that's an instance of a struct. What doesn't make a lot of sense to me is abusing struct to artificially group all the parameters for what should be a multi-parameter function in a struct. If you're grouping these values together only because you saw them next to each other in an parameter list, I think you're making a mistake. Sure, that could get you something like Python’s kwargs, I suppose. You could supply arguments to all of the parameters by name, using designated initializers… …but no. I don't think it's worth it to create all these bespoke struct types for each of your distinct function signatures. It's a lot of work for little or no gain. If nothing else, it will penalize you on machines whose calling conventions would turn this into a stack argument when some or all of it could have been passed in registers. IMO, the values’ presence next to each other in an parameter list isn't a strong enough reason on its own to put them together in a struct. I wouldn't do that just to replace the parameter list with a single struct containing all the parameters. It can make sense to group some of the parameters together into higher level struct parameters. That fits in the category I opened with. Question: Other than backwards compatibility, what might be some use cases in C++ for functions to return a raw pointer (* MyObject) to an object rather than return a reference or smart pointer to that object?
Answer: The last part is the easiest part. You only want to return a smart pointer if you’re transferring some degree of ownership. Otherwise, you should either pass a reference, a raw pointer, or maybe even a value. See this answer for more details on when you should or shouldn’t pass a smart pointer around: Why not a value? Before we proceed, ask yourself: Is there a reason I wouldn’t just return a value here? Don’t be overeager to return references or pointers when a value would be just fine. Most of the time you want value semantics anyway—i.e. you want something that behaves like your own independent copy of a value. C++ has continued to make value semantics cheaper and cheaper. If you want something that behaves like an independent copy of a value, consider actually returning a value directly. The cost of actually doing so can actually be quite low: And of course the return statement can be shortened to the following, unless the constructor is explicit: So do consider just returning a value if you can. Reference vs. Raw Pointer With smart pointers and actual values out of the way, we’re left with reference vs. raw pointer. Here, it really depends on the expectations of the caller. From my perspective, this breaks into four broad categories identified by these questions: Value-Like Value-like refers to something you operate on directly. It could be a numeric value like 42, or it could be some fancy class. The key point is that you’re going to directly consume or operate on the return value. Most operators and operator-like functions ought to return something the caller will treat as a value. For those, you’ll want to return an actual object with that value or a reference to one. If you don't return a value, I would return a reference as opposed to a raw pointer here. lf you opt to return a reference rather than a value, I’ll assume you didn't return a value instead for a good reason. In some cases, you really must return a reference, as when you need to return a reference to *this. Other times you're chaining a sequence of mutations on a specific value, such as operator<< does on a std::ostream object like std::cout. Iterator-Like Iterator-like refers to something that you’ll use to access an object indirectly, and perhaps objects near it. Iterators are usually associated with lookups and loops. Iterators may also support pointer arithmetic and/or increment operators, depending on their iterator category. I usually think of iterators as short-lived—I’m performing some action in a container and the iterators keep track of where I'm at in the moment. (See the next section for other uses.) For operators and functions that return an iterator or something iterator-like, you want to return something that behaves like a classic C pointer, complete with pointer arithmetic, etc. That includes returning an actual raw pointer. In fact, some iterators are nothing more than type aliases for raw pointers. Handle-Like (Non-Owning) By handle-like, I’m mean an object that allows you to refer to a specific object, and only that object. Usually, handle has other connotations, such as participating in ownership of the object. Smart pointers already have the ownership angle covered. The main properties I’m interested in here are: The latter two are what distinguishes handle-like from iterator-like for me. C++ iterators sometimes get used in a handle-like way, by this set of definitions. (std::span comes to mind here.) Anyway, I digress. Containers (including arrays) cannot hold references, but they can hold objects and pointers¹ to objects. If all you have is a reference, you can use a reference wrapping class or take the address of the object to compensate. However, if you know the caller will likely want to refer to a collection of objects in a container, then you probably ought to pass back a raw pointer. Classes can have reference members; however, they tend to be inconvenient. In particular, the compiler defines the default copy/move assignment operators as deleted² if the class has a reference member. Therefore, if: you probably want to declare the data members that refer to these objects as raw pointers, not references. When you initialize that member, you need to initialize it with a raw pointer. If the hypothetical function in the question is providing the initializer, it probably should return a raw pointer. Summary You’ll only want to return a smart pointer if there’s a transfer of ownership. And in many cases, you ought to just return a value. If you’re left with a choice between raw pointer and reference, there are a handful of places that you might choose to return a raw pointer. It depends on what your callers expect. References are more value-like, while raw pointers are more iterator-like or handle-like. And, there are a few C++ quirks that might cause you to prefer a raw pointer even though a reference otherwise would be a good fit. ¹ This is technically redundant, as pointers are themselves a type of object. References, OTOH, are not. ² Defined as deleted is not a contradiction. It means the compiler has a definition, and the definition explicitly says that operator is deleted.
