Question: Do switch statements (specifically in C) take advantage of branch prediction?
Answer: tl;dr: Yes. ∗ *Indirectly and implicitly. Longer Answer: Indirect and Implicit I wouldn’t word it quite the way it’s worded in the question, but I think I know what you’re getting at. If nothing else, I would assign the action to the correct actor: Compilers that optimize for speed take as much advantage of the hardware as they can, and that includes branch predictors. Thus, those compilers generate code for switch statements that takes advantage of branch predictors. Suppose I’m tasked with tuning compiler X to improve performance for platform Y. I’m going to run my benchmarks, compiled with compiler X of course, directly on platform Y. If platform Y has various branch predictors that affect the compiler’s output, I’ll see those effects when I measure performance, whether or not I explicitly take the branch predictor into account. When I tune the performance of code generated for switch-case statements specifically, I’d investigate which lowering strategy performs best on that platform. Again, the best choice is going going to depend on the details of the microarchitecture, including any branch predictor structures. As a result, whether I intended to or not, I will have adapted my compiler to take what advantage it can of the branch predictor. That can happen without outputting any special “branch predictor helper” instructions or anything else. I just need to figure out what works best on the hardware, in the presence of the branch predictor. My generated output takes indirect advantage of the branch predictors. I’m letting them do their thing and benefitting—on average, at least. And, this happens implicitly. There are no explicit instructions saying “branch predictor, do this.”* (*Well, there could be—branch hint instructions have popped up in various architectures from time to time. From what I’ve seen, they haven’t been very popular and their use has all but disappeared in practice.) Lowering Strategy? Wha? In compiler parlance, the process of taking a higher level construct and mapping it to lower-level constructs is called lowering. Switch-case statements are high level constructs. C’s isn’t particularly high compared to, say, C#’s. But it’s still well above assembly language. There isn’t one way to generate code for switch-case statements. Far, far from it. Several years ago, Roger Sayle published a nice paper at the GCC Developer’s Summit that surveys a number of techniques. I’d posit this is just the tip of the iceberg. Link: https://www.nextmovesoftware.com/technology/SwitchOptimization.pdf I’ve linked to that paper multiple times, as switch-case questions seem to come around rather regularly on here. So how does that apply here? A given switch-case statement might map to a branch table on one platform, and a tree or list of if-else statements on another platform, due to differences in branch prediction. Branch Predictor Differences and Switch Statements There are a wide variety of branch predictor structures out there. People have built careers around branch prediction. I’m not going to pretend to cover everything. I’ll just hit a few broad categories that might affect switch-case. On a simple machine with little or no branch prediction hardware, you might map a dense switch-case table to a simple branch table. Likewise for a more complex machine with very rich target prediction support. For the latter, the target predictor needs to do a good job of guessing which case will be taken in the switch-case. It might use some combination of execution path and recent local and global branch history to help it predict a branch target. For machines in-between, you might investigate lowering the switch-case to a decision tree or some other structure, based on what works best for the branch predictor. If your predictor can handle many nested, unresolved branches, you might even lower it to the equivalent of an if-else stack. If the compiler knows some cases are taken way more than others, it might tilt toward an if-else stack anyway. Punchline Yeah, compilers that optimize for performance take advantage of branch predictors, at least indirectly. These days, compilers expect this to happen implicitly. Branch hints have fallen out of style. As a result, switch statements benefit, along with any other constructs that rely on branches with runtime dependent behavior. For switch statements specifically, there’s a wide variety of strategies for lowering to machine code. The best strategy to select with depend on the branch predictor characteristics of the platform you’re targeting. If the compiler tuners have done this tricky job well, the compiler’s heuristics will pick a pretty decent match for the machine most of the time.

Question: A queue can be implemented using singly linked list in two ways. One implementation has front at head and rear at tail of the linked list. Other has front at the tail and rear at the head of the linked list. Which implementation is efficient and why?
Answer: Before we get wound up on front, back, head, or tail: the question is really getting at whether the each link in the list should point to an older entry or a younger entry. It suggests there's only two options. There are more than two options; however, I suspect that you were given these two options for a reason. The fact that the question allows the labels front and back to be assigned independently of head and tail also suggests that they haven't locked down their nomenclature. If I look at, say, the C++ standard library, its notion of front and back are pretty unambiguous for std::list and std::forward_list. (The latter is a singly-linked list.) They avoid the terms head and tail. I have seen code bases that swap the meaning of head and tail, so I can understand why the C++ standard library avoids that. In my answer, I will do my best to avoid terms you haven't locked down. And finally, it's not explicitly stated in the question, but let's assume this queue is strictly first-in, first-out (FIFO), as opposed to, say, a priority queue. Thought Experiment Suppose you work in an office with one of those Take-A-Number systems: This is in a budget-strapped office, however, and the system broke down ages ago. The display is broken, and they're reusing the tickets. As people arrive, they draw a random ticket from the box. As people get called, they put their ticket back in the box. That sounds like a real mess, doesn't it? Fortunately, everyone coming to your office is motivated to get in and out efficiently, and nobody there is going to tolerate anyone cutting in line. All the folks in the lobby are willing to help out. What do you ask them to do? Here are some options: Let's walk through these. Option 1 This one is easy for you, at least at first. You just have to remember the ticket number for whoever walked in the door last. When it's time to figure out who to call up next, you ask them for the ticket number of the person before them. Keep doing this until you find the person waiting longest. That's not too bad with 2 or 3 people waiting. I think it gets old pretty quickly, though. On the plus side, as new people arrive, you can quickly say “Hey, remember the guy before you has ticket number X.” Option 2 This feels a little better than option 1, because now each person can you the number of the next person to call. The problem is that when someone new arrives, you don't have any way to help them figure out who arrived just before them. So, you both go down the line asking person by person until you find the end. Ultimately, option 2 doesn't seem much better than option 1, does it? Option 3 Finally, you’ve had enough with options 1 and 2. Then inspiration strikes: if you remember the number for who's been waiting longest, and who arrived most recently, now you can avoid asking all the folks in line what order they're in. When you're done with one person, you can ask them who's next. And when a new person walks in, you can tell the person who was previously at the end of the line that this new person is after them. You just keep track of the two ends of the line. That works pretty well, but now you have two numbers to remember. Option 4 Let's say the stress of working in this underfunded office is starting to get to you, and you can only reliably keep track of one number. How do you cope? You can ask the last guy who enters to keep track of the guy who was waiting longest for you. Now everyone only has one number to remember. When someone new arrives, the guy who was previously at the end tells the new guy the ticket number of who's been waiting longest, and then takes note of the new guy's ticket number. You just have remember who arrived last. When it's time to call the next person, they can tell you the number for who's next or you can ask the guy at the end for that number. When the next person is called, the guy at the end can ask the guy who was just called what ticket number follows him. Analysis If you followed that thought experiment, you probably figured out I was constructing singly linked lists in different ways. If you replace “ticket number” with “pointer” or “reference,” it should be even more obvious. And if you know your data structures, you probably identified some implementation choices one might make to optimize them. Options 1 and 2 correspond to the two options in the question. Both options are equally bad as presented: Here, d is the average queue depth. Option 1 in C code: Option 2 in C code: Since a FIFO has equal numbers of enqueue and dequeue steps, both end up being O ( d n ) , where d is the average queue depth and n is the total number of elements you’re passing through the queue. If d is proportional to n , then processing the entire queue is O ( n 2 ) . If you put all of the elements in the queue before you withdraw any, you're definitely O ( n 2 ) . Option 3 is a straightforward tweak of option 2, and it provides both O ( 1 ) enqueue and O ( 1 ) dequeue. This approach is quite common in the real world. It's so common that option 2 feels like the special case. That said, data structures courses will likely start with option 2 above and walk through an example like this one to justify constructing option 3. With this tweak, processing n elements is O ( n ) , regardless of the average queue depth. The big annoyance with Option 3 is that you now need two pointers to keep track of the two ends of the list. Option 3 in C code: OK, OK. I’ll admit that I don't feel like introducing a structure to manage the two pointers, or working through all the corner cases to ensure I have managed them correctly. It's not really that difficult, but it is tedious. Option 4 is one that I don't see mentioned as often. It manages the singly linked list as a circular list. Now the last node in the list points to the first node rather than holding a null pointer. Some environments such as the Linux kernel make heavy use of circular lists. In Linux's case, those are doubly-linked, however. As with Option 3, enqueue and dequeue are both O ( 1 ) , and processing n elements is O ( n ) . In order to make this work, you need the list pointer to point at the most recently added element in the queue—i.e. the last element . From there you can easily find the first element, as the last element closes the circle by pointing to the first. Option 4 in C code: Nifty, eh? Summary The italicized points in first two bullets above suggest the question you were given is meant as a setup or prompt. Once you discover neither approach works well, you can explore ways to tweak and improve. At least, I hope that's the case. I really hope they aren't teaching you to parrot canned answers by rote. That's what books and Wikipedia are for.¹ Addendum The above assumes linked lists even make sense for what you're trying to do. These days, they rarely do. See Jerry Coffin's answer for more details. And yes, in C++ I really do just use std::vector whenever possible. ¹ Or ChatGPT / Gemini / Poe / etc. if you love having complete BS presented as confidently, clearly, and insipidly as correct information.

Question: In C++, do developers commonly construct individual objects first before copying them into a container? If so, isn’t the original object still taking up memory? Shouldn’t they instead ‘emplace’ or ‘move’ objects into the container?
Answer: There is a lot wrapped up in this question. Let’s unpack it a bit. Cheap to Copy In C++, an object is simply a region of storage which has an associated type. There are plenty of other details that go with it, but that’s the kernel at the heart of it. Notice I didn’t say class type. You can have int objects, char objects, void* objects, etc. IMHO, as a matter of design, most objects ought to be cheap to copy. Objects with primitive types—int, float, raw pointers, etc.—are cheap to copy. Most class types with default copy and move constructors and assignment operators likely are as well, up to around 16 to 32 bytes in size. Now obviously, that’s more tenable with some collections of types than it is with others. And even if it’s true that most of your objects are cheap to copy, eventually you’ll end up with some class type that’s expensive to copy. Now what? Expensive to Copy; Cheap to Move If your class is expensive to copy but can be made cheap to move, then you should probably make it movable. Make sure you mark your move constructor and move assignment noexcept. If you’re using default move assignment and move constructors—which under ideal circumstances, you are—then that detail’s taken care of. Consider std::vector. An actual instance of std::vector is typically around the size of 3 pointers. Under the hood, it may actually hold 3 pointers, or maybe a pointer and a couple size_t members. It doesn’t really matter. This is a class type that’s cheap to move into a fresh std::vector—i.e. move construction—because it needs to do is twiddle a few lightweight fields. Move assignment can be a little more expensive because you might need to destruct whatever was in the vector previously. It’s also potentially expensive to copy. If I have a std::vector with millions of elements, copying that unnecessarily will be a drag, even if it’s std::vector<char>. Expensive to Copy or Move These shouldn’t be as common as your other class types. In my experience, these most commonly are classes with large internal arrays. In many such cases, move construction and move assignment are identical or nearly identical to copy construction and copy assignment in cost. Consider this class: Tell me again why you wouldn’t use std::vector, or maybe std::unique_ptr<T[]> for something like this? There definitely can be good reasons to have a large, fixed internal buffer like this, but in my experience other options are more attractive most of the time. The intersection of “places where such a type definition makes sense” and “reasons to copy/move it enough times its cost becomes noticeable” should be close to empty. In any case, if this class type is neither cheap to copy nor cheap to move, you’ll want to think carefully about making very many instances of that object that aren’t on the heap. If you’re instantiating one of these as a local variable and you intend to copy or move it to some other place, you’re going to incur a cost you might have avoided. (And if the class type truly has a large internal array like Elephantine above, you’re itching for a stack overflow.) If you allocate these objects directly from the heap, then you should probably manage their lifetimes with std::unique_ptr or std::shared_ptr. Those are relatively¹ cheap to move and/or copy. And, you can (and should!) use even cheaper raw pointers and references to interact with these objects most of the time. Use the smart pointers only to manage lifetimes. See this answer for more details: But Containers…? Yes, about this container you mentioned. I’m getting there. As you mention in the question, you can construct objects in place in a container using emplace(), emplace_back(), etc. There’s usually no harm in doing so,² but it doesn’t always bring noticeable gains. In many cases, it produces essentially identical code to using insert(), push_back(), etc. Here’s a quick example I just plopped into Compiler Explorer: (https://godbolt.org) Can you spot a meaningful difference between the versions output by Clang here? Me neither. If your object is cheap to copy, there isn’t a meaningful advantage to using push_back() with an instance you just created vs. emplace_back() to construct in place for a std::vector, or insert() vs. emplace() for something like std::set. If your object is much cheaper to move than to copy, then you’ll want to use std::move to put it in the container if you aren’t constructing it in place. At that point, there isn’t really a big difference between push_back() and emplace_back() or between insert() and emplace(), as the non-emplacement versions will just forward to the move constructor. In fact, it may even generate identical code. I whipped up another quick example to feed through Compiler Explorer, using std::unique_ptr as my movable type. Let’s play “spot the difference” again. This time, I opened 3 compiler views with the same settings, so I could scroll the three copies next to each other. … Nifty, eh? If you have good reason to construct your expensive-to-copy-or-move class directly in the container, then yes, you can gain a noticeable advantage constructing it directly in the container. That’ll work best for for container types that allocate individual nodes for each object, such as the various map and set containers and std::list. The container’s internal node management takes the role std::unique_ptr would otherwise take in managing the lifetime of the object. If you use something like std::vector<T> with a class type that’s expensive to copy and expensive to move, you’re going to be grumpy when std::vector<T> decides it needs to grow its capacity(). It’ll need to make an expensive copy/move from the old storage into the new. I wouldn’t use std::vector<T> with such a type unless I was darn sure I could reserve() enough storage to ensure size() always remains within the capacity(). Otherwise, you probably want a container of pointers to objects allocated on the heap. You’ll need pointers anyway if your type is polymorphic. If that container also manages the lifetimes of those objects, those should be smart pointers. Once you have a container filled with pointers—smart or raw—you’re back in the “cheap to copy or move” territory again. It doesn’t matter much whether you use emplacement or not. Still Taking Up Memory…? To be honest, that’s probably the least of the concerns most of the time in this context. Also, if you allocate anything huge as a local variable,³ it’s likely going to bloat your stack frame for the life of the function it’s in, even if it only lives in an inner block. Other objects might reuse part of the space, but not all of it for something huge enough to matter here—our friend Elephantine above, for instance. Focus more on the cost of construction, destruction, copying, and moving. Once you get that part right, proper memory usage usually follows as you’ll have moved things around to where they ought to go. You can always focus on the handful of cases that remain, if any. How Common…? Hopefully, the rest of my answer above makes clear that with proper class design, most of the time it shouldn’t matter so much. And in the places it does matter, you likely have a design challenge that probably requires more thought than simply choosing between insert() and emplace(). I don’t have a good sense of how commonly C++ programmers make outright design errors that result in many needless copies of expensive-to-copy structures. It can happen to the best of us unintentionally. With the right reflexes and good design, it ought not to happen often. Honestly, it’s going to depend on the programmer’s level of expertise, and likely whether they’re programming in a modern C++ style or not. I expect a different result for casual C++ programmers and kids fresh out of school than I do from seasoned professionals that have honed their craft. And then there’s always the contingent of folks that learned one way of doing things and never refined it from there, regardless. At my previous $DAYJOB, we had extensive internal guidance—some of which is now available as Tips of the Week (TotW) the Abseil website—on how to design your code to avoid many of these pitfalls. I don’t always agree with all of the advice as given, but even the advice I don’t agree with brings with it some insight. For instance, this Abseil TotW highlights that you may not have as many copies as you think in your code: https://abseil.io/tips/166 The C++ Core Guidelines also offer many tips, some of which address your concern about needless copies. The tips are broader than that, covering elements of C++ design as well. Taken together, I think you’ll naturally end up doing the right thing more often than not. Links: Good luck! ¹ They’re not as cheap as raw pointers, although std::unique_ptr comes closest. std::shared_ptr has some additional costs as it’s designed to work with threads. Still, either will be cheaper than copying/moving an instance of your expensive class. ² This Abseil Tip of the Week highlights some potential gotchas: https://abseil.io/tips/112 ³ I’m referring to the object itself, and not the resources it owns. An instance of std::vector is usually about the size of 3 pointers, regardless of its current capacity().

Answer: Why do we learn arithmetic when we have calculators? To learn how it works, for one thing. There is no one best sort algorithm for all purposes. Hopefully, your coursework will make that clear. It’s so broad a topic that Knuth devoted half a book to it. If you’ve never read any of Knuth’s The Art of Computer Programming, I’ll tell you right right now that material is dense. Half a book of TAOCP is easily multiple lighter-weight books. It sounds like you’re probably in a Data Structures and Algorithms course. That’s categorized as a computer science course, but it’s really a kind of math class in disguise. The purpose of the class isn’t to memorize a bunch of algorithms, or at least I don’t think it should be.¹ That’s why we have reference books. The purpose is to see not only how many types of algorithms work, but also to teach you how they’re constructed and how to analyze them. It should be teaching you how to think about algorithms. It should be preparing you to write your own algorithms when the need arises. Yes, your language of choice comes with a sorting function, and it’s probably faster than what you’d write in class. What happens when you don’t have access to a library sort function? Or what if you have data that has properties that work against the built-in sort? How would you be able to tell? That last question—“How would you be able to tell?”—is something your course should be teaching you. It should also teach you how to reason about the problem so you can start working toward a solution. Besides, somebody had to write that sorting function in the library. Those things don’t magically pop into existence. And every so often, someone stumbles on a new way to do things, whether it’s sorting or something else. Why shouldn’t that be you? ¹ I imagine more than a few are, sadly.

Question: Is it possible to get multiple simplified Boolean expressions when using k maps or Quine-McCluskey method to simplify an expression?
Answer: Not exactly. First, let me state what I think you’re asking. Karnaugh maps and Quine-McCluskey simplify individual Boolean expressions. If you have multiple expressions to simplify, you perform the procedure in turn for each one. And, once you’re done, you can quickly spot if any of the terms in the final expressions are the same. I don’t think that’s quite what you’re interested in. What I think you’re asking is whether we can spot opportunities to share terms among multiple expressions using either of these tools. That’s the question I’m going to address today. Sell Some Quine Before Its Time…   ...find yourself an itch to scratch —Weird Al Yankovic First, let me get something out of the way: I’m not going to cover Quine-McCluskey (Q-M). In their default forms, Q-M and Karnaugh maps (K-maps) are functionally identical. K-maps are quite well matched to human visual pattern matching. Q-M’s tabular form is more suited to electronic digital computers, not wetware versions like myself. 😉 Also, I’m going to spend a bit of time up front on using K-maps for a single Boolean expression. Hopefully it won't be a complete retread of what you learned in class. Rather, my goal is to hopefully have you see K-maps a little differently than you might have learned in class. Not the Optimum You’re Looking For? Let's consider what K-maps and Q-M do and what they don't do. In their classic forms, these procedure reduce a Boolean logic equation to a minimal canonical sum-of-products (SOP) or product-of-sums (POS) representation. They optimize the number of minterms (SOP) or maxterms (POS) required to realize the logic function. They don’t directly give you an optimum logic realization.¹ Minterms and maxterms assume you have access to each input and its inverse for free. The SOP and POS forms also assume there's no limit on fan-in for any of the gates. (Fan-in is the number of inputs to each logic gate.) As someone once joked with me, with large enough fan-in, any Boolean function can be computed in two levels logic! Fan-in is not the only way in which the simplified form isn't necessarily the optimal form. Suppose I wanted to implement XOR using only NAND gates. After going through the K-map exercise,² I am left with: X O R ( a , b ) = a ¯¯ b + ¯¯¯ a b Great! That's just 2 minterms in my SOP equation. There are only two minterms, one for each 1 in its truth table. Not bad, right? It turns out you need 5 NAND gates to implement that equation directly from this expression. I need two NAND gates just to produce ¯¯¯ a and ¯¯ b . ¯ Those then feed into the three NAND gates implied by my SOP expression above. Source: Wikipedia. But guess what? You can implement XOR with just 4 NANDs! Source: Wikipedia. Don't get me wrong: K-maps are useful. (And by extension, Quine-McCluskey should be as well.) By default, they simplify Boolean logic expressions down to their prime implicants (the minimum set of minterms) or prime explicants (the minimum set of maxterms), but that's not the same as finding the optimum logic realization. A Worked Example: What a Capital Idea! Just because K-maps don’t necessarily give you what you want by default, that doesn't mean you can't use them to help. It just means you have to use them a little differently. While writing this answer, I recalled this question from 4 years ago. It involved constructing a logic circuit to identify whether a given ASCII character is an uppercase letter. I managed to find some of my handwritten notes from the time, so let’s walk through it. Uppercase ASCII characters occupy the range 41 16 through 5 A 16 . If you prefer binary, that’s 0100 0001 2 through 0101 1010 2 . ASCII itself is only a 7 bit code, but for now I’m assuming we’re going to decode a full byte. I’ll immediately adopt a strategy of matching these in parallel and ANDing with whatever we compute for the lower bits. There are only 11 different XOR patterns for 4 variables, so you might at least check those out. Obviously, the set grows if you include XNOR. Let’s Play Checkerboards Let’s try to optimize across the two K-maps for b 4 = 0 and b 4 = 1 for our single logic expression. Rather than the ordinary K-map methodology, let’s look at the maps in a more ad hoc manner, to find ways to poke 0s and 1s where we need them. For reference, these are our two K-maps again: b 4 = 0 b 4 = 1 b 1 , b 0 → b 3 , b 2 ↓ 00 01 11 10 00 0 1 1 1 01 1 1 1 1 11 1 1 1 1 10 1 1 1 1   b 1 , b 0 → b 3 , b 2 ↓ 00 01 11 10 00 1 1 1 1 01 1 1 1 1 11 0 0 0 0 10 1 1 0 1 When b 4 = 0 , we want a 1 whenever any of b 3 , b 2 , b 1 , or b 0 is 1, and a 0 when all four are 0. As long as whatever we do to pull apart the b 4 = 1 table is consistent with that, we’re going to be in good shape. But, we need to be sure to cover all of the b 4 = 0 table. OK, What’s the Point of all That? So far, I’ve focused on optimizing a single Boolean expression. But, you might have noticed I took a very different approach to thinking about how employ K-maps to optimize the expression in the second take. I managed to squeeze two more gates out of the realization and reduce the critical path from 6 gates to 5. The K-maps served as a guide to help me identify potential subexpressions I might find useful for synthesizing the complete truth table. In the end, I needed to make one logical leap. I guessed that a particular algebraic transformation was true after eyeballing the relationships among values, and then verified that it was actually true after the fact. The exact path I followed to this optimal form, however, wasn’t particularly formal. I remember back in Calculus II, one of my classmates asked if there was some way to systematically identify what step to take next when working a complex integral. Our professor gave an honest but disappointing answer: Not really. You just need to practice the strategies and try to gain an intuition for what works and what doesn’t. And, of course, there are the nice tables inside the cover of our textbook for reference and inspiration. Once you’ve gotten out of the mechanical “find the minterms” / “find the maxterms” mode of thinking, you’re in better shape to do something interesting with a system of K-maps to find interesting common subexpressions. Question: Are there any number systems besides decimal, hexadecimal, octal, and binary that are used frequently?
Answer: As David Vanderschel's answer points out, sexagesimal (base 60) is quite commonly used. In addition to time, it shows up in the degree-minute-second coordinate system used for navigation and angle measurement. Bucking the trend, weekdays are modulo 7. It might be a stretch to call that a base, unless you have a project manager with a perverse sense of humor, numbering weeks in base 7 as well. But hey, that gives you 103 7 weeks a year… In computing, base 64 gets used regularly for encapsulating data in strings of printing characters. Base 85 also gets used, but mostly under the hood, such as in PDFs. Si prefixes essentially act like base 1000 or base 1024, depending on which set you're using and the domain you're in. Question: Is it better for us to use binary system instead of decimal system?
Answer: In what context? And what is your metric for judging “better”? In general mathematics, there isn't really a difference. They're just different ways of displaying a numeric value. Some values display as repeating fractions in binary that don’t in decimal, but that doesn't change their values. It's a different story for computing machinery. For instance, if you're building a mechanical calculator, a decimal implementation is probably more compact than a binary version. That said, if you group up your binary digits into groups of 4, then you could build a hexadecimal mechanical calculator and get even more numeric range in a similar footprint. The columns get pretty tall, though. Grouping your binary digits into groups of 3 and using octal might be more reasonable. Digital electronic computers⁰ use binary levels¹ for their internal signaling. Therefore, ultimately, every numeric value will have a binary representation of some form when operated on by a digital electronic computer. That binary representation, however, may be encoded in a way that makes decimal oriented computations more convenient. For instance, ENIAC used binary pulse trains and ring counters to encode digits 0 through 9. Other early computers used various encoding schemes that used 4, 5, or 6 binary digits to represent a decimal digit. Look up BCD, Excess-3, 2421, bi-quinary, and qui-binary for some examples. Some modern machines still offer hardware support for binary representations of decimal digits, including decimal floating point! As of 2008, IEEE 754 includes decimal floating point, including decimal32 and decimal64 formats which hold exactly 7 or 16 decimal digits of precision. Otherwise, most modern machines work in various binary encodings that do not make special affordance for decimal values. Most of the time, it doesn't matter much. It primarily makes a difference for fractional values. Unlike pure mathematics, computers arithmetic⁴ generally works with finite-precision values. As a result, some values will need to be rounded, and rounding will occur on binary digit boundaries rather than decimal digit boundaries. Which one is better? Decimal arithmetic is probably what you're most accustomed to. Most handheld calculators⁵ implement decimal arithmetic, albeit in a binary representation. It's certainly what most banks are accustomed to. Financial calculations should be rounded consistently with decimal arithmetic. Binary arithmetic is what most computers are suited for natively. For integer and rational arithmetic, there really isn't a meaningful difference other than that native binary is much more dense than binary coded decimal formats. There's vastly more hardware support for binary integer arithmetic than there is for decimal integer arithmetic. There aren't any rounding differences or anything like that, so most of the time you will neither notice nor care.⁶ It probably matters more for floating point. Binary floating point is more space efficient than decimal floating point, although not dramatically so. Binary floating point hardware is far more common than decimal floating hardware. And, it offers the keys to the Secret Robot Internet! I can't decide for you which one is better, because you haven't offered any criteria to judge them and rank them. But, I can point you to other answers with more information, so you can decide what computational approach is the best fit for whatever application you have in mind. The second link below has a nice addendum re: Benford's Law that you might find interesting. … ⁰ Yes, there are analog electronic computers and hybrid analog-digital electronic computers. There are also a minuscule number of quantum computers. ¹ At least, the relevant ones. There were ternary computers that had used three leveled logic.² I’m also ignoring storage technologies that may use more levels for denser storage, such as MLC flash and the 8087’s coefficient ROM. ² Not to be confused with TRI-STATE™³ logic, which describes binary-level outputs that have a third, undriven state. ³ TRI-STATE™ is a trademark of Texas Instruments (formerly National Semiconductor). ⁴ Not including computer algebra systems that might offer symbolic evaluation and symbolic representations of irrational values such as e , π , √ 2 , etc. Also excluding rational arithmetic. ⁵ Handheld digital electronic calculators, of course. Question: What are column weightings in number systems (computer science)?
Answer: This isn’t really a computer science question. It’s a math question. Computer science just happens to be a place many people encounter it for the first time in a meaningful way. By that, I mean that most of the time most of us perform decimal arithmetic without really thinking too hard about the framework that underlies the notation. Reintroducing Decimal Consider the decimal number system. If I give you the number 3210, you know its value, right? But what does each of its digits bring to the table? You have: 3 × 1000 + 2 × 100 + 1 × 10 + 0 × 1 = 3210. What do you notice about each of those multiplicands? They’re powers of 10. If I rewrote it in terms of powers of 10, you have: 3 × 10 3 + 2 × 10 2 + 1 × 10 1 + 0 × 10 0 = 3210. Notice a pattern? In a positional-weighted number system, we say each position has a different weight. Typically, that weight is a power of whatever numeric base (or radix) the number is represented in. These positions can also be referred to as columns, as you need to line them up in columns by weight when performing addition. As you move to the left, the weight increases by a factor of the base. If we assign 0 to the least-significant digit position, then the digit in position n (counting from the right) has weight b n in base b . Suppose I gave you the numbers 123.4 and 4.567. What do their values expand to, when written in the form above? Digits to the right of the decimal point—or, more generally, the radix point—also have weights that are powers of 10. They’re just negative powers of 10. Suppose we number the positions to the right of the radix point with increasingly negative position numbers, starting at -1 with the digit to the right of the radix point. When we number the positions that way, the property that position n gets weight b n holds for these positions as well. For the two values above, we have: 1 × 10 2 + 2 × 10 1 + 3 × 10 0 + 4 × 10 − 1 = 123.4 4 × 10 0 + 5 × 10 − 1 + 6 × 10 − 2 + 7 × 10 − 3 = 4.567 If you want to add these together, you need to line them up so that the digits with the same place value (i.e. weight) are in the same column. 10 2 10 1 10 0 . 10 − 1 10 − 2 10 − 3 1 2 3 . 4 + 4 . 5 6 7 1 2 7 . 9 6 7 This should all seem really familiar. You’re probably not accustomed to spelling it out like this, though. Most of us learn how to do this in grade school and internalize the mechanics as reflex, just as Paige Fox has internalized how to solve systems of equations without realizing it in the comic below: Binary Positional Weighted Numbers The reason this comes up in computer science and adjacent fields is that computers typically work with numbers encoded as a collection of 0s and 1s, aka. binary digits or bits for short. Thus, it’s natural to represent numbers in a binary positional weighted manner, aka. base 2. Decimal quickly gets inconvenient. Base 2 means each position now takes on a power of 2 rather than a power of 10. Each digit’s weight is determined as before, only with a power of 2 weight. For instance, the number 1011.01 2 is: 1 × 2 3 + 0 × 2 2 + 1 × 2 1 + 1 × 2 0 + 0 × 2 − 1 + 1 × 2 − 2 = 1011.01 2 Note: The subscript 2 above indicates a value written in base 2. For values in a base other than 10, I will be sure use a subscript to indicate what base they’re in. I’ll occasionally use it for base 10 as well. Now, what is that value in decimal? We can replace the powers of 2 by their decimal values if we care to know: 1 × 8 + 0 × 4 + 1 × 2 + 1 × 1 + 0 × 0.5 + 1 × 0.25 = 11.25 The same rules for lining up digits by weight apply in base 2 (or any other base, for that matter) as they do in base 10. That includes rules for handling carries and borrows when adding and subtracting. I won’t get into those here. I invite you to explore on your own. Binary's Buddies: Octal and Hexadecimal Values written in binary tend to be long and unwieldy. That’s why you’ll most likely encounter one or two other bases, such as base 8 and base 16. These are known as octal and hexadecimal, respectively. You’ll often see hexadecimal shortened to hex. They work the same way as binary and decimal above, only in terms of powers of 8 or 16. Why do we use octal and hexadecimal? They’re both powers of 2: 8 = 2 3 , 16 = 2 4 . That makes it easy to convert between either of those and binary. Each octal digit corresponds to a group of 3 binary digits, and each hexadecimal digit corresponds to a group of 4 binary digits. Binary Octal Hex 0000 2 00 8 0 16 0001 2 01 8 1 16 0010 2 02 8 2 16 0011 2 03 8 3 16 0100 2 04 8 4 16 0101 2 05 8 5 16 0110 2 06 8 6 16 0111 2 07 8 7 16 1000 2 10 8 8 16 1001 2 11 8 9 16 1010 2 12 8 A 16 1011 2 13 8 B 16 1100 2 14 8 C 16 1101 2 15 8 D 16 1110 2 16 8 E 16 1111 2 17 8 F 16 The letters A, B, C, D, E, and F are actually digits with values 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, and 15 in hexadecimal. For instance, D 16 = 13 10 . Now, you might notice I only showed 4 binary digits in the table above, but I said octal groups into 3s. Each number has implicit 0 digits to the left and right of it—possibly after an implicit radix point in the case of values without a fractional portion. These leading and trailing zeros do not change the value of the number, and so we often don’t write them.¹ We can write the binary value I gave above in octal and hexadecimal by grouping up digits in groups of 3 or 4, anchored on the radix point: 1011.01 2 = 13.2 8 = B .4 16 The leading and trailing zeros I mentioned both came into play when I performed the octal and hexadecimal conversion above. In case it wasn’t clear how everything got grouped, let’s do that again with some of the implicit leading and trailing zeros made explicit: 000000001011.010000000000 2 = 0013.2000 8 = 00 B .400 16 Do you see it now? How about if I add some breaks in there: 000 000 001 011.010 000 000 000 2 = 0013.2000 8 0000 0000 1011.0100 0000 0000 2 = 00 B .400 16 All of this is otherwise just basic math in a standard positional-weighted system. We use these bases in computing because they’re convenient. They aren’t specific to computing or computer science. They’re popular in those fields because they’re useful. Other Encodings and Uses for Binary, Octal, and Hex Now, you may encounter other encodings as well. For instance, there’s binary coded decimal (BCD), which groups bits into groups of 4 like you would for hexadecimal, but only uses digits 0 through 9. You get a binary pattern that looks like a decimal number when written in hexadecimal form. For instance, the decimal value 1234 10 would be encoded as 0001 0010 0011 0100 2 , which would be written in hexadecimal as 1234 16 . This brings me to two different points: With regards to the second point: Any string of bits can be grouped up into groups of 3s or 4s and rewritten as octal or hexadecimal. That’s just a shorthand way of representing the binary pattern. A binary pattern need not represent a number in positional-weighted form. It need not represent a number at all. For instance, the NOP opcode on the 6502 processor has the bit pattern 1110 1010 2 . You could also write that as E A 16 . It means the same thing. You could try to interpret that as an integer, but its value (250) isn’t particularly meaningful. Final Thoughts I haven’t talked about numbers with limited precision, nor have I talked about signed numbers. Computers generally work with numbers of finite, fixed sizes such as 8 bits or 32 bits. And you’ll definitely encounter a couple different ways to represent signed numbers. Sign-magnitude numbers just dedicate a bit to storing the sign. It’s like prepending a + or - in front of each value. That’s easy enough to understand. Two’s complement, on the other hand, assigns a negative weight to the leftmost digit. Now, you might wonder “What leftmost digit? I thought you said there’s implicit leading and trailing zeros!” That’s correct. The computer, however, might limit you to some fixed number of bits, such as 8 bits or 32 bits. The leftmost digit is whatever the most significant place value is, within the width you’re operating on. I won’t dive into how two’s complement works, but I invite you to experiment with it. And in case you’re wondering: yes, there’s such a thing as ten’s complement in decimal. That found use in old-school mechanical adding machines: Oh, hey! Just look at those columns! ¹ There are places where we do, such as dollars and cents ( $ 1.20 ) or when indicating precision. For instance, 3.000 implies a more precise value than 3.0 or simply 3.

Question: How is the number 10 made in the decimal system just because it represents ten digits, 0-9?
Answer: It’s called decimal because it’s base ten. The prefix deci- means ten. In any numeric base b , the number 10 b = b , assuming the traditional positional-weighted number system we normally use. Here, the subscript b indicates the number is in base b . In base 8, 10 8 = 8. In base 16, 10 16 = 16. In base π , 10 π = π . The digits 0 through 9 are somewhat arbitrarily chosen, but we’ve standardized on them. You could pick any collection of symbols to represent the digits, and those are the symbols we chose. With ten distinct symbols, you can use a single symbol to represent each decimal digit.

Question: Which memory has a high capacity and high access speed?
Answer: You're going to have to quantify what you mean by: Here's a thought experiment for you: A C-130 Hercules military transport plane has a cargo capacity of about 20,000 kilograms. A recently developed optical disc roughly the size of Bluray disc claims a capacity of 125TB. (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06980-y) For the sake of an estimate, let's say these weigh about the same as a Bluray disc—about 16g each. That means you could carry about 1.25M of these discs in the C-130, on the basis of weight. Assuming they fit inside the C-130’s massive cargo area, than translates to about 156 EBs (exabytes) of data. I think that qualifies as high capacity. If a C-130 loaded in this manner took flight once an hour, the total bandwidth would be about 43PB/s (petabytes per second), if I did my math right. That sounds pretty fast to me. The latency would be extremely terrible, though. Hopefully, my thought experiment highlighted the importance of parameterizing and constraining the question correctly. If you confine yourself to silicon based RAM, such as standard DRAM and SRAM, you probably want to consider scale-invariant parameters such as bandwidth per pin and capacity per pin. Pin, in this context, refers to a signal wire on a data bus. You can achieve crazy bandwidth numbers by building exceptionally wide interfaces connected to exceptionally wide memories. Likewise, the capacity of the memory increases with interface width as well. That's why you need to normalize based on the interface width to compare memory technologies. Another factor to consider is latency. The bandwidth-delay product describes how much data must be “in flight” to achieve 100% utilization on a memory interface. If your processors and DMA engines can't get that much work in flight, then the usable bandwidth drops accordingly. People often confuse bandwidth and latency. L1 caches, for example, have high bandwidth and low latency. I could build a high bandwidth DDR subsystem that matches the L1 cache’s bandwidth, but it would be about 2 orders of magnitude higher latency. Having more bandwidth than you can utilize in a sustained manner still can be helpful, as it reduces the degree to which a burst of activity might increase latency. Question: Why is C faster than C++?
Answer: Is it? Let's look at that lower left corner: Source: https://benchmarksgame-team.pages.debian.net/benchmarksgame/index.html These are box-and-whisker plots. They’re also known as box plots and Interquartile Range (IQR) plots. The two “whiskers’ extending from each box represent the “minimum” and “maximum” data points. The top and the bottom of the box represent the medians of the upper and lower halves of the data. The thick bar in the middle is the median of the data—half the data is above, and half is below. This diagram illustrates: Source: https://www.simplypsychology.org/boxplots.html While their distributions differ slightly, the data shows a dead heat between C, C++, and Rust. And, of course, that's on this particular benchmark suite on this particular benchmark machine with the particular compiler versions they've chosen to use. Languages don't have a speed, but implementations do. These implementations of these languages are quite close in speed on these implementations of these benchmarks. The median is lowest (fastest) for C, but the worst-case data point is lowest (fastest) for C++. If we instead distill this down to one number, the geomean,¹ the story remains the same for these three languages. If anything, they’re even more tightly clustered. And, as many folks will quickly point out, you could always tweak your C code to compile with a C++ compiler and you should see the same performance for the converted program as the original in most cases.² Which is Fastest, Really? With the Benchmark Game out of the way, you might be wondering “Which is fastest, really?” There isn't a simple answer. I know you probably want a simple answer, but tough noogies. If you actually care about performance and pay attention to how things actually work, you’ll know that simple answers are rarer than you’d like. I will say, however, that in my experience it's easier to eke more performance out of certain kinds of programs in C++ than it is in C. That's particularly true when you have limited time to develop and debug your software, and when you need to keep your code relatively maintainable with proper abstractions in place. In particular: I could rattle off a littany of specific bits and bobs that I feel give C++ an edge. And likewise, others can rattle off a littany of C++ features that routinely cause surprising performance issues. You pay for what you use, but you may not always understand the costs when you choose a particular design. IOW, it's not just the language implementation that matters, but also the program’s implementation as well. Benchmarking vs. Development These languages give you sharp tools that provide a great deal of control over the final outcome. Given unbounded time to optimize and debug, an expert C programmer may or may not pull ahead of an expert C++ programmer on a given task. You might get a very different result if you constrain those programmers’ development time and coding style to meet typical development timelines and maintainability requirements. In my experience, I am able to spend more time exploring higher level algorithmic optimizations in C++ than I am in C. For instance, I wrote a rather complex constraint-solver-based CPU test case generator in C++ several years ago. I implemented some sophisticated algorithmic optimizations that I arrived at through experimentation and incremental refinement. I would never have explored many of these in C, because the effort required would have been too great. In C++, in many cases I could just tweak a few templates and type definitions to hide the change behind a low overhead abstraction. The compiler handled the rest, or flagged an error where I needed to make a local change. Punchline In the end, the fastest language for you is the one that enables you to produce the fastest code. With C and C++, that depends quite a lot on you, what skills you have, and what constraints you have to operate under. Footnotes ¹ Why geomean (geometric mean)? See the first addendum below. See the second addendum for a further exploration on geomean vs. box-and-whisker/median. ² One notable exception may arise with code that benefits from C99’s restrict; however, many C++ compilers offer a version of that as an extension in C++. Addendum: Why Report Geomean? Randall R Schulz asked in the comments why benchmark suites typically report geometric means (geomean). Here's what I replied: Excellent question. This is common in benchmarking as it tends to deemphasize outliers, but in a way that's neutral to whether you're computing speedup ratio or slowdown ratio. Suppose I compare A and B on 8 benchmarks. On 7 of them, B gets a 2× speedup and on one, B gets a 32× speedup. By speedup, I mean time(A)/time(B). What if I had instead measured slowdown from A to B (time(B)/time(A))? Then we have seven benchmarks with 0.5× “slowdown,” and one with 0.03125× “slowdown.” The arithmetic mean and harmonic mean swap between the two. The geometric mean doesn't. In terms of speedup B/A, arithmetic mean favors A, but it also favors B in terms of speedup A/B. This is inconsistent! A similar inconsistency arises with harmonic mean. Geometric mean is consistent between both. In real life, we often compare two machines that trade wins on various benchmarks. Arithmetic and harmonic means will favor one machine over the other. Geometric means put them on a common footing. Likewise, geometric means work better when comparing machines A and B to a common reference machine R. With geomean, the ratio between the speedup time(A)/time(R) and time(B)/time(R) is the relative speed time(A)/time(B). Is this perfect? No. But it's a reasonable default when trying to gauge “what speedup should you expect on average, assuming the benchmark suite is fairly representative?” SPEC uses geomean for its reporting as well. In SPECint_rate 2006 for instance, most machines I’ve looked at blow away libquantum, while returning more consistent speedups on the other benchmarks. The geomean deemphasizes this one outlier pretty effectively. Median might also work; however, benchmark suites tend to be small and tend to exhibit some notable differences in individual benchmark scores. Only one or two individual benchmark scores will get directly reflected in the final result for the suite. The others will only get reflected indirectly by how they influence the sorting amongst the full suite. Median works best for identifying a representative run across many runs of a single benchmark within a suite. Mode only really works when you have highly quantized results so that many values are repeated. Thus, median and mode require much larger data sets with different properties to become reasonable. Addendum 2: Geomean vs. Median Isaac Gouy pointed out in the comments that I’m not immune to the dictum: Technical work needs reviewing for the same reason pencils have erasers: To err is human. − Freedman and Weinberg I had misinterpreted the median line in the box-and-whisker plots as the geometric mean. The Benchmarks Game site offers both sets of data. I’d forgotten that the box-and-whisker plots showed the median, and a quick visual comparison made it appear they’d overlaid the geomean onto the box-and-whisker plots. Mea culpa. I also hadn’t noticed that some of the languages switched rank between the two graphs, and a couple went missing. Let’s take a closer look at that. vs. Language Rank By Median Rank By Geomean Delta C (gcc) 1 1 − Rust 2 2 − C++ (g++) 3 3 − C# (.NET) 4 4 − Chapel 5 5 − Classic Fortran 6 ? ? Julia 7 6 ↑ 1 F# (.NET) 8 10 ↓ 2 Ada 2012 (GNAT) 9 7 ↑ 2 Java 10 8 ↑ 2 Swift 11 11 − Go 12 9 ↑ 3 Haskell (GHC) 13 12 ↑ 1 Free Pascal 14 ? ? Lisp (SBCL) 15 14 − I’m not sure what happened to Classic Fortran and Free Pascal. I don’t see why they shouldn’t have stayed about where they started, actually. Let’s assume for the moment they just got dropped for some reason. Let’s pick on two big movers: F# and Go. F# has some massive outliers above the “maximum” in its box plot. While geomean does deemphasize outliers, it doesn’t ignore them. Median, however, completely ignores them. If I take the worst data point and make it 10× worse—which is about the ratio between the “maximum” and the outlier—the median won’t move. The geomean will. Go also has a massive outlier above it, but it’s only off by a factor of 2 from the “maximum.” Otherwise, the upper half of its data set is pretty tightly clustered about the median. Unlike most of the other languages, Go has a much longer tail downwards than it does upwards. Go’s median is about as close to the top of its box as Rust’s is to the bottom of its own box. Again, the median alone won’t capture this, but the geomean will. The median is a bit too reductive on its own. It tells you the middle data point, but not much about what’s going on above and below it. It makes sense to report it as part of a box-and-whisper diagram, as that gives you a sense of the overall shape of the curve. You can quickly see how far off from a nice bell curve you are: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interquartile_range As you shift the Q1, median, and Q3 around, you can imagine the underlying curve stretching and compressing accordingly. The distribution may not look anything like a distorted bell curve, but it’s useful for getting a quick impression. You need the entire box-and-whisker to get that quick impression, though. Median alone doesn't capture it. Geomean, OTOH, at least captures some of the characteristic of the data to either side. It still boils everything down to a single number, but at least that number is shifts in response to all the samples, including outliers. If you’re forced to go with a single number, I’d pick geomean. In the case of F#, the outliers above pulled the geomean up relative to the median. In the case of Go, the median was actually near the top of the “meaty” part of the data, and there was a long tail downward. That pulled the geomean down with it. Which is better? The box-and-whisker plots are more informative. They give you an idea of how consistently the language implementation performs. C, Rust, and C++ are very consistent performers. So’s Go, for that matter. F# is pretty inconsistent, with around a factor of 5 between its “minimum” and “maximum,” and an outlier that’s 10× above its maximum. The geomean makes a nice single figure of merit for the “Don’t make me think too hard” crowd. Any single figure of merit is going to lose nuance. Geomean at least has reasonable mathematical properties that make it difficult to game, and it does change value if any of the data points that comprise it change.

Question: Is a memory block the same size as a cache line? Why is a cache line 64 bytes nowadays, while a memory page (assuming a page in virtual memory is the same size as a memory block) is 4 KB?
Answer: I can't say I’ve encountered the term memory block without some other context that made it clear what exactly they were referring to. I have seen the term cache block, which is more or less synonymous with cache line.¹ If you saw the term memory block in a document describing caches, it's probably referring to the range of memory that would be held in a cache line if cached. In any case, there's pretty much no relationship between the size of a cache line and the size of an address translation page. The two features exist independently of each other and serve different purposes.² Cache Line Size The optimal cache line size depends on the locality of data, the access pattern, and the transfer characteristics between the cache and main memory. Smaller cache lines reduce the amount of pollution caused by fetching data that you don't actually need. They require more cache tags. Larger cache lines provide a better prefetch-like benefit when it turns out you do need all the bytes in the line. A few decades ago, memory was slow enough, buses were narrow enough, cache sizes were small enough, and latency was low enough compared to processor speed that a 16 byte cache line size made sense. Bandwidth, processor speeds, and working set sizes have gone up while baseline unloaded memory latency for a typical PC hasn't changed all that much. Currently, 64 bytes seems to be the sweet spot for many applications (although some would benefit from 128 or 256). DDR technologies have largely optimized for 64 bytes as well. Page Size Virtual memory page size, OTOH, usually wants to be much larger. It's primarily concerned with virtual address translation and privilege checks.³ Virtual address translation isolates processes from each other, the OS kernel, and the hardware. Page-sized memory transfers happen rarely, as compared to cache misses. The optimal page size depends on some of the same application characteristics that cache line size does, but at a different granularity. Unlike caches, typical virtual address pages are not directly involved in fine grain data movement between cache levels. Larger page sizes won't pollute caches or tie up buses with large burst transfers. They may, however, increase the physical memory footprint of a program by reducing the granularity of control the OS has in allocating pages to it. Larger page sizes improve the hit rates of translation lookaside buffers (TLBs), and reduce both the cost and frequency of table walks in response to a TLB miss. Back in the 1970s, some notable minis had 512 byte page sizes. That makes sense given how much smaller RAM capacity was at the time. Nowadays, systems use bigger minimum page sizes.⁴ As the question noted, 4KiB pages are pretty common. They're also probably smaller than optimal. Some big iron went larger than a 4KiB minimum ages ago. IIRC, Alpha debuted with 8KiB pages. IIRC, POWER and SPARC both headed toward a 64KiB minimum page size for larger systems many years ago. Consumer gear also is also going larger, finally. AIUI, Apple has gone to a 16KiB minimum page size for its phones and ARM-based Macs. I hear they won't be alone for long… ¹ Most resources I’ve seen consider them synonyms. I recall one that made a distinction for sectored cache lines, but I don't think that's common. And the there's resources like this one that can't decide even within the space of a sentence: ² The two can interact, particularly in VIVT and VIPT cache architectures, and to a lesser extent in PIPT caches. A good cache architecture will take the page structure into account. Large pages often lead to more consistent performance in large, set-associative PIPT caches by spreading lines more evenly among the sets. For instance, each line in a 2MiB huge-page resides in a different set of a 16-way, 32MiB PIPT cache. ³ Secondary backing storage—i.e. paging to disk—has far less to do with this these days than many people think. Memory virtualization does make it easier for an OS to page portions of physical memory to disk. That's far from its only use, or even its most important use. That said, there are many systems that aligned disk block sizes and/or file system block sizes with virtual memory page sizes either out of convenience, or to simplify the design of the system. ⁴ All the mainstream virtual memory systems in use these days that I am aware of support some from of “huge page” that's larger than the minimum page size. A system with a 4KiB minimum page size might also support sizes like 64KiB, 2MiB, 32MiB, and 1GiB for example.

Question: Does Java sometimes transform the values you are adding? I have a while loop that adds integer and decimals, and my decimal value got turned into a bunch of 9s. Why is that?
Answer: First: There's no “sometimes” about it. Every literal numeric constant in your program is converted (transformed) into an internal binary representation. All of them. Which representation depends on the data type you're working with. For instance, i and j both get initialized to the same binary representation in the fragment below: Now onto the meatier part of the question. When you say “decimal value,” I assume you mean a decimal fraction such as 4.2, and not just any number written in decimal, like 42. The latter would be in contrast to, say, hexadecimal. The decimal value 42 is 0x2A in hexadecimal, as I alluded to in the example above. By default, floating point arithmetic is binary floating point. Some environments do offer decimal floating point support; however, Java’s float and double are binary floating point types. Likewise in C, C++, C#, and most languages. Decimal floating point, when it's available, is rarely the default in modern programming environments. Floating point is essentially scientific notation: you have some number of significant bits—its precision—and an exponent that specifies a scale factor. Each floating point operation gets rounded to its specified number of significant digits at the end of the operation. Suppose we have values written in scientific notation with 3 decimal digits of precision. Now let's add 2.34 × 10 2 and 1.23 × 10 1 . First, we align the values by scaling to a common exponent, and then we add: 2340 × 10 − 1 + 123 × 10 − 1 2463 × 10 − 1 Next, we round the value to the specified number of significant digits and normalize it by picking an exponent that makes the digit to the left of the radix point greater than 0 but less than the radix. We're currently working in decimal, and so our radix is 10. In radix 10, the radix point is also called the decimal point. Rounding 2463 × 10 − 1 to 3 significant digits and then normalizing gives 2.46 × 10 2 . We round down because the portion we're rounding away is below the midpoint between the two values we can represent in 3 significant digits. If we had added 1.26 × 10 1 rather than 1.23 × 10 1 , then we would have rounded up to 2.47 × 10 1 . Stop here and study the arithmetic if you don't follow how we ended up with 2.46 × 10 2 , or how we would have ended up with 2.47 × 10 2 if we had rounded up. Binary floating point works on the same principles, except it operates in radix 2, not radix 10. Where you're probably getting confused is that your programming language has you enter floating point values in decimal; however, the underlying representation is binary. Most decimal fractions don't have an exact representation as binary fractions. 0.75 does: 1.1 2 × 2 − 2 . 0.1 , on the other hand, has a repeating binary pattern: 1.100110011 … 2 × 2 − 4 . Binary floating point therefore stores binary approximations of most decimal fractions. Furthermore, when it rounds, it rounds on power-of-2 boundaries, not power-of-10 boundaries. This isn't limited to fractional values. Try the following arithmetic in a float in Java: Try it, and see if you understand what it does. See if it makes more sense if you write the values in hexadecimal: Finally, try it a third time with 0xFFFFFF instead of 0x1000000. It's tempting to regard floating point arithmetic as “fuzzy” or “inaccurate.” Some historical floating point implementations were truly dodgy, with questionable rounding and, erm, flexible precision behavior at times. Modern IEEE 754 floating point is much more careful about precision and rounding. Intermediate results for basic operations are computed precisely with arbitrary precision, and then the result is correctly rounded to the target precision. The biggest place I see most people get confused is that they're accustomed to rounding decimal values to decimal digit boundaries. The computer is rounding on binary digit boundaries rather than decimal digit boundaries.¹ I’ve written many, many answers regarding the behavior of floating point arithmetic. My most recent answer on the topic is probably a useful starting point for you. It points to previous answers that dive into a lot more detail. As I discuss in the answer above, decimal floating point arithmetic isn't necessarily more accurate or more precise than floating point. If you need very specific rounding, say for monetary computation, floating point in any radix might be inappropriate. You might instead look up scaled integer—aka. fixed point—arithmetic. Beware, however: integers can also experience precision issues! For instance, the largest Mega Millions jackpot as of the time I write this was $1.602 billion dollars. Writing that out longhand, that's $1,602,000,000. What's that in cents? Try it and see. What, if anything, should you change in that example? ¹ And this is true for any implementation of IEEE 754 binary floating point, regardless of whether it's a software implementation or hardware implementation. I’ve seen answers that suggest this is a hardware artifact. It is not. It's how binary floating point arithmetic is defined. IEEE 754 decimal floating point² rounds on decimal digit boundaries, regardless of whether it's implemented in hardware or software. ² Yes, IEEE 754 defines a decimal floating point format as well, as of 2008. Previously it was specified in IEEE 854. And yes, there are hardware implementations of it.

Question: How does a computer understand binary? Does the program get filtered down to binary so the computer hardware can process electronic currents?
Answer: A computer doesn’t really understand binary any more than a light switch understands on and off. In the answer linked below, I link to several other answers I’ve written on that part of your question: Now, that question mentions “hexadecimal digits,” but hexadecimal is generally just used as a shorthand way of writing binary values. Computers are just machines—the electronic equivalent of clockwork, really. Charles Babbage’s computer designs were mechanical. Electronically controlled switches are pretty easy to make. Since the invention of the transistor and the integrated circuit, we can make them cheaply, en masse. These days you can get billions of transistors on a single chip for just a few dollars. The simplest type of logic circuit to implement with these switches has inputs and outputs with two states.¹ It’s a short jump to label these states 0 and 1, and build up from there. Once you have a methodology for building simple logic gates, you can build up more complex computations with multiple gates. You might start with AND, OR, and NOT. A two-input AND gate outputs 1 if both of its inputs are 1, along the lines of “If the first input is 1 and the second input is 1, then output 1, otherwise output 0.” OR is similar; just replace and with or in that sentence. And NOT is even simpler: “Output 1 if the input is not 1; otherwise output 0 if the input is not 0.” Mathematicians had already explored logic built up in this fashion, long before the electronic computer. George Boole formalized that into an algebra, and introduced the world to it in 1847. George is the reason we now refer to Boolean algebra and Boolean logic. Link: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra You can use these logic gates to construct larger logical units that perform arithmetic and other useful computing circuits. That’s the basis for modern digital computers. George Boole wasn’t the first to fiddle with binary—far from it. I survey a little more history of binary computation in this answer: The second part of your question asks how a program gets translated so that a computer can execute it. You didn’t quite use that wording, but that’s essentially what you’re asking. We programmed early electronic computers by physically rewiring them. You hooked up the various functional units in whatever way your computation required. If you wanted to perform a different computation, you rewired the machine. Then, bright folks such as Konrad Zuse, the folks working on the Manchester Baby, and the folks on the EDVAC team all realized that you could build other logic circuits that would effectively rewire the computational part of the machine on the fly. After all, we have all these electronic switches, let’s have them manage that wiring. One switch configuration sets up the machine to “add this to that.” Another configures the machine to “multiply that thing with this other thing.” We can represent those switch configurations as strings of binary digits also. Now we just need to feed a sequence of these binary strings to the computer to sequence the computation. The easiest way to do that is to store it in a memory attached to the computer, just like we do with the data it processes. We call that invention the stored program computer. We call the collection of valid binary strings that reconfigure the machine to execute our instructions machine language or machine code. Link: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stored-program_computer Machine language isn’t much fun to program.² The first big development to improve on this was assembly language. Assembly language is a more human readable form of machine language. It’s definitely more approachable, but still quite close to the hardware. Since then, we’ve developed higher level programming languages. Tools such as compilers then translate that code into assembly language or machine language. For instance, suppose I want to sum the squares of the integers 1 through 10. This fragment of C code will do that: The key portion of this code is a for-loop. Before the loop, we set sum to 0. At the start of the loop, the variable i gets initialized to 1. Then we iterate, multiplying i by itself and adding that product to the variable sum. We add 1 to i and repeat the loop body until i becomes larger than 10. The compiler translates this code to assembly language or machine language. Since assembly language is mostly just human-readable machine language, I’ll stick to assembly language for now. A simple compiler might turn the code above into assembly language code that looks similar to this: This is a made-up assembly language for a made-up processor, but anyone who has programmed a couple different assembly languages could tell you it’s pretty representative for a modern RISC-like machine. In the code above, R0, R1, and R2 are registers. These are circuits inside the processor that hold a value for the processor to work on. R0 holds the variable sum, R1 holds i, and R2 holds a temporary value. The assembly language above breaks down as follows: And that’s it! Each of those short words such as MPYR and CMPI are known as mnemonics. They’re just short names to help programmers remember what each operation performs. The suffixes I and R above mean immediate and register. Immediate means “I’ve given you one of the values to work on immediately in this instruction.” Register means “the values to work on all come from registers.” Conceptually speaking, the computer will execute the machine code that corresponds to the assembly language above one instruction instruction at a time. It basically just goes down the list: do this, then this, then this, etc. Branch instructions just tell it “OK, go to this other instruction and continue from there.” It’s really that simple. The corresponding machine code for a program like the example above would be a sequence of 1s and 0s that directly encodes those human readable instructions. Suppose I used 8 bits (1 byte) to specify the operation, and 8 bits each to specify up to three operands. To keep things simple, every instruction will have 4 bytes, even if some aren't used. I could assign bit patterns for the operations—operation codes, or opcodes for short—like so: …and so on. You might notice that except for the branch, the last bit of the opcode is 0 for instructions that take their inputs solely from registers, and 1 for instructions that take an immediate value. Many machine languages work this way. In the earliest, simplest machines, that bit may directly control a logic circuit that picks where to get the input from for an arithmetic operation. Similarly, the first bit is 0 for arithmetic-like instructions, and 1 for the branch. Again, that might trigger a circuit that determines whether the arithmetic units get fired up, or the instruction-fetching unit gets redirected to a different instruction. Unsurprisingly, modern machines are more complicated, but the principles hold. Let’s translate the assembly language example to machine code. Here’s the assembly language for reference: And assuming I made no mistakes, the corresponding machine code might look like this: Oof! That’s no fun to read, and not much fun to write, at least for anything longer than a quick example. It's slightly easier to follow (but only just) when written in hexadecimal next to the original assembly instructions, such as in an old school assembler listing file generated during assembly. In this example, the first column is the instruction address: Doing this by hand is super tedious and error prone. Good thing we have a machine managing the translation for real world programs! :-D I touch on that in this answer: Real world machines are somewhat more complex, and real-world compilers are more sophisticated than my example above. That example, however, should give you a taste. There’s quite a lot involved in developing a proper programming language and translator (aka. compiler) for that language. I talk a little more about that in this answer: Hopefully, my answer gave you a useful glimpse of the big picture, and some jumping-off points to drill down deeper. That very last answer may go deeper down the rabbit hole than you’re interested in just yet, but at least it has a cool picture of the ENIAC. :-) ¹ And sometimes there’s a third state that represents “no value.” Gates capable of setting their output to this third state often go by the trademarked name TRI-STATE™. ² At least for most programmers. John von Neumann apparently didn’t see the point of an assembler, and there are handfuls of people who don’t mind hacking about directly in machine code. Most programmers, however, would much rather not work at that level.

Question: How a transistor amplify a signal without changing its frequency? Yes, I know that it takes power from an external battery source and amplifies the signal but how does it creates the same waveform like the small signal.
Answer: A typical Class A inverting amplifier is a bit like a see-saw with the fulcrum off-center. A small movement on the left translates to a large movement on the right, in the opposite direction. And, of course, since I mentioned Class A: a single-transistor inverting amplifier typically needs biasing so that it rests in the middle of the range when you're not moving it: The spring I added at the left places the right hand side roughly in the center of its range when at rest. Otherwise, I can push up and down on the left side and get the corresponding wider swing on the right. That's pretty similar in character to how a single transistor Class A inverting amplifier works. And, if the see-saw wasn't perfectly rigid, the “output” at the right might be a little out of phase with the input. Obviously, if you start digging into the physics of see-saws vs. transistors, the metaphor breaks down. It's still reasonable for the explanation above. So here's the thing: if you wiggle the left side at a particular rate, the left and right hand sides oscillate at the same rate. When the left goes down, the right goes up; when the left goes up, the right goes down. (At least, after a short delay, potentially.) There's nothing here that can change frequency under normal circumstances. I suppose clipping and whatnot introduce significant harmonics, but I don't think that's what you had in mind. My question for you is: why did you thing a transistor would change the frequency of a signal? Shifting the pitches in an analog signal with analog components is somewhat less trivial than a single transistor inverting amplifier. (That's not to say it's necessarily difficult super difficult. Look up heterodyne for one example.)
