Question: What can I do to improve my logic in programming? Everyone keeps saying “code code code code”, but how can one code all the time when they can't even build a logic to tackle the issue easily?
Answer: First go read Comet’s excellent answer for a good philosophical description of why this is fundamentally challenging: Next, read Steven’s excellent answer for some solid advice on how to take on the challenge successfully: And now I will add my own 2¢. Actually, I'm going to go in a similar direction as Alice Baker’s excellent answer on learning a piece of music: I’ll quote the relevant bit for framing: The biggest mistake most students make is to PLAY the music they’re supposed to be learning instead of WORKING the piece of music they’re supposed to be learning. When you PLAY a piece of music, you run through it at full tempo and ignore your mistakes. You slop through the difficult parts. You don’t take the time to figure out sensible fingerings. Then, you go back and do the same thing again. The thing about practicing is, practice doesn’t make perfect. Practice only makes permanent. If you practice mistakes, you’ll get those mistakes more firmly embedded into your head and your muscle memory with every repetition. When you WORK a piece of music, you dissect it with a scalpel and forceps, right down to every sixteenth-note. And you break it down as much as you have to. If measure 42 is giving you a difficult time, then you play measure 42 over and over again until you get it right. Once you’re mastered measure 42 all by itself, you play measures 41–43 over and over again until you get them right. I’ve bolded what I consider the most important paragraph. Practice Properly You’ve stated in your question that you’ve received the advice to code, code, code. Or maybe it's given as practice, practice, practice. If you’ve been practicing, but you're not improving, then perhaps you're reinforcing mistakes, or at least not focusing on what you need to improve. Programming is different from playing music. With music, you're performing a prepared work, and the challenge as a musician is to get your body and musical instrument to do what's necessary to realize the composer’s work. Retyping the same program a hundred times won't make you a better programmer.¹ I'm not about to suggest you do that. The relevant mistakes programmers make—both beginners and senior developers—are at higher levels than that. Often, they're much more subtle. Let's say you just completed a program to find all the primes below 1000. (If you followed my suggestion and read Steven's answer, you’ll recognize the example.) And let's say you’ve debugged it, so it’s more or less correct. Congratulations! Don't get too comfortable, however. You're not done yet. Ask yourself: You have a working, nominally correct program. Before continuing, make sure to commit it to revision control. Digression: Revision Control You might think revision control is overkill for beginner code and personal projects. I'm here to tell you that I wish I had gotten religion on revision control years before I finally did. Pick a modern one that works offline, such as Git or Mercurial. Git is more widespread, while Mercurial is more user friendly. Why is revision control important? It can make you fearless about changing your code. You can roll back to any previous commit. You can fork a new version and modify it independently. You have at least some protection against a 3AM nightmare like this: It was working a few hours ago. I don't know what I changed, but it's broken now and I have no idea how to fix it! Just about everyone ends up in that state eventually if they're not careful. I know I have. And, I must confess, I've been there more recently than you might imagine. I didn't bother to commit my most recent intermediate, working version. I lost several hours—practically a day—to that. And, I still don't know what I screwed up, so I can't learn as effectively from the mistake. Revision control can't protect you as effectively you if you don't use it consistently. Working the Code OK, so you’ve got your working prime number program. Can you improve it? First get the quotidian stuff out of the way. Clean up the formatting. Check your variable names. Make sure everything is as clean and consistent as possible. Polish your code so that it can be read and understood by other programmers that aren't familiar with your code. You’ll be surprised how many improvements—minor or otherwise—suggest themselves at this stage. Awkward code tends to assert its awkwardness at this phase. Pay attention to it and fix it if you can. Going back to Alice’s advice: Don't just write the code. WORK THE CODE. While you don't need to take every program to the nth degree, I would recommend sticking to good code hygiene and best practices whenever possible. It will pay dividends in the long run. You’ll find it hard to not write nicely formatted code with decent variable names, etc. You might not think variable names and formatting and such matter for a throwaway program you write for yourself. I've been surprised many times by: To give you a real world example: a program I wrote as a summer intern² as a stop-gap while we waited for a compiler ended up pressed into service for architecture analysis and design verification. I upgraded, cleaned up, and extended that program for about 13 years. After that, someone else took it over for another 4 years, making it 17 years old once we retired it. The Next Level Suppose you get to a point where you can't see ways you would improve it. Or maybe you see parts you know aren't great but you don't know how you would do better. Now’s a prime opportunity to improve your game! And of course, commit the intermediate versions along the way. Once you’ve gotten as far as you can that way, change it up: Eventually you’ll get bored of primes. Pick some other challenge and work that. You might also take a look at existing open source projects and see if you can make meaningful changes. It might be awhile before you're in a good position to do that, though. The Next Language Once you get comfortable in one programming language, you might learn another programming language. I would suggest picking one that's enough different from the one you already know that you need to learn something new that isn't just a syntax tweak. Still, don't pick one that's so different that none of your skills transfer. For example, if you know a C-like language or Java-like language, maybe try something like Python next. Now take programs you have already written, and try implementing them in this new language. You might be tempted to perform a direct translation. That might work, but it's unlikely the code would look idiomatic in the new language. Instead, try to implement a version that looks and works idiomatically for the new language you're learning. With any luck, it should open your eyes to different ways of structing the program. Can you apply this new insight to programs you write in the language(s) you already know? The Punchline In the end, there's no replacement for experience. Practice is important, but as Alice warns us: on its own, practicing doesn't make perfect, practice makes permanent. Make sure you practice with purpose and intent. Reinforce good habits whenever possible. Weed out the bad habits. Work your code into the best shape you possibly can. Then find other resources—skilled programmers, books, blogs—that can help you take it further. Over time, you’ll ratchet your skills set upward. And, if you followed my advice about revision control, you can take a look back at all those older versions and appreciate just how far you’ve come.³ Further Reading I heartily recommend Kernighan & Pike’s The Practice of Programming. It's less about algorithms and languages, and more about the art and engineering. It sounds like the kind of book you might find rather useful right now. Also, make sure you use good learning materials. If you study bad code without understanding it's bad code, you’ll reinforce mistakes. Addendum: Elegance vs. Cleverness I mentioned elegant code above. Do not confuse that with clever or tricky code. For instance, way too many people are hung up on cute tricks like swapping two values without a temporary, or figuring out whether a stack of if-statements is faster/slower than a switch-case statement. In C++, the standard way to swap two items is simply: And yes, the using declaration is idiomatic.⁴ You only need it once per scope. Python uses parallel assignment for its swap idiom: And in clever-tricks-ville, the three-XOR-swap is de rigueur: a ← a ⊕ b b ← a ⊕ b a ← a ⊕ b The first two are elegant. The third is clever and tricky. It's also brittle and buggy. C++’s swap idiom will pick the most efficient way to swap the two values, regardless of their type, as long as their types match. Suppose you develop your own data type that includes a custom swap operation for efficiency reasons. This idiom makes that custom swap available to generic code that may not know your data type even exists. The C++ standard library uses this idiom internally so it automatically customized itself to your data type, at compile time. That's pretty elegant, IMHO. Python's idiom is concise and clear. Furthermore, it can swap any two values, including None. Again, it's generic, clear, clean, and broadly useful. Or, in a word, elegant. The three-XOR-swap? Very clever! Very tricky! Also very specific to integers. It actually pessimizes code on modern processors. If a maintenance programmer hasn't seen it before, they have a greater burden to figure it out. And, it's brittle and potentially buggy: If you replace a and b with a i and a j , it breaks badly when i = j . Therefore, be wary of advice on competitive coding sites and certain homework-help sites. There are certainly plenty of clever tricks on display there, and not very much elegance. There's also plenty of bad advice and wrong advice. Picking up coding habits from competitive coders is a lot like picking up table manners from competitive eaters. Clever and tricky code can be a lot of fun, whether it's for competition or just personal enjoyment. It's a lot like doing stunts on a bike, or other tricky maneuvers. By all means, have some fun. You might even indulge in some code golf someday. Clever tricks do have their places in real-world production code. With modern compilers and hardware, those places are very few and far between,⁵ and grow increasingly rare. So, by all means, have fun with these cute and clever tricks in a sandbox of your own. Just understand that that's not how you should program day to day. I suggest getting solid on the basics before indulging in too much overly tricky, clever code. As Brian Kernighan put it: Debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first place. Therefore, if you write the code as cleverly as possible, you are, by definition, not smart enough to debug it. So when someone suggests you to reverse the direction of a for-loop or to replace a multiply with shifts and adds “for performance,” take it with a gigantic grain of salt. There are very specific places where that might be useful advice, and there's a 99.44% chance you're nowhere near those places right now. ¹ It might make you a better typist, though. I think there are more useful ways to reach that goal as well. ² Actually, it was a coworker’s masters thesis code. I took it and extended it several different ways. I didn't start from a blank sheet of paper. ³ And once you're thoroughly horrified, you might be tempted to squash away some of those commits. Or, maybe you’ll hold onto them and use them as a warning to others. I have some code I keep around for that purpose… ⁴ The C++ Core Guidelines call this a customization point. See https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#c165-use-using-for-customization-points for more details. ⁵ Tiny embedded systems are over-represented in that list by orders of magnitude.

Question: If I multiply 8-bit two unsigned integer binary number, I will be received 16-bit binary number. However, if I am received 17 bit (257 words), Is multiplication overflow number? If overflow number, what will product be?
Answer: I’m not exactly certain what you're asking, but I will take a crack at it. Here's roughly how I interpreted the question, taking into account a potential translation issue from OP’s native language: When I multiply two 8-bit unsigned binary integers, I receive a 16-bit product. However, if I multiply one of those values by the word 257, will the product require 17 bits? If it overflows 16 bits, what will it look like? If you multiply two 8 bit unsigned numbers together, the product always fits in 16 bits. For example, 0xFF × 0xFF = 0xFE01. Or if you prefer decimal, 255 × 255 = 65025. Now, you can multiply 257 by any unsigned 8-bit value and the product will still fit within 16 bits. Why? Recall this identity from algebra: ( n + 1 ) ( n − 1 ) = n 2 − 1 Suppose we say: n = 2 8 = 256 = 0x100 Then by the identity above we have: ( 2 8 + 1 ) ( 2 8 − 1 ) = 2 16 − 1 = 65535 ( 257 ) ( 255 ) = 65536 − 1 = 65535 ( 0x101 ) ( 0xFF ) = 0x10000 − 1 = 0xFFFF All three rows above mean the same thing. I just wanted to make the relationships between powers of 2, decimal, and hexadecimal clear. We’ve used this identity to prove that 257 multiplied by the largest 8-bit unsigned integer value (255) fits within 16 bits. All smaller 8-bit unsigned values will therefore also fit when multiplied by 257. The constant 257 is actually kinda useful. Consider it in hexadecimal: 0x0101. Now consider an arbitrary 8-bit hexadecimal value 0xIJ, where I and J are unspecified hexadecimal digits. Here's the fun part: The product 0x0101 × 0xIJ = 0xIJIJ. It doesn't matter what the two digits I and J are. Multiplying an unsigned byte by 0x0101 will replicate the byte twice in the result. Perhaps this is why you're asking about multiplying 8-bit unsigned values by 257? It's easier to see, in my opinion, if you write it out in hexadecimal. If you're going to program at this low of a level, it's worth your time to get comfortable with hexadecimal arithmetic.

Question: What is the difference between "struct" and "class" keywords in C/C++?
Answer: Ah, that somewhat mythical language C/C++. C and C++ are two different languages. See? Yeah, yeah, I know. I needed an image for this answer's “preview” view. C/C++, as best as I can tell, is C code that’s been mechanically converted to C++ in a manner that clearly belies its origin as C code, but it now requires a C++ compiler to compile it. It’s popular in certain homework-help sites and C++ course material that hasn’t updated much since the Turbo C++ era. Compare and contrast: Behold! It's the C/C++ language spotted in the wild! This “C++” implementation simply swapped out malloc() for new, and changed /* */ comments to // comments for some reason.¹ Also, whoever wrote the comment at the top has a unique understanding of what a reference is. There are no C++ references in the “C++” code above. That “C++” code above is an example of the language that I associate with “C/C++.” A proper C++ implementation would probably wrap that linked list up in a class so you can avoid the error-prone pattern of passing a pointer to the head pointer. But, I digress… C only offers struct. C structs are aggregate types, which in C means they have one or more independent data members. That’s it. In C, both arrays and structure types are aggregate types. C++ only offers classes.² When declaring, defining, or referring to a data type, the C++ struct and class keywords both specify a non-union class type. The only difference between a class declared with struct vs. class is the default visibility of members and base classes: struct defaults to public visibility while class defaults to private. That’s it. The two keywords are otherwise interchangeable when declaring a class. You’re even allowed to switch between class and struct with different uses of the same type name, although I understand Microsoft’s C++ compiler isn’t too keen on that.³ They’re also interchangeable when declaring a scoped enumeration. These declarations are equivalent: They’re not always interchangeable, though. For instance: You can’t replace class with struct for the type template parameter T. You can, however, replace it with typename. I generally use typename there instead of class anyway, as the deduced type need not be a class type. Consider the declaration of std::max: It’s perfectly legitimate for T to resolve to a non-class type such as int. I believe type template parameters and template template parameters are the only places where struct and class aren’t interchangeable in C++. ¹ C officially added // comments in C99 about 25 years ago. Both languages now support both comment types. ² A given C++ class may or may not be considered an aggregate type. It depends on the details of its declaration. The exact rules also depend on what version of the C++ standard you’re using. From CppReference: ³ At least some MSVC versions mangle names differently for the two. I don’t know whether any recent versions fix that; however at least one page I found suggests Microsoft has fixed this. Question: Do the POSIX select() and poll() system calls provide asynchronous I/O functionality? If so, how? Don’t they cause the calling process to block until a fd is ready or a timeout occurs? If so, how is it that consonant with asynchronous I/O?
Answer: The data movement for synchronous I/O takes place during the function call that requested it. When the function returns, assuming it completed successfully, the data has at least moved into or out of the buffer you passed into the request. For example: On successful completion, this call returns the number of bytes read into buf[] from fd. This assumes fd is opened as a blocking file descriptor, which is the default. It's a similar story for writes: Synchronous means “at the same time.” Here, the I/O transfer happens entirely within the time the function call is active. For the examples above, only the data transfer between your buffer and the OS is synchronous with the function call. The OS may apply its own buffering, prefetching, and scheduling independently. That’s pretty much standard these days in desktop OSes, although they also typically offer ways to turn that off. (Look up the O_DIRECT and O_SYNC flags for an example.) Go back far enough and you’ll find such buffering wasn’t always prevalent. MS-DOS had very limited buffering capability,* and IIRC it was mainly limited to buffering a handful disk sectors for reads. So, back in the MS-DOS days, a read() or write() to a file on a floppy disk would likely spin up the floppy drive while your program sat there twiddling its thumbs. (*I’m not counting the various disk caching add-ons that added more sophisticated disk caching. Those came towards the end of MS-DOS’ run. I’m thinking of something like MS-DOS 2.1.) And keep in mind: Even with OS-level buffering and caching, there are limits to what it can do. Large enough transfers will eventually have to wait on the hardware. With select() and its modern variants poll() and epoll(), the I/O itself may have already happened. For example, if I have a daemon serving multiple connections, I can find out which of the sockets sent me data since the last time I checked. Likewise, I can find out which sockets are ready to accept more data to send. The data itself moves asynchronously. As Paul mentioned in his answer, something other than select()/poll()/epoll() actually initiated the transfer. The transfer itself may have completed a long, long time ago. For incoming traffic on network sockets, the transfer was initiated by whatever was on the other end of that connection. Under normal circumstances, that isn’t the same process that called select()/poll()/epoll(), and it’s most likely not even on the same machine. Where you might be getting tripped up is that this operation is a synchronization operation. When those calls tell you an fd is ready for read or write, your process is now synchronized with that fd. That doesn’t mean the data transfer was synchronous. The transfer executed asynchronously your task up until now. You need a synchronization operation because the transfer was launched asynchronously. The timeout on these calls exists so that you don’t spin rapidly asking again and again “Are we done yet?” If you don’t have other work to do, you may as well wait. It’s a waste of resources, however, to tie up a CPU rapidly asking for the completion status while you wait. The timeout tells the OS that you’re willing to yield the CPU for a bit until you have I/O to work on or too much time has passed. If one of the file descriptors you’re waiting on is finishing up a transfer, that portion of the transfer is synchronous to the function call. That doesn’t mean the I/O is fundamentally synchronous. It just means you’re waiting a little until you’re synchronized. If you had performed enough other work before the select()/poll()/epoll() call, the I/O would have had a chance to complete before the call. And remember, these calls take a set of file descriptors, and return immediately if any member of the set is ready. You only block if none of them is ready. You don’t know which of the descriptors in the set you’re waiting on will become ready for you to act on. When one (or more) file descriptors becomes ready, the others may be blocked waiting for data from the network or in the middle of transferring data. Do these calls provide asynchronous I/O functionality? No, not on their own. They’re a piece of the puzzle, but not the whole picture. They provide a mechanism for synchronizing with asynchronous I/O. You still need other calls or a peer on the other side of a network link to actually initiate the data transfer.

Question: Why would you use C++ in embedded code if you want to omit the use of STL, complicated templates and exceptions, isn't that just C?
Answer: STL is an outdated term.¹ It’s the C++ standard library. The main features I avoid in embedded C++ are dynamic memory allocation² and exceptions. Exceptions aren’t necessarily bad; however, they tend to increase codesize even when they don’t affect performance. Templates are quite useful in embedded code. I use them to customize classes for my environment. For instance, I can code up a generic driver for a peripheral with a class template for its interface. I can then instantiate interfaces for that driver at whatever address(es) I need to for a given device. I can apply the same technique for more generic components as well, such as buffer pools, queues, semaphores, etc. I’ve seen similar techniques in C, but they usually involve a big mess of fragile macros. Prior to C23, only C++ offered constexpr. C++’s constexpr, consteval, and constinit allow me to evaluate quite a lot at compile time, including lookup tables and compile-time configuration. C++ also offers stronger type checking, function and operator overloading, namespaces, virtual dispatch, references, and lambdas all of which are useful features even in an embedded environment. The C++ standard library offers a number of useful features that don’t require dynamic memory allocation. I might not be able to make use of most C++ standard containers, but that’s not all the C++ standard library has to offer. Given all that, I’d say C++ in an embedded environment provides many advantages over C. It isn’t “just C.” ¹ Technically speaking, STL should only refer to a portion of the C++ standard library corresponding to the template library Alexander Stepanov wrote in the early 90s. We're coming up on the 30th anniversary of STL’s adoption into the C++ standard library in a couple months. Since then significant standard library functionality has been built on and around it that go well beyond the original STL. Microsoft still uses the name STL to refer to its C++ standard library overall. I guess at this point they're unlikely to let the name go? ² To be clear, I mean on the generic heap, such as you’d use with new/malloc by default. Dedicated resource managers with resource pools established before or during program startup are a different story and far more common. Static pools of uniform objects aren't subject to the fragmentation, footprint growth, and unpredictable performance of a generic memory allocator. Any heap use in the sorts of embedded programs I have in mind ought to be confined to runtime configuration at startup.

Perhaps you should step back a bit. 8 bit computer architecture isn’t a monolithic entity. There are many different 8 bit architectures out there, and you’ll find a wide variety of architectural choices among them. Compare these different 8-bit processors: The list above isn’t exhaustive. Rather, I tried to pick distinct architectures that make different tradeoffs. While these processors have some things in common, they also have many notable differences. The only thing truly in common with all of them is that they are widely considered 8 bit architectures. And the “bitness” of architectures isn’t necessarily well defined: What is your actual goal? They integrate many peripherals and I/O ports, using the CPU to orchestrate them all. Please, don’t let me dampen your enthusiasm. I’m merely suggesting you take a different approach. You’ll probably get more useful input that way. ¹ If 12-bit instructions aren't weird enough for you, check out the PIC16F84. It has 14-bit instructions. Question: What are the applications of 8-bit multiplication in computer architecture?
Answer: It Depends.™ “In computer architecture” isn't a meaningful qualifier for this question. It might be more interesting to ask why a particular architecture chose to include that feature, especially if it also includes other multiplication instructions that seem better matched to the architecture’s bit-width. An 8-bit multiplier multiplies 8-bit values. That much is obvious. Without further information, we don't know whether that produces an 8-bit or 16-bit result, or some other less-common size. If it produces a result larger than 8 bits, then we also probably need to know whether the inputs are both signed, both unsigned, or a mix. If the machine is an 8 bit machine, such as a small microcontroller, then the answer may be as simple as “any application that needs multiplication.” An 8-bit multiplier sounds like a good match for an 8-bit machine. But what if it's on a 32-bit or 64-bit machine? One answer could be “backward compatibility,” if the machine is a modern extension of an older, narrower architecture. The x86 falls into that category. The original 8086 was designed to easily port 8-bit software from the 8080 and 8085. Therefore, it included instructions that operate on 8 bit values alongside instructions that operate on 16-bit values. Modern 32-bit and 64-bit x86 processors still include support for that >40 year old instruction set. Another answer might be “performance optimization for 8-bit data.” This one is less obvious. An instruction that performs an 8-bit multiply on a single pair of operands is unlikely to be noticeably faster than a multiply instruction that operates on larger inputs on a modern machine. However, suppose that 8-bit multiply is part of a SIMD instruction set. A single instruction might perform 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, or more 8-bit multiplies in parallel. Now that's potentially interesting. If you're dealing with a lot of 8-bit data, such as video or images, then an 8-bit integer or fixed-point multiplier might come in handy for operations such as filtering and color space conversion. In recent times, machine learning inference models have explored using various tiny-float representations to squeeze larger parameter-count models into the same amount of physical memory. This can increase the complexity of the model without increasing the required bandwidth dramatically. A SIMD 8-bit tiny-float multiply instruction would be quite useful in such an application. Those sorts of optimizations make it possible to squeeze ML inference models into places like the driver assistance systems in modern cars, smarter motor controllers for EVs, and even various inference tasks on modern cell-phones. EDIT: As Bill Smith points out in the comments, 8 bit integer multipliers also show up in some of the same places I mentioned tiny-float. Google’s TPUs offer a metric heckload of 8-bit multiplies. <snark tone=light-hearted> These sorts of optimizations only really matter if you're building real-world hardware with real-world size, energy, and performance constraints. They're more interesting to the hardware architects and engineers who need to address the engineering challenges of realizing an application in actual hardware. Pure computer scientists need not concern themselves with the practicalities of the physical implementation. That's merely a frustrating inconvenience that needs to be abstracted away. In an ideal world, we’d only need to prove our implementations are correct and mathematically prove their efficiency. Running them on actual hardware is an exercise for others. Let the engineers figure it out. We shouldn't worry too much about what actual hardware is like, regardless of what that heretic Knuth might say.¹ </snark> The above is just intended as some mild, light-hearted ribbing towards Ian Joyner’s answer. Don't take it too seriously, please. Ian does make a good point, and all kidding aside, you should go read it. It's good software development advice.² Most programming should not worry about these sorts of microoptimizations. Too many programmers get caught up in optimizing details that don't really matter. They often end up with overly complicated, inflexible solutions that are difficult to understand, develop, maintain, and debug. Don't pursue those sorts of microoptimizations without good reason to.³ Continue to use proper abstractions wherever possible to separate your application’s needs from the underlying implementation details. If done properly, decent tooling will handle the mapping efficiently for you most of the time. That said, there are significant application spaces that demand squeezing computations down as far as possible to meet practical constraints. If you're studying processor architecture tradeoffs, it's worth keeping the target applications, their target performance levels, and their energy/performance/cost constraints in mind. ¹ Consider the fact that Knuth demonstrates algorithms in TAOCP using MIX and MMIX assembly, rather than a higher level language. He’s even told us some of the reasons why: People who are more than casually interested in computers should have at least some idea of what the underlying hardware is like. Otherwise the programs they write will be pretty weird. … By understanding a machine-oriented language, the programmer will tend to use a much more efficient method; it is much closer to reality. ² If you ignore the moralizing over high-level vs. low-level programming. They both have their places. Don't assign a value judgment to them. ³ Consider these other Knuth quotes: Programmers waste enormous amounts of time thinking about, or worrying about, the speed of noncritical parts of their programs, and these attempts at efficiency actually have a strong negative impact when debugging and maintenance are considered. We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil. Yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%. … You're bound to be unhappy if you optimize everything.

Question: Why do we use floats to store decimal numbers instead of a pair of integers if the latter gets rid of precision issues?
Answer: First, let’s back up a tick. What exactly do you mean by decimal numbers? Which of these did you mean? And what exactly do you mean by “precision issues”? Which of these describes what you’re referring to? I suspect you’re referring to the second bullet in both lists. Your question, however, is technically asking about the first bullet in both lists. You should probably first review the difference between precision and accuracy: Roughly speaking, precision refers to the smallest change I can represent relative to the range of values I can represent, ignoring the sign.* For example, an unsigned 32-bit integer offers 32 bits of precision. If I increment an unsigned 32-bit integer by 1, its value changes by 1 / 2 32 of the range of values it can represent, assuming it didn’t overflow. I have 32 binary digits (bits) of precision to work with. In decimal, that unsigned 32-bit integer covers the range [ 0 , 4 294 967 295 10 ] . That means 32 bits of precision is roughly equivalent to 9 decimal digits of precision. Now 4 294 967 296 10 is an awkward-looking value in decimal, but it’s merely 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 2 in binary. Equivalently, the decimal value 999 999 999 10 is the awkward looking value 11 1011 1001 1010 1100 1001 1111 1111 2 in binary. Unsurprisingly, a nice-looking number in one radix might look messy in another radix, even if you just stick to integers. Accuracy refers to how close my value is to the ideal “infinite precision” value. For example, if I divide 100 by 3 using one of the integer representations above, I get 33. That’s off by 1 3 from the exact value 100 3 = 33 1 3 . Does binary vs. decimal change this in any way? No. Let’s say I have two data types that require about the same amount of storage in a computer: Other than the difference in range, is one of those better than the other in some way? Mathematically speaking, not really. They both have limited precision, but they’re otherwise both valid ways to represent an integer with limited dynamic range. If my integers fit in the interval [ 0 , 999 999 999 10 ] , both are equally useful and usable. Now let’s look back at that division example. In both formats, when I divide 100 by 3, I get 33. That is the most accurate value I can represent in either integer format. In fact, any integer representation that has enough precision to hold both 100 and 3 will have that limitation. You’re probably muttering “But I asked about floating point!” I’m getting there. In fact, let’s go there now. Here’s the key detail you need to keep in mind: Now let’s take our integer representations above and add an exponent to scale the value. For the 32-bit format, the exponent is a power of 2. For the 9 decimal digit format, the exponent is a power of 10. Now lets compute 100 divided by 3 in both formats. How close is each of these to the ideal “infinite precision” value? For the first one, we have: ∣ ∣ ∣ 2 236 962 133 10 2 26 − 1 3 ∣ ∣ ∣ = 1 201 326 592 10 (Note: 2 236 962 133 10 = 1000 0101 0101 0101 0101 0101 0101 0101 2 ) For the second one, we have: ∣ ∣ ∣ 333 333 333 10 10 7 − 1 3 ∣ ∣ ∣ = 1 30 000 000 10 Huh. Neither one of them was exact, and the binary representation was closer to the exact value by almost a factor of 7! Now, you’ll probably point out that the 32-bit binary representation has a little more than 4 times the range as the 9 decimal digit representation, and that that has something to do with it. That’s quite true. But let’s say I shorten the binary representation to 30 bits, so the maximum value it can hold is 1 073 741 824 10 . That’s much closer to 999 999 999 10 . Now we have: ∣ ∣ ∣ 559 240 533 10 2 24 − 1 3 ∣ ∣ ∣ = 1 50 331 648 10 That’s still closer to the exact value. It’s almost as if binary isn’t the problem. That’s because binary isn’t the problem! So what is the issue, then? The issue is that all computer numeric formats make tradeoffs, and those tradeoffs come with different consequences. The standard binary floating point types such as IEEE 754 binary32 and binary64 represent their significant digits as an ordinary binary value. Any rounding or truncation applied to the significant digits is performed in terms of binary digits. The representable values exist at power-of-2 boundaries. Most decimalized fractions do not land on power-of-2 boundaries. Thus, when you convert something like 0.1 10 to a binary floating point format, the converted value isn’t exactly 0.1 10 . It is, however, the nearest representable binary floating point value (unless you have broken software and/or hardware). Is that inaccurate? Sure. But it’s the most accurate you can be in that representation. It’s also not fundamentally a problem with binary representations. As the 100/3 example above demonstrates, decimal representations also have values they can’t represent exactly. In your question, you mentioned using a pair of integers to represent the value. You didn’t say exactly how you’d use that pair, but I’d guess you’re hinting at representing a value as a ratio of those two integers. Sure, you could do that, but it’s no panacea. Integers have finite precision, unless you decide to use arbitrary precision arithmetic. However, for an apples-to-apples comparison, we should keep the total number of bits (or decimal digits) that I get to play with fixed. If I split my 32-bit integer into a 16-bit numerator and 16-bit denominator, now my dynamic range drops dramatically. Assuming I stick with unsigned values, the maximum value I can represent drops to 65 535 10 . My effective precision becomes is now roughly 16 bits, if I hold the denominator fixed. For any given denominator, I can vary the value by 1 part in 2 16 . It gets a little more complicated than that once I start performing arithmetic on values with different denominators. I’ll quickly run into cases where I need to round to the nearest representable value, because I can’t represent the exact value. It’s possible to work out the ordered sequence of all representable values, so that you can look at how close or far they are from each other. I think you’ll find that the effective precision approaches what you started with on average (for a suitable definition of average), but it’s far from uniform and messy to reason about. I could repeat the exercise with decimal digits. I’d have to split my 9 decimal digits between numerator and denominator. The answer turns out essentially the same. So… exactly what problem are you trying to solve? Do you want arithmetic that rounds in a manner consistent to how you’d round with pencil and paper arithmetic performed in decimal? That’s available if you want it. For instance, there are decimal floating point formats and libraries that provide support for them. They’re not more accurate. But, they will round values in a manner consistent with rounding in decimal. You could also use scaled integer arithmetic (also known as fixed point arithmetic), where the scale factor is a power of 10. For instance, if you’re working with monetary values in dollars, you might want to scale all values by 100 to track values in cents or 1000 to track values in mills. (1 mill = 0.001 dollar.) That will give you control over which decimal digit boundary you round your arithmetic at. You’re still rounding, though. You’ll still run into precision issues. But, they’ll feel more natural because your results will match the result you’d get when rounding pencil-and-paper arithmetic to decimal boundaries. Banks and other financial institutions use techniques like these, as do most desk calculators, because they’re using the computer to implement the same arithmetic that used to be performed by hand, in decimal. They use decimal rounding so that you don’t see subtle differences in rounding between the by-hand computation and by-computer computation. That doesn’t make the result more accurate. It simply makes it match the expectations of people who expect decimal rounding behavior. In reality, as my 100/3 example above demonstrates, when you compare a binary format to the nearest decimal format that fits in the same number of bits, you’ll find that most results are slightly less accurate for the decimal format. [See addendum for another interesting reason decimal suffers.] There’s no silver bullet. Computers use a variety of numerical representations because no digital representation is ideal. I’ll leave you with links to a few other answers I’ve written on this topic. They link to even more answers I’ve written on floating point and numeric representations. It might surprise you to learn that you’re not the first person to ask about this. The Perl answer below digs into rational arithmetic a little more. … … Enjoy! Addendum I realized while writing a comment that I neglected another reason decimal computations sometimes produce less accurate results, particularly with decimal floating point: Benford's Law! Benford's Law governs the distribution of the leading digits of numbers. For scale-invariant numbers—numbers that follow a power-law distribution—smaller leading digits are vastly more common than larger leading digits. Link: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benford%27s_law A surprising number of data sets and computations fit the distribution predicted by Benford's Law, or come close. This reduces the effective precision of a decimal representation accordingly. For decimal floating point, it potentially affects every non-zero value. For decimal fixed-point, it reduces the utility of the most significant digit somewhat. Binary is immune to Benford's Law—at least for the leading digit—as there is only one possible non-zero leading digit in binary: 1. * This ad hoc definition works well enough for integers, but isn’t sufficient as-is in general. Another simple definition is “number of significant digits;” however, for machine integers we often forget about all the leading zeros on small values. Those count towards the integer precision.

Question: If I have the magnifying cam, soldering kit, and have previous experience soldering, can I put an 8th gen processor chip on a Pentium board for my laptop that won’t post, or will it not be compatible?
Answer: Pentium? As in one of these bad boys from 30 years ago? Not a chance! Everything about how it interfaces to the system has changed, except maybe the ground plane, and even that might not be sufficient. Voltages, signaling rates, protocols, bus types, chipset, … everything! It's not just a wiring problem. It's an everything problem. The answer won't really change for motherboards intended for other processors either—including more recent processors named Pentium—unless those processors were designed to compatible system integration specs. Chances are good that a desktop processor won't even work in place of a laptop processor in the same product generation. Update As Andre pointed out in the comments, there are some adaptors that could allow a laptop processor to fit into a desktop processor socket. Going the other direction may be possible, but I would worry about power delivery and thermals. The two processors—what belongs on the board, and what you intend to adapt to the board—need to be closely enough related for that to even be a potential option. Even then, that's only a necessary condition, not necessarily a sufficient condition. Both likely need to belong to the same product generation, or maybe belong to the corresponding “tick” and “tock” of two consecutive generations. Tick-tock refers to Intel®’s long-standing practice of introducing a major microarchitecture update on a mature process, and then shrinking that design as an inaugural product on the next. Obviously, that broke down recently for Intel® 10nm, but it still applies to older generations. You may need to build a custom BIOS to get things working properly. Product SKUs aimed at desktop vs. laptop have different requirements for power and thermal management. That assumption may be hard-compiled into the stock BIOS on a particular mobo. You need to combine the correct processor details that with the mix of peripherals and their topology on the motherboard you transplanted the chip onto. The stock BIOS may not be prepared for your Frankenstein combination. Ultimately, it's a research project, and not one with a large payoff beyond self satisfaction if you pull it off.

Question: What's the point in code editors to track the lines and the columns if the columns change anyway in the file depending if the person is wrapping the code or not?
Answer: You need to distinguish between what's displayed on the screen, and the underlying file that display represents. Display vs. Underlying Representation On modern systems, plain text files are stored as a sequence of variable length records. Each record consists of a sequence of zero or more characters followed by a terminator.¹ Each of those records represents a single physical line of code. The terminator itself is the end-of-lihe sequence, which is typically one or two characters—e.g. LF or CR+LF. If you go back to the punched card days, each physical line was represented by a single card. The terminator was implicit. Also, some older systems represented text files as a sequence of variable or fixed length records in a structured format managed by the environment. I’ve described one such system at the end. However it's stored, that file is what the compiler operates on. The compiler reads the file directly. It's not scrolling through somebody's editor viewing the file. Any diagnostics reported by the compiler will likely report the physical line number and possibly the character number within the physical line within the where it detected the error. Diagnostics include remarks,² warnings, errors, etc. Your editor displays a representation of the text file. The editor must interpret various aspects of the file in order to construct the display representation. For instance: The first bullet above is the feature that brought you here. In the code-oriented editors I’ve used, the line number reported by the editor represents the physical line number (i.e. the record number) in the file as it will appear on disk. If you set the editor to line-wrap, a long physical line may be displayed in multiple rows on the screen. Those still correspond to one physical line in the file. Consider this example: I told my editor to display line numbers along the left. Notice that line 3 occupies three rows of the display, but only advances the line number by 1. If your editor doesn't do that, I would consider getting a different editor. Physical vs. Logical Line You might wonder why I said physical line above. The reason is that many programming languages allow you to concatenate multiple physical lines into a single logical line. Recall the punched cards mentioned above. The physical width of the card puts an upper limit on the number of characters that it can hold. A classic IBM punched card holds 80 characters; some go higher. And as mentioned above, some older environments have structured storage that store text files as a sequence of records; those records may have some maximum length. Meanwhile, you might have some code that legitimately does not fit within that width, but still needs to be on one line for some reason. FORTRAN addressed this by interpreting a + in column 6 as a continuation character. You could concatenate several physical lines—up to 40 in the reference I just consulted—into a single logical line. In C and C++, preprocessor directives must reside entirely on one logical line. The preprocessor³ interprets a backslash at the end of a physical line⁴ as an indicator to concatenate the next physical line to the current logical line. To the C preprocessor, these eight physical lines form one logical line, thanks to the backslashes at the right: The concatenated lines aren't usually shown to the programmer, unless they ask to see them. They're usually just handled internally. Therefore, error messages reported by a compiler typically correspond to the physical source line, not logical. The logical line number isn't as useful for reporting diagnostics. An Example of Structured Storage Text Files My first computer was a TI-99/4A. It used structured file formats where the system managed the structure. This might seem a little alien to those of us that have only experienced the “bag of bytes” files we have today on PCs and *NIX systems. From what I recall—and could verify with a quick search—two formats were commonly used for text files: The DIS/VAR 80 format allowed up to 80 characters per line. Each line started with a byte indicating the length of the line. It could only be read in SEQUENTIAL mode. The DIS/FIX 80 format had fixed length 80 character records. I don't know offhand how it handled lines shorter than 80 characters, although presumably the unused portion at the end of theine had a fixed fill value. Answer: The implementation language for your compiler and/or interpreter shouldn't dictate your language design, IMHO. Everything may seem to make sense locally, but when you put it all together… bam! That's also how we end up with jokes like this: Spouse 1: “Honey, could you pick up a loaf of bread at the store on your way home? Question: In C++ what is the underlying difference between std: :cout and fprintf? Is one better or faster than the other?
Answer: They are different kinds of things. std::cout is an instance of std::ostream. It's the C++ analog of stdout as opposed to printf. I can hear some of you saying “But wait! Those are handled by helpers outside, most of which aren't members of std::ostream. The <iostream> library includes a set of operator overloads for operator<< that handle converting various data types for output and outputting them to a std::ostream. Some of these are member functions of std::ostream, but most are freestanding functions. Those operator overloads implement the actual format conversions between the internal representation and an output string. They are also responsible for delivering the converted value to the output stream. And, unlike the printf family functions, you can add your own overloads for operator<< to format output for your custom types. These operator-overload functions are what your program calls when it outputs values via std::cout or other std::ostream instances. As of C++20, there's std::format, which provides a format string model similar to printf, while also enabling you to provide your own formatting functions for custom types. It formats to a string you can print via std::cout. Question: How does UNIX understand that he needs to call tty? How does a tty understand that they want to print to stderr and not stdout?
Answer: How does UNIX understand that he needs to call tty? Who is “he”? Also, TTYs are devices. You can open their device nodes as files. You don't call them like functions. How does a tty understand that they want to print to stderr and not stdout? It doesn't. A TTY device doesn't know anything about stdout or stderr. Those concepts don't exist at its level. The names stdin, stdout, and stderr are the names C gives to the default C file streams set up by the runtime environment prior to entering main(). On a UNIX™ or POSIX system, those three streams are associated with file descriptors 0, 1, and 2. File descriptors are not a C concept, they're a UNIX™/POSIX concept. Other operating systems may use different concepts below file streams. In UNIX™/POSIX, the exec() family of calls replace the current process with a new process for the new program, while retaining a subset of open file descriptors and environment variables. This allows a shell to set up what files it wants associated with file descriptors 0, 1, and 2 before it exec()’s the target program. For an interactive program, all three might be associated with some TTY device such as /dev/tty42 or /dev/ttyS0 or something. Inside a C program, the C runtime library wraps these file descriptors in its FILE* stream abstraction. That's where stdin, stdout, and stderr come in. Those provide a higher level interface, with optional buffering, etc. Typically, stdin and stdout are buffered by default,¹ while stderr isn't.² That buffering is part of the C standard library, and can be reconfigured by your program. Look up setbuf() and setvbuf() for more details. The TTY is oblivious to all this. It just services read and write requests for all the open file descriptors that are associated with it. The division of labor in a UNIX™/POSIX environment is roughly as follows: Now, there's a whole lot more you can dig into with the UNIX™/POSIX terminal interface, and OS-specific APIs and concepts around it. Controlling terminals, cooked/raw, various line disciplines, etc. etc. I’m not going there. I focused on the lowest common denominator: how stdin/stdout/stderr connect a UNIX™/POSIX terminal device. My answer is also specific to UNIX™/POSIX. Other OSes may do things differently. ¹ In fact, the runtime environment could select between line buffered and fully buffered. It might select line buffering for stdin or stdout if detects that it's connected to a TTY. See the UNIX™/POSIX isatty() function. ² At least within C’s FILE* abstraction. Question: What server can compute a 256-bit or 192-bit? If it can be done, how much time will it be?
Answer: In a comment on the question, I asked: A 192-bit or 256-bit what? If you are just asking about arbitrary precision computation, you don't need a server for that. The 8-bit computers of my childhood are overkill for that. The response was: I mean iterate from 1 to 192 bit I started to write the reply as a comment, and I’ve decided to turn it into an answer. And what exactly do you mean by iterate to 192 bit? Do you really mean count sequentially from 1 to 2 192 ? If so, then no. Let me rephrase that. There’s no freakin’ way. To give some context, let’s associate powers of 10 to convenient powers of 2 just above them: To a first order approximation, the Earth has been around over 1.7 × 10 16 seconds, or about 17 quadrillion seconds. That’s about 2 54 seconds. The U.S. Summit supercomputer is good for about 2 60 FLOPS (floating point operations per second). For the sake of estimation, let’s use that as a proxy for our counting rate. That’s extremely generous, as that the supercomputer achieves this score with parallel computation. I had stipulated a sequential count up above, so I really do believe I am being generous. If we started that computer counting when the Earth was formed, it would have only counted to about 2 114 by now, or about 20 thousand decillions ( 2 × 10 34 ). You’d need 2 78 times that amount of time to reach all the way to 2 192 . Thats about 5.4 × 10 39 seconds, or about 173 decillion years. Yeah, no. Ain’t happening. Even if I’m pessimistic by a factor of a million, it ain’t happening. A billion… A trillion… A quadrillion… it ain’t happening within the Earth’s estimated remaining lifespan. Even if I’m pessimistic by a factor of decillion, it still ain’t happening within a single human lifespan. These numbers are sufficiently large that they defy most people’s ability to reason about them. They’re still small compared to, say, the number of atoms in the observable universe—estimated to be somewhere between 10 78 and 10 82 , according to a quick search. They’re still stupidly huge compare to any numbers we normally encounter. So the answer is no. No traditional digital computer can count sequentially from 1 to 2 192 within any reasonable amount of time. One additional thought: Your question refers to a “server,” I assume as a proxy for “a fast computer.” Most beefy servers are fast in the same way freight trains are fast. Freight trains* can haul a tremendous amount of freight at highway cruising speeds. No supercar can haul anywhere near as much freight from point A to point B as a freight train can, in the time it takes the train to get from A to B. But no freight train can keep up with a supercar’s acceleration, nor would any be able to match the supercar’s top speed. If I want to increase the total throughput of a rail line, I don’t make the train run faster. I add more boxcars. That’s very different from a supercar. With the supercar, you can’t increase the passenger capacity. You can just tweak the vehicle to accelerate faster or boost its top speed. Therefore, if you want to run one single thread super fast, a typical server may not be the fastest option. *I picked freight trains on purpose, as it’s a different story with high speed passenger rail. Freight trains are more analogous to the beefy dual-socket servers with many dozens, or perhaps hundreds, of processor cores. Those tend to run at lower clock speeds to maximize efficiency and deliver maximum aggregate throughput.

Question: A modern CPU with billions of transistors, when running a normal program, how many of those transistors are actually used? Do the not used transistors still consume electricity and generate heat?
Answer: A “normal program” could include anything from good ol’ vi all the way to your favorite 4K video encoding and editing software. Obviously, they're going to make different demands on the device. But, let's not get ahead of ourselves, shall we? Dead / Dormant Silicon Most of the transistors on a die have a specific purpose. Not all of them, but most of them. And some have specific purposes, but they won't actually do much while you're using the computer. Let’s dig into that, shall we? − Some percentage of the die would be whitespace, because wire routing and other placement constraints can't make effective use of the area. Physical design tools may fill that with spare gates. These do nothing, and are tied to ground to make sure of it. Why bother? Chips have bugs. Also: It’s free (chip) real estate! Fixing the bugs requires changing the logic. Sometimes, you can find a fix that just requires rewiring a couple gates, or inserting another term into an equation. With spare gates, you can do the equivalent of an old-school blue wire fix, patching in a spare gate or three. These are called ECOs—engineering change orders—in the business. Now, you can't easily do that on already-manufactured devices.¹ The real goal is to make it easy to cheaply deploy the fix to production. A full mask set for a chip can cost $millions. A metal-layer fix, OTOH, is an order or two less expensive, typically. Ever look at the stepping info for a modern processor? Some vendors use a letter and a number, like A1, B0, or C2. A full spin bumps the letter up by one and resets the digit to 0. A minor spin—such as you’d see with a set of metal fixes—bumps up the digit by 1. Minor spins consisting of metal fixes might take you from A0→A1→A2. A major spin involving a full new mask set would take you to B0. − Another portion of the die has redundant structures. Why? Chips have manufacturing defects. See that little RAM block over there, with 512 columns and 256 rows? Well, that’s its functional capacity. It actually has extra columns and extra rows—perhaps 514 columns and 258 rows. That way, if there is a silicon defect under the RAM, we can configure the chip to use a spare row and/or column in place of a defective one. RAMs have a nice, regular, dense structure. Their transistors are often smaller than typical logic transistors. They’re quite susceptible to defects. At the same time, that nice, regular structure lends itself to easy repair. Another fraction of the die has built-in self-test (BIST) logic for the same reason. Memory BIST is a fairly obvious feature to include. This finds the defects I mentioned above. Logic BIST uses various test patterns—often generated by automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) techniques—to find defective logic. Patterns can test for stuck-at-1, stuck-at-0, opens, shorts, and other sorts of defects in logic gates. Some test patterns may be generated on chip, while larger test patterns may be driven from outside by a chip tester. Also, there’s usually additional supporting logic on the die, such as checksum logic² on buses and critical signals, to measure the chip’s behavior to determine whether it passes the tests. − And that brings us to the next portion of the die: In-circuit debug and test logic. Why? Chips and software both have bugs, and chips have manufacturing defects. The in-circuit debug and test logic connects nearly all of the flip-flops in a design into a gigantic shift registers known as scan chains. Scan chains provide access to nearly all of the flip-flops via test access ports (TAPs), usually connected over something like JTAG. (JTAG is named for the group that standardized it: the IEEE Joint Test Access Group.) One or more of the scan chains may be for boundary scan. Boundary scan, as its name implies, goes around the edge of the design, allowing you to inspect and exercise I/O pins and whatnot. In some cases it might exercise interfaces between certain blocks as well. The rest go into the heart of the logic. Remember those ATPG test patterns I mentioned above? Scan chains are the path to get those patterns up into the logic. That same scan logic provides incredible visibility for an in-circuit debugger. However, once you start shifting one of those scan chains under JTAG control, most modern chips won’t be able to continue execution. Scan dumps are great for diagnosing chip bugs in the field, but not so great for diagnosing software issues. Therefore, the TAPs also usually provide access for dedicated software-oriented debug functionality. This includes logic for inspecting memory, CPU registers, and caches, as well as setting breakpoints, tracing system buses, measuring code performance, etc. Depending on the design, some of that same logic may be accessible to software running directly on the chip. However, in many chips, a good fraction of it is only usable with an appropriate hardware debugger attached. And crucially, it’s only activated when it’s being used. Otherwise, it’s not doing anything. − And there’s one more bit of dedicated logic to complement everything above: process characterization logic. Why? Chip manufacturing has variability. You may have heard of speed binning. Different chips with the same design may perform differently due to variations in manufacturing, and speed binning is just one of the ways we try to get as many useful devices as possible out of the process. Or, as they say in the industry, to improve the yield of the process. Different dies on the same wafer can vary due to local variations in the process. Different wafers can vary either intentionally by skewing the process parameters slightly, or unintentionally due to variation in the machinery itself. Process characterization logic has small test structures designed to measure and validate process parameters. Is this a fast or slow die? Does it run hot or cold? Are the transistor thresholds on the high or low side? This logic may only provide coarse characterization rather than finely detailed measurements, but that’s okay. Its goal is to let the tester program know which bin this chip landed in, process-wise. − I can hear some of you in the back muttering about the elephant in the room I haven’t mentioned yet: intentionally disabled logic. Why? Chip defects can’t always be worked around locally. Also, we may want multiple SKUs from a single die. If there’s a chip defect big enough to take out an entire CPU core, it may³ be possible to just disable that core. If the defect takes out an entire RAM instance in the cache, it may be possible to reduce the advertised amount of cache on the device. Just create a new part number with a correspondingly lower core count or cache capacity. Disable the defective blocks and sell it as the lesser device at a lower price. It’s usually better to make some money than it is to make no money. If demand for these lower-spec devices outstrips the natural amount you get from disabling defective blocks, then you might purposefully disable good cores or good cache memory just to create more lower-spec devices. In order to make that work, the chip needs to be designed with that flexibility. That means there’s additional logic to conditionally disable and isolate blocks so they don’t negatively impact the rest of the device. You don’t want a defective CPU shouting the digital equivalent of “Potato potato potato! I can count to potato!” at all the other cores. This isolation logic, when present, is configured once at chip reset time. It remains static at run time. Some of this may occur at a finer granularity as well, and sometimes for different reasons than defects or differentiated SKUs. For instance, it’s illegal to ship certain technologies such as high speed crypto to certain countries. Rather than make a completely different die for those markets, we instead design those blocks so they can be disabled at manufacturing time on a subset of the chips produced. And for a historic example of differentiated SKUs, there’s the i486DX and i486SX. At least initially, both used the same die, with the FPU disabled on the i486SX devices.⁴ (Later revisions actually removed the FPU, so it truly was a smaller, less expensive die.) The i487SX is actually just an i486DX with one extra pin on the package. Once plugged in, the i486SX is disabled. “One processor for the price of two!” ;-) − And finally, you might wonder how we configure all the bits I mentioned such as RAM repair and disabling CPU cores. The answer is: on-chip fuses or other non-volatile storage. Some portion of the die is dedicated to storing details programmed at manufacturing. Process characteristics, RAM repair, enabled/disabled cores, enabled/disabled RAMs, etc. are all details that might get encoded in fuses. Or, if your device has on-chip flash, it might use that instead. Alongside that information is typically some manufacturing details such as fab, lot, wafer, die coordinates, manufacture date/time, and a device-unique identifier. These details allow correlating a specific device back to the exact set of machines involved in its manufacture. If the device fails at any point in manufacturing or out in the field, this information can be used to help root-cause the failure. A faulty machine or process excursion might cause a bunch of devices to fail in a similar way. This manufacturing metadata allows us to tie their failures together to understand what they have in common. Additionally, we can use this information on healthy devices to correlate their characterization data as well. That allows process engineers to tune the process to maximize yield and minimize avoidable defects. − Here’s the important part that connects these together: All of the logic I just described is typically dormant under normal operation. Most of these transistors fall under the general heading DFx, which is a shorthand for Design for _______. Much of what I described above falls under the specific headings Design for Test, Design for Manufacturability, and Design for Debug. It doesn’t take up a huge percentage of the die, but it’s pervasive, and—under normal circumstances—idle. Dark Silicon This is different from the dead/dormant silicon I mentioned above. Dark silicon, as I’ve heard the term used, refers to perfectly functional silicon that you can use at (nearly) any time. However, due to power and thermal considerations, you can’t use all of it all of the time. There are devices with large vector units, matrix engines, or other accelerators that can’t make use of all of the functionality simultaneously. It might draw more power than can be safely delivered and/or heat up the chip too much. Software can only make use of a subset of the logic on the die safely. On mainstream devices, there’s typically some chip management logic—quite possibly a small embedded microcontroller!—that monitors what’s in use and what software wants to use. It also keeps an eye on temperature and incoming voltages. It manages which blocks are turned on and which are turned off. It might also adjust voltage and frequency delivered to various blocks to keep as much turned on as possible, albeit at a lower performance point. That brings us to the final portion… The Rest of the Chip The rest of the silicon is nominally active. That said, depending on what you’re doing, much of it may still be idle. CMOS logic burns power two ways: When a CMOS logic gate holds a static output value, very little current flows through the gate. The little current that does flow through is called leakage. The amount of leakage current depends on the type of transistors in the gate, as well as the voltage across the gate, and the transistor’s junction temperature. Leakage determines the static power of a logic block. When a CMOS logic gate switches from 0→1 or 1→0, a little bit of current flows directly through the gate while it switches, as there’s a momentary resistive path from V D D to V S S . Additionally, the wire(s) it drives have capacitance, and that capacitance needs to be charged or discharged. The activity factor of a given gate is the percentage of cycles that the gate switches its output value through a full 0→1→0 cycle.⁵ Multiply that by the clock rate to determine the number of times it switches per second. That, combined with many of the same parameters that affect leakage, determines the dynamic power of that logic block. And then there are the clocks themselves. These go all over the place and drive a ton of logic. Even worse, they toggle at twice the maximum toggle rate of the logic they drive. If we say the clock’s activity factor is 100%, all of the logic driven by that clock will have an activity factor of 50% or less—usually much less. As a result, clock networks can draw a huge amount of power on their own. Modern chips dynamically manage the voltage and frequency supplied to each major logic block to try to minimize both types of power dissipation. Lowering the voltage reduces leakage power at the expense of switching speed. Lowering the frequency reduces the number of times the clocks and logic in that block switch per second. Modern designs also aggressively clock gate. If a given piece of logic doesn’t need to change state unless some specific condition is true, then the registers that drive it don’t need to be clocked. You can locally disable the clock to those registers. If a larger part of the design is going to be idle for awhile, you could gate the clock at an even higher level. With these techniques, the actual switching rate for most of the nominally-active logic on the die can be quite low most of the time. That’s how you can have a beefy multicore system that runs nice and cool. But, once you start really crunching some numbers, it can heat up very quickly. And if your cooling solution doesn’t keep up, that chip management logic will whack you with a thermal throttle. The Punchline I’m sure I missed some finer details, but I think this captures the broad categories that your question touches on. If you’d like to know more, ask in the comments. ¹ You might use a focused ion beam (FIB) device or similar on a handful of devices to test a fix. You’re not going to do that for all the devices you’ve already shipped. ² Examples include single-input signature registers (SISRs) and multiple-input signature registers (MISRs). The ones I am most familiar with are lightweight linear-feedback shift registers (LFSRs). To a first order approximation, you can think of these as taking the CRC of everything that happens on a particular signal or group of related signals. ³ Depending on the nature of the defect, it’s possible that the entire die is compromised in ways that aren’t obvious initially but will cause failure later, as noted by Alex Witkowski at the link below the next footnote. Manycore processors such as Cerebras’ WSE would have approximately 0.00‰ yield if 100% of the processing elements must be fully functional. AsAP2 with its >1000 cores wouldn’t be much better. And AFAICT, RAM repair is present on pretty much any modern silicon with more than a smattering of RAM and a fuse block or some flash. ⁴ While popular rumors suggested the i486SX was made from i486DX dies with defective FPUs that were disabled once found defective, that’s not actually the case. According to Alex Witkowski, one of the engineers behind the i486SX, the FPUs on the converted dies were simply never tested. The SX/DX distinction was a bond-out option; however, to bypass FPU testing you needed to make the decision before you connect bond wires and put the chip in the package. I’ll add that tester time is expensive too, and so the shorter test time saves money as well. ⁵ That means a signal that switches from 0→1 or 1→0 every clock cycle has an activity factor of 50%. For single-data-rate signals, the activity factor is always 50% or less.

Question: Why does any power of 6 have a remainder of 1 when divided by 5?
Answer: I’ll be generous and fill in an important detail: Any positive,* integer power of 6 has a remainder of 1 when divided by 5. In other words, when k ∈ Z ; k > 0 : 6 k ≡ 1 mod 5 In case you haven’t seen it before, ≡ means “is congruent to.” Informally, that means the remainder for the value on the left equals the remainder for the value on the right after dividing by the modulus. (If the remainder is negative, add the modulus to make it positive.) Or if you prefer, for a , b , c , k ∈ Z ; c ≠ 0 : a ≡ b ( mod c ) ⟹ a = b + k c Note: For the remainder of this answer, a , b , c , k ∈ Z ; a ≠ 0 ; c ≠ 0 ; k > 0. So why is 6 k ≡ 1 ( mod 5 ) ? Because: 6 ≡ 1 mod 5 In general, when you compute a b modulo c , you only need to keep the remainder modulo c at each step, because the multiples of c in the result disappear modulo c . Why? Allow me to demonstrate informally with an example: ( a + 1 ) k ≡ 1 mod a If you set a = 5 , you have the scenario in your question. First, consider k = 1 : ( a + 1 ) ≡ 1 mod a Hopefully it should be obvious that the remainder of dividing a + 1 by a should be 1. So what about k = 2 ? ( a + 1 ) 2 = a 2 + 2 a + 1. Notice that all of those terms except 1 are divisible by a . Therefore: ( a + 1 ) 2 ≡ a 2 + 2 a + 1 ≡ 1 mod a In general, the only terms that will survive modulo a are the ones that aren’t multiplied by a . They all boil down to: ( a + 1 ) k ≡ 1 k ≡ 1 mod a Now what if I added some other number than 1 to a ? For example, what about ( a + 2 ) k ( mod a ) ? I’ll leave the algebra to demonstrate the following as an exercise for the reader: ( a + 2 ) k ≡ 2 k mod a Try it numerically with a = 5. You’ll find as k goes 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , … that ( a + 2 ) k cycles 1 , 2 , 4 , 3 , 1 , … . Try it with other values of a . You might find this property surprising, but it really shouldn’t be. Consider a = 10. The modulus 10 gives us the last decimal digit of whatever number we’re considering. Now consider 11 k . What’s the last digit of 11 k in decimal? It’s 1 of course. When I multiply to values a and b , only the rightmost digit of a and b can affect the product a ⋅ b . Write out a product long-hand like you learned in grade school to convince yourself. See that rightmost column? There’s only one digit that contributes to the sum in that column: the product of the rightmost digits of the multiplicands. When you have some other modulus, the same thing happens, just in a different numeric base—the same base as your modulus. Taking the remainder modulo 6 is the same as finding the rightmost digit in base 6. Hopefully my ad hoc explanation helps. I could have brought in more formality, and walked through modular arithmetic. I’ll be honest: I’ve never had a number theory course, and my own self-directed learning is sufficiently spotty that I’d probably stuff up the explanation. But, I also see no issue with building up an intuition with the tools we get from algebra class. After all, you have to start somewhere if you’re going to dive into number theory at all. *And I believe you can extend that to non-negative integer powers; however, it’s late and I don’t feel like working through the zeroth power case just to verify.

Question: Is C or Basic better for programming on the Intel 8086 processor?
Answer: It depends on your goals. By today’s standards, the 8086 is roughly 40 years out of date, give or take. Its 32-bit younger brother, the 80386, came out 39 years ago (1985). I suppose you could be charitable and say it’s only ~30 years out of date, as there were many 8086 and 8088 machines still happily churning along (albeit slowly) in 1994. Apparently, Intel® kept making 8086 CPUs until 1998, probably for embedded applications and low-end DOS-based portables. Given the 8086’s age, I’ll assume you have an eye toward retrocomputing. BASIC, particularly GW-BASIC or QBASIC, will give you that retrocomputing feel of being back in the 80s, programming a Turbo XT PC clone using whatever language was available with MS-DOS or PC-DOS. C would wring more performance out of the machine. I don’t know of any modern compilers that target the 8086. You may need to dust off an old version of Turbo C++ (which includes a C compiler) or other MS-DOS compiler from ~30 years ago. You’ll be learning an older dialect of C, likely without many of the nice features C99 added. Also, to use more than 64K of RAM, you’ll need to learn about different compilation models (Tiny, Small, Compact, Medium, Large, Huge) and what “near” and “far” pointers are. The near and far keywords were quite common extensions on those old C compilers for a reason. Of course, to squeeze the most out of an 8086 or 8088, you’ll need to learn assembly language. You could easily beat the C compilers of the early 90s with hand coded assembly on an 8086 or 8088. If you know what you’re doing, you can push an old IBM PC pretty far. … Of course, to pull off the tricks that demo crew accomplished, you’ll need to learn about the rest of the hardware in the machine intimately as well. The differences between the original IBM PC and the clones will become much more apparent if you try to squeeze out every last drop. Welcome back to the era of 40-pin DIPs and 5V TTL. Happy retrocomputing!

Question: If the interpreter translates Python to an intermediary language line by line, then to machine code, why doesn't it directly compile it to a machine code and make it like C?

Many Python constructs have expensive semantics. This answer unpacks this concept further: While that answer focuses more on Perl than Python, the principle remains the same. What makes C different from Python or Perl is that its language semantics are tied to an abstract machine model that is fairly similar in character to typical assembly languages.
