Question: How would I design a DFA to recognize the language consisting of all strings ending with 001 over the alphabet set {0,1}.?
Answer: Since this question is from 2017, my guess is OP has earned whatever grade they were going to earn for their class. I don’t know how OP would design this DFA, but I can describe how I might do it. I would start with a direct path from the starting condition to our accepting condition. At the beginning, you’ve seen nothing. You’re in the Start state. If you see a single ‘0’, go to the 0 state. If you see another ‘0′, go to the 00 state. And finally, if you then see a ‘1’, go to the 001 state. As the double-circle indicates, that’s an accept state. Obviously, this DFA isn’t complete. Now, what should happen when you’re in the Start state and you see a ‘1’? We’re waiting to see a ‘0’, so let’s transition back to the Start state in that case. OK, so far, so good. The 0 state indicates we’ve seen a single ‘0’ after zero or more ‘1’ symbols. What should happen if we see a ‘1’ in this state? We need to start over! So, let’s transition back to the Start state. The 00 state currently indicates we’ve seen two consecutive ‘0’ symbols after a ‘1’ symbol. We also already know what should happen if we see a ‘1’ while in this state: we transition to the 001 state, our accept state, because the last three symbols we’ve seen are ‘0’, ‘0’, ‘1’. But what if we see more than two consecutive ‘0’ symbols? We really should allow for more than two consecutive ‘0’ symbols. As long as the last two symbols were ‘0’, ‘0’, we can remain in the 00 state. Any extra ‘0’ symbols don’t change anything for us. Therefore, if we see a ‘0’ while we’re in the the 00 state, let’s transition back to the 00 state. Nice! Now every state except the 001 state has a transition for both ‘0’ and ‘1’. What should happen if we see a ‘0’ while we’re in the 001 state? When we reach the 001 state, the most recent symbol we saw was ‘1’. If we see a ‘0’ next, we should transition to the state that corresponds to “zero or more ‘1’ symbols, followed by a ‘0’ symbol.” That’s the 0 state. And finally, what should happen when we see a ‘1’ while in the 001 state? We need to start over! Once we see that ‘1’, we no longer match the sequence we’re interested in, ‘0’, ‘0’, ‘1’. Furthermore, the ‘1’ itself isn't a prefix of our desired sequence. That means we need to go back to the Start state if we see a ‘1’ while we’re in the 001 state. And that’s our complete DFA. Ta da! You should test the DFA. To get you started, try the input strings below. I think if you try the set of inputs detailed above, you’ll traverse every edge in the graph at least once, and you should end in each state at least once. Mission accomplished! Question: Why doesn't AMD or Intel make processors with built-in RAM like Apple did? Is this intentional with the intention of preventing RAM manufacturers from becoming extinct?
Answer: As Pierre Leclercq's answer points out, Intel® has done something similar: Before that, Intel® released versions of Sapphire Rapids with HBM on the same package. But let's also be clear about what Apple did and didn't do. Apple mounted LPDDR chips to the top of the same chip package as the M1 chip. They did not integrate system RAM onto the same die. It’s not “built in.” It's soldered on. Jonathan Kang makes that clear here: And contrary to much speculation, this did not lead to noticeably lower latency for DDR access, either. I believe this was more of a yield and cost play than anything else. Addendum As Franklin Veaux's answer points out, the POP architecture also makes it much easier to scale up to very high bandwidth memory interfaces as well. A 400GB/s LPDDR5-6400 interface requires a total of 512 bits of data channel plus probably over 350 control lines.¹ That’s a lot of high speed signals to route out from under a BGA. Double those numbers for the 800GB/s M1 Ultra. I disagree that bandwidth is the primary reason to go POP, as Apple uses POP across the entire line, including its entry level M1 with only ~68GB/s of memory bandwidth. They’ve most likely been using POP for years in their mobile and tablet products. I’ve architected a chip that’s in production that didn’t resort to POP, but delivers more LPDDR4x bandwidth than the baseline M1 and the same bandwidth as the baseline M2 and M3. I do absolutely agree the POP architecture enables Apple’s eye-popping Max and Ultra bandwidth numbers (400GB/s to 800GB/s) at a reasonable manufacturing cost.² POP allows Apple’s UMA to scale up to higher BW without going to more exotic manufacturing techniques at the board level. In a more traditional PC without integrated graphics, the GPU(s) have their own private high bandwidth memory separate from the CPU. In Apple’s UMA, the GPU, CPUs, and Neural Engine (NE) all share the same memory interface.³ FWIW, the CPUs on an M1 Max can only make use of about 2/3rds of the bandwidth anyway. The rest of that bandwidth is for the GPU and NE. I’ve focused on M1, as that’s the device I know the most about. M2 and M3 should have a similar calculus. I don’t know offhand if the CPUs are able to achieve higher peak memory throughput than the M1 Max. ¹ It depends on how many channels the LPDDR5 is divided into. I estimated a lower bound based on 16 × 32-bit channels. LPDDR5 naturally has 16-bit channels, but I believe it permits pairing them to share a single Command/Address (CA) channel as LPDDR4 did. AFAIK it doesn’t allow larger groupings, but I also don’t see any reason why that couldn’t work other than signal integrity. The control signals are highlighted in purple boxes below. The WCK, RDQS, and DMI signals are per-byte, regardless of whether you’ve paired up channels. The actual signal count could be reduced slightly if some signals such as CS were shared by more than one channel. They could ditch several more by dropping masked-write and data bus inversion support (DMI pins). I also see no immediate reason Apple couldn’t try to group four 16-bit physical channels into a single 64-bit channel, as long as they can get good signal integrity on the CA channel. They might need to work with their DDR controller/PHY vendor to get custom training algorithms, but Apple’s pockets are deep like the Marianas Trench. With a WCK:CK ratio of 4:1, they might just make it work. If you trim out DMI, you would only need 7 CA, 8 RQDS, 8 WCK, 2 CK, and 1 CS, for a total of 26 control lines. 8 × 64-bit channels would require 208 control signals. At burst length 16 (BL16), that gives a 128-byte burst. That matches M1’s cache line size of 128 bytes. ² OTOH, the retail price on the higher end models may still cause some eyes to water. ³ This also applies to x86 chips with integrated graphics. Those are unified memory architectures as well, only without the Apple buzz, or Apple’s Neural Engine for that matter.

Question: How does Rust do direct control of memory addresses and hardware registers, if it is memory safe and doesn't handle memory directly using pointers? How can Rust be used to write device drivers if it is memory safe and does not handle low-level stuff?
Answer: Don't confuse language semantics—what a program means—with how that meaning is achieved. Also, don't assume there isn't a way to lower the guard rails a bit. Semantics vs. Generated Code Rust’s memory safety comes from its language semantics. It tracks resource ownership at a language level. The language semantics restrict how you use references, and force you to explicitly manage ownership. Most of Rust's memory safety guarantees come from these carefully constructed language semantics and the strict implementation-enforced rules that go with them. Most of Rust's rules are checked and enforced at compile time. Additional memory safety comes from other checks that may happen at run time, such as array bounds checks. Once it has proven your program doesn't break any compile-time rules, the Rust compiler has wide latitude on what code it might generate. Most of the checks disappear at that point. The compiler will emit code for any run-time checks it deems necessary as well. For example, it can omit run-time array bounds checks where it can prove the index stays in-bounds, and insert them otherwise. Will it use pointers in that generated code? Not exactly, but the effect is the same. The pointers you probably have in mind are a high level language construct. Pointers in C are typically just machine addresses, but they're wrapped in a data type that captures details about what type of thing it points to. They offer scaled pointer arithmetic and an abstraction for null pointers. They're addresses underneath, but they have some higher level semantics on top. The code generated by C compiler manipulates addresses and issues memory accesses consistent with the original program’s meaning, but it usually does so with the same mechanisms it uses for integer arithmetic. You might have written p++ in your code; under the hood could be implemented by an ordinary integer add. If the thing it points to is 42 bytes in size, you might see 42 getting added to an integer register’s contents. Most processors don't have a distinct pointer data type in hardware, particularly one that encodes the type of thing it points to. Some do—perhaps as an optional feature—but the current crop of mainstream processors don't. More commonly, addresses are just integer values, manipulated by ordinary integer arithmetic. The only thing special about them is that the compiler generates memory access instructions that use those values as memory addresses. A Rust compiler needs to generate code to access memory as well. It will use the same hardware functionality that C used for pointers. It's just happens to start from higher level constructs such is its reference types to do so. Once you get past the compile-type ownership checking, Rust references are essentially a subset of C pointers. They can't be null and they don't offer pointer arithmetic. The Rust compiler should otherwise generate similar code to what C would for pointers used in the same restricted manner. For large portions of a driver, the ownership tracking either doesn't come into play, or will be self-contained to resources the driver maintains itself. It doesn't get in the way of the driver logic managing its own resources. That's not enough, of course. It's a good thing that's not all Rust offers… Unsafe Rust Rust lets you explicitly write unsafe code. When it comes time to actually touch the hardware and access hardware registers and so on, Rust’s memory safety and borrow checker and whatnot are out of their element. Also, Rust can only see what’s in your Rust code. If you drop a Rust module into, say, the Linux kernel, the Rust compiler has no way of knowing how resources are managed in the kernel at large. That's why the language includes Unsafe Rust. Compared to ordinary Rust, Unsafe Rust has certain “superpowers,” as the documentation calls them: You can take five actions in unsafe Rust that you can’t in safe Rust, which we call unsafe superpowers. Those superpowers include the ability to: Link: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch19-01-unsafe-rust.html So, when it comes time to actually fiddle the part of the computer you can kick,* you can drop into Unsafe Rust for just the few bits that need it. Likewise when you need to exchange resources with parts of the software not written in Rust. Update! Gabriel J. Ferrer added the following great detail in a comment: I’ve written a lot of low-level Rust and what you write is accurate. Where Rust’s checking is helpful with device drivers and the like is that if your hardware has a region of memory-mapped I/O, you can use an unsafe block to encapsulate that region in an array. From there, you can access the hardware using bounds-checked array accesses. So the only time you need to use unsafe is to specify the region of memory containing the hardware one needs to access. Beyond that, it is all safe code. A nice example of this is with the following code for accessing the VGA buffer on Intel: Link: https://os.phil-opp.com/vga-text-mode/ Punchline P.S. I haven't actually written any Rust myself. If any Rustaceans see egregious errors or omissions in my description above, chime in below. *That’a an old joke definition for hardware.

Question: In C programming, when would you use OS-specific system calls (e.g. open) if there is a corresponding higher-level function (e.g. fopen)? Don’t you lose portability using the former?
Answer: I use OS-specific functionality when I need that OS-specific functionality. Higher level APIs are more portable, but they often offer the lowest common denominator amongst a broad range of potential targets. That doesn’t mean my entire application needs to rely directly on those low-level, OS specific APIs. How about a real-world example? I’ve written an Intellivision emulator that’s portable among a large number of 32-bit and 64-bit targets. It mostly relies on standard C and C++ for its core logic and functionality. It does implicitly rely on 32-bit int and a few other minor details not guaranteed by the standard. But, those details that it does rely on, such as 2′s complement signed integers, are pretty common. But, since it’s a video game emulator, it needs graphics and sound and real-time control input. Those aren’t part of the language! Now, I could write native code for some OS’s graphics and sound frameworks, or even a bare-metal backend for embedded targets. That’s not what I chose to do. Instead, I structured most of my emulator to output to an internal layer with graphics, sound, and event handling interfaces. That internal layer then targets various backends. I’ve currently implemented backends that talk to SDL and SDL2. I know one person implemented a Mac Classic backend many, many years ago. For the remainder of my answer, SDL refers both to SDL and SDL2, since they’re similar in scope and purpose. The SDL libraries make extensive use of OS-specific APIs for graphics, sound, raw event processing, multithreading, and so on. It maps its own APIs to other OS-specific and environment-specific APIs including OpenGL, Vulkan, Carbon, Win32, etc. Some of SDL’s APIs parallel standard library APIs, but offer some additional capability, or better integration with the rest of SDL. For example, both C and C++ now offer threading support. I’ll still use SDL’s threading support as I know it’s available on platforms which don’t have the recently-added standard library support, and it’s integrated with SDL’s other functionality. SDL’s backends likely call into OS-native APIs directly rather than rely on the standard library, as that support isn’t guaranteed on older platforms. And, of course, I insulate the rest of my application from SDL by confining it to my own internal platform-layer abstractions. How about open() vs. fopen()? For most programs that just need a generic file stream, fopen() is the way to go. It’s portable, it’s integrated with other parts of the library (fprintf(), fscanf(), fread(), fwrite(), etc. etc.), and so on. One answer states open() is not buffered while fopen() is. That’s not 100% true: setvbuf() can change the buffering associated with a standard C file stream. That includes making it unbuffered. The open(), close(), read(), write(), lseek(), etc. APIs are POSIX APIs that work in terms of file descriptors. I use these APIs when I specifically need to work with functionality that requires file descriptors. For example, if I want to memory-map a file with mmap(), I need a file descriptor. If I want to connect stdin, stdout, and stderr to different files/devices—say as part of a fork()/exec() sequence—I need file descriptors and dup2() or similar. Some use cases, such as memory-mapping a file, are performance oriented. Others, such as setting up stdin/stdout/stderr for file redirection, are purely about functionality. In a large, portable application, these bits should be grouped together into an internal library or subsystem, and invoked through an internal API or interface. For targets that offer the POSIX APIs, they can reuse the POSIX backend. For targets that don’t, you need a different implementation behind that internal interface. Most of your application won’t directly depend on those OS interfaces. The small, OS-specific and/or target-specific subsystems will. When it comes time to port your application to a noticeably different environment, you will need to rewrite those OS and target specific portions. The rest of your application may not need to be touched at all. If the rest of your application does require changes, that hints that you haven’t encapsulated the target platform dependencies adequately. That’s an opportunity to refactor the code and move more of those dependencies behind abstracted interfaces. If you’re just getting started with programming, you’re probably not accustomed to building up internal abstractions as part of developing your code. You probably have user interface, business logic, and algorithm implementation welded together in the same function, and that function might even be main(). For example, suppose you’re asked to input 10 integers into an array, and then print the largest and smallest elements in that array. I use that example, because I see questions like that one repeatedly here on Quora. A typical answer for such a question would likely include the user-interface I/O, the code for scanning the array, and so on all in one function, main(). You could factor that apart: Let’s assume I’ve introduced an ArrayInt abstraction that’s similar to C++’s std::vector<int>, in that it manages a dynamically allocated array that knows its own size. PairInt holds a pair of integers. You might get main() down to: Naturally, that collection of internal abstractions would be pretty weird if the listed functions were the only functions offered. I’ve only described the bits that this particular use case would need. Each of these might be built on other internal library pieces as well. For instance, GetArrayInt() might call a GetInt() function that checks that you actually input an integer, for example. You could call GetInt() directly if you needed to get just a single integer. If you really look at the code, you might notice something: It’s no longer tied to stdin/stdout. DisplayMessage() will display a message in whatever manner makes sense to your target. In a windowing environment, that message will likely end up in a window somewhere. Likewise for getting input. If you wrote this with printf() and scanf() and such directly intermingled with the rest of the code, your UI will be tangled with your other logic. If someone asked you to take input and provide output some other way, you’re modifying the same code that holds the business logic and the min/max algorithm. You can get away with that in a toy homework program. It gets ugly as your application grows. The common thread here is abstraction.

Question: Why does for example decimal 193 = 11000001 and 1 = 1, 9 = 1001, 3 = 11 (1-1001-11) does not provide same binary? Is it possible somehow calculate that decimal 193 would be as 1-1001-11 in binary without needing separate every decimal?
Answer: 193 in decimal is equal to 11000001 in binary, not 0001–1001–0011. The latter is called Binary Coded Decimal. BCD uses 4 bits to represent a decimal digit. It’s really decimal, just encoded in binary to make it easier to work with in digital logic. You’re asking why 193 10 = 11000001 2 . That implies you’re working with numbers in an ordinary weighted positional number system. That’s the sort of number system we use every day. Each position in such a number has a different place-value associated with it. Each place-value is a power of the numeric base. As you move to the left, each place value increases. The ratio between adjacent digits’ place values equals the base. The digit just to the left of the radix point (aka. decimal point in decimal) has the value b 0 = 1 in base b . The digit immediately to its left has place value b 1 , and to the left of that is b 2 , and so on. To determine the overall value of the number, you multiply each digit by its place-value, and sum up the products. For instance, 193 10 is a decimal number. I added the subscript 10 to emphasize that it’s decimal. The place-values for its three digits are 10 2 , 10 1 , and 10 0 . Thus, the value of 193 10 is: 1 ⋅ 10 2 + 9 ⋅ 10 1 + 3 ⋅ 10 0 = 1 ⋅ 100 + 9 ⋅ 10 + 3 ⋅ 1 = 193 10 Binary works identically, except instead of powers of 10, you have powers of 2. The value of the binary number 11000001 2 is given by: 11000001 2 = 1 ⋅ 2 7 + 1 ⋅ 2 6 + 0 ⋅ 2 5 + 0 ⋅ 2 4  + 0 ⋅ 2 3 + 0 ⋅ 2 2 + 0 ⋅ 2 1 + 1 ⋅ 2 0 = 1 ⋅ 128 + 1 ⋅ 64 + 1 ⋅ 1 = 193 10 And, of course, the subscript 2 on 11000001 2 indicates binary. Keep in mind that binary and decimal are just representations of numbers. 11000001 2 and 193 10 are the same number. 11000001 2 is its binary representation, and 193 10 is its decimal representation. And, for completeness, 0001 2 1001 2 0011 2 is its binary coded decimal (BCD) representation as three 4-bit numbers representing its three decimal digits. I mention BCD, because I anticipate you’ll eventually encounter that in class too. To convert a decimal number to binary, there aren’t really any great short cuts. You can multiply each decimal digit by the binary representation of its decimal place value, and then sum that up, but it isn’t particularly convenient. And, if you’re not accustomed to working in different numeric bases, you might find it confusing. In practice, we don’t generally convert between decimal and binary (or other bases, such as hexadecimal) by hand very often. We let the computer do that for us. But, it’s useful to know how to translate between the two if you need to write the code to tell the computer how to do it. It’s also useful to understand what you’re looking at, and how it relates to how computers represent data internally. The simplest way I know of to convert decimal integer to binary by hand is to start with a table of powers of 2. For example, 2 7 = 128 is the largest power of 2 that’s not larger than 193. Tada! That’s it. A table might make that easier to read: n 2 n Remaining 2 n ≤ Remaining? Question: Why do computers use more than one representation for signed numbers?
Answer: For the same reason humans use multiple representations for numbers: because some representations can be more useful than others in different contexts. For instance, two’s complement arithmetic is really just arithmetic modulo a power of 2. It makes use of the fact that − k ≡ 2 n − k  mod  2 n We used a similar trick with ten’s complement arithmetic back in the day of manual adding machines. But, instead of a power of 2, we used a power of 10. What's neat about that realization is that as long as you keep the result modulo the given power of 2 (or 10), the same mechanism works equally well for signed and unsigned arithmetic. N’s complement approaches work reasonably well when your digits are always all aligned by place value, as they would be for integers and fixed point arithmetic. Chose N to match your arithmetic base, and choose the power of N based on the number of digits. For fixed point, you’ll also have to account for a scale factor, but that's not difficult, as it's fixed. Sign-magnitude representation is more useful when you're dealing with a wide range of magnitudes. If you keep your numbers normalized, as we do with scientific notation ( 1.234 × 10 5 ), it's really easy to multiply or divide two numbers looking only at their significant digits, and then adjusting the sign and exponent separately afterward. In fact, that's the principle of operation for multiplication and division with basic slide rules. They do get more than a little help from logarithms, of course. The markings help you switch between linear and logarithmic domains easily though. And, uncoincidentally, IEEE 754 floating point uses sign-magnitude. IEEE 754 isn't the only floating point representation, but it's presently the most common. IEEE 754 doesn't need to use logarithms to multiply and divide, however.

Question: Why don't more programmers use regular expressions? Somehow, most of the programmers I know prefer to use split/substring with index, etc.
Answer: There are a solid handful of good answers here that deserve your attention. In no particular order, I suggest reading each of these: I won't repeat the “now you have two problems” joke from Jamie Zawinski (aka jwz). I suspect he might be tired of it. [See: https://www.jwz.org/blog/2014/05/so-this-happened/] Instead, pun dog to the rescue. I share this as a self-aware fan of Perl, BTW: As the other answers I linked point out, regular expressions are: I generally agree with all of those points. In their classic form, regexes are essentially machine code for a certain category of finite state machines. They just happen to use opcodes that map to punctuation so that it's possible to get by without an assembler. ;-) OK, that's not literally true. Still, it's a sufficiently useful metaphor to capture the essence. I give my own take below. I will try not to retread too much ground already covered in the answers I linked. Please, go read them! I’m here to recount my own experience. Regexes On The Fly One place I absolutely love using regular expressions is in my text editor (Vim) and with the classic UNIX™ utility grep and its younger cousin egrep (“extended grep”).¹ In both of those use cases, I am writing a regular expression on the fly for a specific, immediate, and transient need. Readability? Maintainability? Who cares?!? Those regular expressions won't persist in any codebase, other than a few that I keep in my .vimrc. They just need to work in the moment. After that, they're gone. There's no consequence to getting one wrong, either. Just hit undo (if necessary) and try again! What about in some software’s codebase? Perl: Regexes as a Lifestyle Perl took awk, sed, grep, C, and a dash of sh (Bourne shell), and munged them all together into one language.² Regular expressions are a first class feature of the language. You would be forgiven for thinking it’s a regular expression engine with a scripting language just sorta tacked onto it. That prints all lines from stdin that look roughly like assignment statements. And, the fact I had to explain that hints why regular expressions are not so great in codebases: They quickly become difficult to follow. That one actually isn't all that bad. But, it still, it's wrapped a lot of work up in a 30-character string. When writing Perl, I do as Perl programmers do and let regexes flow. I set a low bar for when to apply a regular expression, as the language really does make it easy. Too easy, perhaps. I avoid complicated back references and conditionals and most of the fancy features. I don't need them often. When I do, I have two choices: Usually the latter wins. After all, if I write at the limit of my cleverness, it's probably beyond my ability to debug. And anyone else that maintains the code is going to be cursing my name. That's not to say I haven't used such beasts. I have at least one program that uses a gnarly regex I found in a cookbook, already debugged. I used it like a black box. In many Perl programs, regular expressions often run afoul of the old saying “If the only tool you have is a hammer, every problem looks like a nail.” Regexes aren't the only tool Perl has, by far. Perl’s regex hammer is really darn shiny, though. It's also comfortable, capable, and nearly always near the top of the toolbox. When you pick it up, its handle is usually still warm from the last time you held it. I focused on Perl so heavily in my answer so far because it's the only language I’ve programmed where I consistently ended up preferring regular expressions over other, more focused constructs. For example, I spotted code similar to this in one of my old scripts: Did that really call for a regex? It feels natural to me in Perl, and unnatural in nearly any other language I use. Elsewhere, I would just compare against the two strings with an ordinary comparison. Other Languages The only other language I made heavy use of regexes in was Lex and its cousin Flex. Programs in those languages specify match patterns and actions for lexical scanners. Lex and Flex use regular expressions to match lexical elements in the input stream. In Lex, a pattern match and associated action might look like this: Other than that, I don't use regular expressions very often at all. There's nearly always a better option. And by “better,” I mean clearer, more focused, and often more efficient option. C++ has added std::regex to its standard library. While I was happy to see it added, I have actually only used it twice, I think, and I can only really remember one major use of it that I will get to at the end. These days, if I have a task that needs a lot of parsing, I will often just reach for a parser generator. Or, if a parser already exists for the input language, I will just grab that instead. If I do use a parser generator, any regexes I write will live in the lexical scanner. The rest of the code doesn't need them. I’ve read a number of stories about regexes blowing up in production. Certain features can result in quadratic or exponential explosion in runtime on adversarial inputs. Many input languages aren't regular, and therefore can't be parsed properly by regular expressions.³ [X]HTML in particular is not a regular language, as this classic Stack Overflow answer reminds us: https://stackoverflow.com/a/1732454  My Favorite (Ab)use of std::regex in C++ Two $DAYJOBs back, I wrote a constraint-solver based tool for generating assembly language test cases to verify a CPU design. The input language looks similar to assembly language, but with details missing. The tool then fills in the missing details by randomly selecting from whatever options remain after applying the constraints. For example, suppose I want an ADD instruction that feeds another ADD instruction. I could write the constraint “ADD => ADD” and the tool would figure out the rest, including allocating and initializing registers, adding code to check results, etc. The => says “The instruction on the right must consume a value produced by the instruction on the left.” In contrast, -> just means “These instructions must appear in sequence.” You could also be more explicit about the connections between instructions by using variables. Suppose I want to add and subtract the same two inputs, and then multiply those together. In this example, I don't really care where they came from either, as long as it came from two other randomly selected instructions rather than constants supplied by the tool: The . means “any instruction”,⁴ while .. in the argument list means “unspecified arguments”. I ran into a design issue: Sometimes I want to specify a subset of the instruction set based on a detail that isn't represented by one of the syntax elements available to me in the pseudo-assembly syntax. For instance, we didn't have separate register files for integer and floating point, so I couldn't use a register constraint to force selecting a floating point instruction. And that's where regular expressions parachuted in to the rescue. Our instruction set mnemonics used a set of very useful naming conventions: I added a feature where you could specify an instruction mnemonic constraint with an extended regular expression. In place of a mnemonic, you’d put a regular expression in-between slashes. The user-supplied regex was then used to filter the mnemonic list. For example, suppose I want to test scalar single precision floating point instructions on values read from memory: That picks instructions whose mnemonic doesn't start with V, thus excluding vector instructions, but does end in SP, thereby giving me all the relevant 3-operand single precision floating point instructions. Or, suppose I wanted to test the shift and rotate instructions, but only on byte operands. This will generate those, and the tool takes care of the rest: That would match SHRB, SHRUB, SHLB, ROTLB, ROTRB, and their vector cousins VSHRB, VSHRUB, VSHLB, VROTLB, VROTLB. Want to test all the multiplies? /MPY/ does the trick, even if we add or remove some multiplies from the instruction set definition. If you want to get dot products into the mix, do /(MPY|DOTP)/. Want a generic move instruction that's agnostic about its arguments? That'll match MV, MVC, VMVK, MVK49, MVK64, etc. etc. Occasionally a regex might allow an unintended instruction; however, I didn't see that as a huge problem. We were generating large numbers of tests, and so the few instructions that snuck through would just get a little extra testing, while the instructions they displaced would get slightly less. Was there a better way? It depends on what you mean by better. This was primarily a one person project, and I had a lot of bigger fish to fry in its construction. My customers were already familiar with Perl and regex, as much of our infrastructure was built on Perl. I could have designed more focused instruction selection functionality. It would have taken more time and more code, and would have been less flexible. OTOH, taking a regex from the user and feeding it to std::regex took less than a day. Had I stayed longer at that job, I probably would have added other, more focused mechanisms for filtering the instruction list. I would probably also retain the regex feature as an escape valve, because it was just so effective! So, I think I made the right tradeoff given the position I was in. I couldn't anticipate all the ways it might be used, but I could see it could be very general, powerful, and flexible. Punchline Regexes are cool and powerful, but best used sparingly—if at all—in most code. Sometimes they're exactly the right tool for the job. Usually there are better, more focused tools available. Go nuts with them in your editor though. ¹ Back in the day, I also used fgrep (“fixed grep”), although modern implementations have made fgrep and even egrep unnecessary. grep -F and grep -E correspond to fgrep and egrep, respectively. egrep is still shorter to type than grep -E, and modern implementations of grep optimize fixed string searches automatically. ² The result was far better than Fish Pork-a-roni a’la Simpson, in my opinion. However, there are plenty of folks that, like Bart, would rather not have nuggified fish porklets. Reference: ³ Although they might be tokenized just fine by a regex based lexer. Question: In C++, inside of a class definition, does it matter if the public section is placed before or after the private section, or can they be in any order?
Answer: Not only can they be in any order, they also aren’t really sections, per se. The public, protected, and private access specifiers can be used more than once, in any order. Each access specifier affects declarations up until the next access specifier. Generally speaking, I would prefer putting public before protected, and protected before private. You typically want your public interface up front, and internal details further down. Occasionally, you need to put some private details above the public details, such as declarations for nested internal types used in the implementation. Most of the time you don’t need to, but sometimes you do. C++ lets you introduce a subset of private declarations above your public declarations, and the rest further down: As I mentioned above, you can switch between public, protected, and private as many times as you like. They aren’t sections.* Still, you probably do want to group declarations that share common access control together whenever possible. And, I repeat the recommendation above: prefer the order public, protected, private when you have an option. You might notice that this goes against the default access control C++ applies to class. Honestly, I think that’s a design error. Yes, you want to keep your implementation details private and should be encouraged to do so. However, you also want to put your public interface first, and deemphasize your implementation details for the casual reader. Putting public first and private last serves that goal. And protected should go between them in the rare case that you have any protected members. Addendum I should also point out that non-static data members are always initialized in the order they're declared within a class, regardless of access control. Therefore, if a public member needs details from a private member as part of its initialization, that can be another reason that it you might need to alternate between public, protected, and private access control. Most coding guidelines I’ve seen discourage public non-static data members unless all data members are public and can vary completely independently. Therefore that situation doesn't come up often—if at all—as long as you follow that guideline. * Prior to C++23, the language did not make any guarantees on the relative address order of non-static members within a class that had different access control. In theory, the compiler could group members by access control. Prior to C++11, the guarantee was even less strong: there was no guarantee on order between members separated by an access control specifier at all. C++23 now guarantees that for all non-zero sized non-static data members declared within a class, the later-declared members have higher addresses than the earlier members, regardless of access control. Question: Is it possible that CPU and other types of caches may become obsolete with increased data transfer speeds?
Answer: Don’t confuse bandwidth with latency. Minimum latency to system RAM hasn’t really budged in a long time, even though transfer rates continue to increase. You can access a CPU register in a modern CPU in a fraction of a nanosecond. You can access data in L1 cache in around a nanosecond, and L2 may only be a few nanoseconds further away.* System memory accesses, on the other hand, take anywhere from dozens to hundreds of nanoseconds. Those latencies are measured from when you request the data until the first chunk of data arrives. Bandwidth describes how long it takes to move a block of data. If you request a block of data in an otherwise-idle memory system, increasing the bandwidth with reduce the amount of time from the first chunk of data to the last. Most CPU loads and stores ask for a single chunk of data, however. Streaming workloads, such as you find in traditional GPU applications, care way more about bandwidth than latency. They’re moving large quantities of data and have a ton of work in flight. The work itself is divided up into a large number of independent streams. Each of those streams runs concurrently, sopping up the available bandwidth. Overall throughput then bottlenecks on memory bandwidth, even if individual streams experience gaps in execution due to memory system latency. General purpose computing cares quite a bit about latency as well. Pointer-chasing workloads are particularly sensitive to latency. If you need to dereference a pointer to get the data, you’re stuck waiting for the data before you can operate on it. If you’re chasing a linked list or tree, each iteration can go no faster than p = p->next or p = p->child. Higher bandwidth does typically reduce the average latency on a heavily loaded processor. In practice, it doesn’t really affect the baseline latency that much, however. DDR5’s baseline latency is similar to DDR4’s, for example. That baseline is much higher than what you see in an L1 or L2 cache. You’re limited by the physics of getting data from waaaaaay over there and up into the processor. The speed of light sets a lower bound, but many other factors (capacitance, inductance, switching speeds, etc) raise the lower bound even higher. *For instance, consider a 4GHz processor with single-cycle register access, a 4 cycle load-to-use latency to L1, and 12 cycle load-to-use latency to L2. Register access takes 0.25ns, L1 takes 1ns, and L2 takes 3ns. That’s roughly in line with an AMD Zen 3 processor at 4GHz.

I don't really see an upside, but I immediately see some show-stopping downsides. Well, show-stopping for me at least. If someone else reading this thinks it's right up their alley, be my guest. Addendum Be sure to see Nathan Hannon's answer, which explores another angle of OP’s proposal: information density. And, as Erik Nilsen Haga reminds us, there can be value in signed digit numeric representations. In those, each digit has an associated sign. As I mentioned in a related comment on Nathan's answer, computers today make use of redundant representations such as carry-save with deferred carries/borrows today, but in base-2. Answer: In what sense does π “complete the circle”? A circle is the collection of points within a plane that are all the same distance from a common point—its center. Notice that π isn’t involved in that definition. Sure, π happens to be the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter. I didn’t need π to define the circle, though. It’s a property that arises from its definition, much like √ 2 is the ratio of the length of a square’s diagonal to the length of one of its sides. In fact, you can find π by integrating the upper half of a unit circle’s distance from the x axis: π = ∫ 1 − 1 d x √ 1 − x 2 Also, π happens to be the ratio of… …and so on. I don’t actually need a circle to define π . For instance, it also happens to arise from the sum of various infinite series, such as: π = 4 ∞ ∑ n = 0 ( − 1 ) n 2 n + 1 = 2 ∞ ∑ n = 0 n ! ( 2 n + 1 ) ! ! = ∞ ∑ n = 0 ( − 1 ) n 4 n ( 2 4 n + 1 + 2 4 n + 2 + 1 4 n + 3 ) = − 3 + ∞ ∑ n = 1 n 2 n n ! 2 ( 2 n ) ! There are many, many more expressions unrelated to circles where π pokes its head in. Sometimes it’s squared or cubed. Sometimes it shows up in the denominator. Heck, it even shows up in physics, such as Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle: Δ x Δ p ≥ h 4 π Going back to the circle and your question: Are there other numbers you might define similarly to π for a circle? Some have proposed that the constant τ be defined as the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its radius. But τ is joined at the hip with π , of course. Because a circle’s radius is half of its diameter, it turns out τ = 2 π . And, of course, π is also one half the period of e i φ , where φ is a real angle in radians measured counterclockwise from the positive real axis. Euler’s formula shows how to convert this into real and imaginary components: e i φ = cos φ + i sin φ If you’ve learned trigonometry, then you likely know the relationship between sine, cosine, and circles. As you sweep φ along the real axis, the expression e i φ yields a unit circle on the complex plane. Euler’s formula pulls both e and i into the mix of interesting numbers that arise in proximity to circles. If you set φ = π , you get Euler’s identity, which I show in two equivalent forms below: e i π + 1 = 0 e i π = − 1 Since τ = 2 π , that also means τ is equal to the period of e i φ . Thus e i τ = 1. Hopefully you can see that π pops up in many places. Depending on what you’re doing, it’s not the only interesting number that arises in proximity to circles. Both e and i may also show up as well. So, what exactly did you have in mind for “completing the circle”? Addendum: The Rule of Zero and The Rule of Five Defaults The Rule of Zero states that you really shouldn't declare any of the five special member functions if you don't need to directly deal with resource ownership. Your class doesn’t have to explicitly manage any resources if its members don’t have any to manage (e.g. plain ol’ data), or the members manage their own resources such as smart pointers, containers, and other well behaved classes do. Once you declare one of the five special functions, you're on the hook for all five. The destructor is one of those five. Fortunately, you can default them all, hence The Rule of Five Defaults: If your base class is copy-only, move-only, or neither copyable nor movable, then some of these members ought to be deleted. For example, if it's a move-only base class, you want to delete the copy constructor and copy assignment. The compiler will delete the default implementation if it would be ill-formed. That means you could use = default even for the special member functions that the compiler will delete. Some compilers may warn about this, however. For instance, Clang++ has such warning that you can enable. If your base class falls into this category, that suggests you're inheriting from an implementation. Question: How do you write programs to run on computers without operating systems?
Answer: Ah, good ol’ bare metal. I’ve written more than a few bare metal programs, including complete video games. I’ve written about Space Patrol a couple times already: My various games and programs for the Intellivision are essentially what you suggest: software running on a machine without an operating system. Technically, there's an EXEC ROM that offers a basic game framework, but my software bypasses it almost entirely. The only part of the EXEC that still runs when my software is running is the interrupt dispatcher. That dispatcher is effectively hardwired into the hardware. I’ve also implemented bare metal firmware, including low level debug monitors, custom file systems, file transfer protocols, menu systems, etc. I’ve ported Doom to run bare metal on a DSP. I’ve even written a run time environment for processors running in RTL simulation. That's so bare metal that the CPU core aren't even on a chip yet! I’ve targeted the 8052, 6805, 8085, CP1610, PIC24H, TMS32C6000, ARM Cortex-A15, ARM Cortex-A53, and probably some others I’ve forgotten. So how do *I* go about this? I get—or in some cases, make—cross-development tools for whatever platform I am targeting. Those allow me to edit and compile my code on my ordinary computer. In some cases, I may be able to run the software in a simulator on my machine as well. Depending on the details of the target platform, I might program the image into EPROM or flash, or download the program over JTAG. With that, I can run the code on the target. When you're running in a bare metal environment, you have the ability to control just about everything. You also have the responsibility to control just about everything. That includes initializing the CPU and peripherals, initializing memory, setting up and handling interrupts (or masking them if you don't want them), and so on. You have to drive everything! Some examples: In Space Patrol, I read each hand controller by reading an 8-bit I/O port and decoding the bit pattern. I made sounds by programming parameters directly into the sound chips. I put text and graphics on the screen by directly writing to the video controller and its attached graphics RAM. My code handles all the interrupts coming in and uses them to schedule all the game’s activities. In my PIC24 projects, I have boot code that configures the CPU clock PLL, initializes RAM and GPIOs, and then falls into the main loop. The main loop then directly implements the application. There's no OS between “reset” and “main.” Just a couple microseconds of housekeeping and then we’re live! In the RTL sim environment, I had some interesting hooks. One of my application areas was a set of benchmarks used to measure the performance of the memory system while the processor was still being designed. I needed some way to get the measurements out of the simulation. I ended up writing some TCL code that ran in the simulator’s external programming interface that set a simulation breakpoint on writes to a certain CPU register. The TCL script would take over and ferry data out to disk—essentially a virtual parallel port implemented in TCL. And on the CPU side, I wrote a library to serialize the data structures of interest and feed them out through this interface. On the other side, a Perl script decoded the information into a nice nested hash. Altogether, four languages were involved: C++, assembly, TCL, and Perl. Now, with the embedded Doom port, I did have a small runtime environment I didn't write myself. My coworker had designed the video card that plugged onto the mezzanine connector, and he and another engineer had programmed up the DMAs and whatnot to form the video driver. That may in fact have run on DSP-BIOS. My Doom port made use of the provided frame buffer driver, but otherwise didn't use any of the other facilities provided. My goal was to keep it as self contained as possible, right down to linking the WAD file into the executable and modifying the zone allocator to directly reference the assets in the linked-in image. For everything else, though, I controlled just about everything from when reset deasserted onwards. It’s a lot of low level work that requires digging into documentation and data sheets that most developers may never see in their entire careers. And, as far as I am concerned, it can be a heckuva lot of fun.

Question: If pi is irrational, then how was its precise sequence of digits found and is still calculated to this day?
Answer: As Balázs Iván József points out in his concise and accurate answer, we don’t know¹ the full sequence of its digits, because: Mathematicians have proven π is irrational multiple different ways that don’t require computing its digit sequence. Why do people still calculate digits of π even today? In some cases, it’s just to test out a large new computer. It’s a popular benchmark that scales to any size computer, and the result can be readily verified. In other cases, it’s due to a deep—and often unwarranted—fascination with its digits. For whatever reason, the digits of π capture a lot of peoples’ imaginations, especially the decimal digits of π . I rarely see anyone go on and on about π ’s digits in any other base. I don’t usually see such fascination with other well known irrationals, such as e or √ 2 . Breathless, inaccurate articles in popular media, combined with and endless drip-feed of math cranks, fuel the fascination further. Some time back, I performed a compression experiment on digits of π , using its binary representation. I started from files containing digits of π in hexadecimal. I received a handful of confused comments, as people aren’t accustomed to seeing π in a base other than decimal. FWIW, I knew ahead of time roughly how the compression experiment would turn out: the “compressed” files would be larger than the original. However, I was a little surprised at how much bzip2 increased the size of the file. Most other compressors just passed the data through in one or more blocks with header(s) saying “this block of data isn’t compressed.” In case you’re wondering, the digits of π in any base don’t lend themselves well to ordinary compression techniques, because they behave like a truly random sequence. They’re not, but the best compression algorithm to compress π is to write a mathematical expression that evaluates to π . Standard lossless compression algorithms aren’t going to do that. In the end, if you use a numeric approximation of π for computations, you probably don’t need more than a handful for real work. Rounding π to 6 fractional digits (3.141593) gives you better than 1 part in a million precision. Rounding π to 12 fractional digits (3.141592653590) gives you better than 1 part in a trillion precision. As my high school teacher pointed out, almost nobody needs more than 20 or so digits realistically, even for navigating the solar system. There are far larger sources of error everywhere else. ¹ I mean “know” in the sense of “having already computed.” We can’t possibly compute the full digit sequence of π because the sequence never terminates nor repeats.² We can directly compute any given digit of π with a spigot algorithm, as Alexey Godin points out in the comments. The digit sequence is fully determined by its definition. Every digit of π is computable in isolation, and therefore in some sense known or at least knowable. It’s possible compute an arbitrarily large, finite number of digits at arbitrary positions within the number on demand. ² In a rational base, at least. π = 10 π after all. I know if I don’t also point that out, someone else is likely to.

Question: Does the Program Counter point to the next instruction to be executed or does it point to the next instruction to be fetched, decoded and executed?
Answer: It depends! It could be both of those or neither of those or some combination of both and neither at the same time. Confused? Read on. On the original x86 architecture, the program counter—aka. Instruction Pointer, IP, EIP, or RIP—isn't directly accessible at all. Branches offer PC-relative displacements, and CALL would push the return address on the stack; however, that's very indirect. x86-64 adds RIP-relative addressing, but that's still “one-way” access. This isn't an accident. If you go all the way back to the 8086 and 8088, you’ll discover that it didn't actually have a dedicated register for the program counter in the implementation. Rather, the bus interface unit (BIU) simply kept the “next fetch address.” That starts out equal to the next instruction address after a control transfer (branch, interrupt, call/return). It then fetches ahead, trying to keep the prefetch queue full. The fetch address doesn't have a fixed relationship to the current instruction address except immediately after a control transfer. If a CALL, relative branch, or interrupt needs the address of the next instruction, the machine would take the program fetch register value and subtract off the number of bytes present in the BIU fetch queue to reconstruct IP. Then it would flush the BIU and set the fetch address to the new target instruction. This worked just fine because the actual value of the program counter doesn't matter at all to most instructions. For features such as PC-relative addressing (RIP-relative in x86-64), what really matters is the reference point used for the address computation. Two common choices are the address of the instruction itself and the address of the first location after it. For function calls, you want the address return to. For interrupts and exceptions, you want the address of the instruction to resume at. Some architectures give you these addresses directly. Others, such as classic ARM, give you an address offset by a fixed amount from what you actually wanted. In many cases, the instruction decode logic can supply the architecturally defined effective PC value to instructions that might need it based on the instruction’s address. That includes PC relative addressing and instructions that might fault. For interrupts, the pipeline might play some tricks to interrupt at a convenient point. The actual address used to fetch an instruction might not be the precise address of the instruction. Modern processors can fetch and decode multiple instructions per cycle. The instruction decoders can reconstruct each instruction’s address, or at least record enough information that it can be reconstructed if/when needed. As long as the machine arranges for those values to get populated with their architecturally defined values when needed, then there need not be an actual physical program counter register anywhere. Since most instructions don't care at all about the program counter address, that gives the machine a lot of leeway. The hardware just needs to fill in the value the PC would have had architecturally for the subset of instructions that need it. Now, old school machines were much simpler. Your question makes more sense for a mainstream microprocessor from 35+ years ago than today's mainstream microprocessors. Let's set the Wayback Machine to the mid-1970s for a moment. On the CP-1600, R7 held the program counter. If you use it in arithmetic, you generally see the address of the first location after the instruction. That may or may not be the next instruction executed. For example, consider: After the MOV, register R0 holds the address of the NOP. The NOP gets executed just after the MOV. In contrast, consider: That instruction will add 42 to the program counter, jumping over the next 42 words of program store. The NOP after it won't be executed next. I believe the PDP-11 works similarly, except that the PDP-11 is byte addressable rather than word addressable. Now let's return to the present. In modern superscalar out-of-order processors, the “next instruction” is a much more complicated concept. Architecturally, you define what the effective program counter value is for each instruction when it executes. You also define the sequence instructions appear to execute. Under the hood, there isn't necessarily a fixed concrete notion of “current program counter,” except maybe at the commit stage of the pipeline. If instructions commit in-order, then the commit stage can say “we’ve committed up through the instruction at address X.” But that's about as far as it goes. As for where the machine is fetching, decoding, and executing? Modern machines can have hundreds of instructions in various stages of execution, most of which are speculative, and many of which will be discarded. It may be fetching from one or more speculative execution paths, well ahead of whatever architectural state that's been committed. In the end, all that matters is that the implementation makes the “right” PC value visible when necessary, based on what the architecture defines. That definition varies, sometimes widely, between different instruction set architectures.

Question: What do you mean by fixed overhead?
Answer: I think it might be best to start with an example. Suppose you want to drive somewhere in your car. For this example, travel time is the only cost I am considering. Most of the time taken for your drive is a function of the distance to the destination, how fast you drive, and traffic conditions. Some of the time associated with a particular trip will depend on more esoteric details of that specific trip. Maybe you need to… Those, along with traffic conditions, are all variable costs. They vary with the details of a specific trip. No matter where you drive to, however, the baseline amount of time it takes to get up off the couch and into the car doesn't really change. If all you need to do is stand up, walk out the door, and hop in the car, there's no other variable cost adding to the travel time. That's a fixed baseline cost. Let's say the straight-line distance to the destination divided by your ideal driving speed represents the fundamental cost of getting to your destination. Every other detail that slows you down from that ideal is an overhead—cost incurred beyond the fundamental cost. That fixed cost in #4 is a fixed overhead that applies to every trip. You can think of the cost in #1 as a sort of fixed overhead as well. For any given pair of starting and ending points A and B, the distance traveled along the most efficient route in the road network will be greater than or equal to the straight-line distance. That additional distance is a fixed overhead for any trip from that particular A to that particular B. You can apply this thought process to a wide variety of situations. For example, the ATM across the street charges $3 per withdrawal, regardless of how much you're withdrawing. That's a fixed overhead. When you do homework for class, you typically need to put your name and other boilerplate details at the top of the page. Those take about the same amount of space and time every time. That identifying information is a fixed overhead. How about another detailed example? This one is a programming example, but it's simple enough that I hope it's mostly understandable for non-programmers as well. Suppose I write some code to sum the contents of an array: This function performs one addition for each element. The fundamental cost of this operation is directly determined by the number of elements and the cost of adding each element to the sum. The ratio between the actual running time and the fundamental running time should asymptotically approach a constant. As the size of the input grows, the running time is roughly proportional to the size of the input. The constant might be larger than 1. If so, you have an overhead per-element that scales with the size of the input. Fixed costs are the reason the run time approaches a constant factor asymptotically. The function call itself has a small cost. Initializing sum has a small cost. Setting up the loop—including testing whether array is empty—has a small cost. These costs don't vary with the size of the input.* They represent fixed overheads that you pay every time you call the function, regardless of the size of the input. [*Depending on the language and how the code’s written, setting up the argument to a function like this might depend on the length of the input. In this Python example, that shouldn't be the case if you're passing an existing array object.] As you’ve probably guessed, the term “fixed” has some context dependence. In the Python example above, I primarily considered the function as a whole. However, I also mentioned that the ratio of actual execution time to ideal should approach some constant asymptotically. If that constant is larger than 1, then you have a per-element overhead. Some of that per-element overhead is a fixed per-element overhead. Possible sources of per-element cost: The first two bullets here are typically fixed per-element costs. The third is not, although it might look fairly constant when amortized across many, many elements. Memory allocation and garbage collection costs tend to have occasional large spikes. Fixed per-operation overheads are sometimes also referred to as “fixed overheads” at the next level out. In those situations, the overhead isn't specified as a fixed quantity; rather, it's expressed as a rate. “Feature X adds a fixed 20% overhead to the running time.” Obviously, the overhead is proportional to the overall amount of work. But, it's fixed overhead per unit of work. Hopefully these examples make sense. I tried to cover fixed overheads as a generic concept. If you have a specific context in mind, that context may have specific definitions of what constitutes fixed vs. variable overheads. If you understand the general approach, theb you should be in good shape to identify which costs in a particular scenario are fundamental vs. overhead, and which overhead costs are fixed vs. variable.

Question: What exactly is the difference between a trace cache and a micro-operation cache? Doesn’t the P4 trace cache also store micro-operations?
Answer: Overview A typical µop cache simply caches decoded µops. That saves energy by grabbing the decoded µops from the µop cache, rather than re-fetching from L1I and re-decoding. Depending on the microarchitecture, the machine may be able to fetch more µops in parallel per cycle from the µop cache than what it can decode per cycle directly from L1I. The Pentium 4 trace cache does cache µops, but it is not a typical µop cache. The trace cache actually stores µop sequences. The entries in the trace cache represent a sequence of operations along the predicted path of execution. A trace may contain µops from instructions that didn’t appear sequentially in the original code. Each trace is indexed by its single entry point. A trace can contain multiple branches that can exit the trace early if the branch was mispredicted. Additionally, the P4 doesn’t have an L1I instruction cache. Rather, the trace cache completely replaces the L1I instruction cache. The P4 trace cache is large—about 80K to 96K bytes depending on model—but I recall reading back in the day that it performs similarly to a 16K byte L1I cache in terms of hit rate. Indexing A typical µop cache is indexed by instruction addresses, with each instruction usually appearing at most once in the µop cache. For example, in Sandy Bridge, each line of the µop cache is associated with a specific aligned, contiguous 32-byte segment of code. A given 32-byte segment of code can occupy up to 3 µop cache lines, as long as it fits. As mentioned above, the Pentium 4 trace cache indexes traces by their entry point. It may cache a given instruction’s micro-ops in multiple different traces, if that instruction can be reached by more than once execution path. Back in the day, I recall reading that the P4 can even unroll some small loops in the trace cache. If so, that implies the same instruction’s µops can appear more than once in the same trace. What that means: If I give you an instruction address, you could quickly determine whether that instruction resides in a typical µop cache by looking up the address. In P4’s trace cache, you can only easily do that with instructions that represent the start of a trace. Performance In both example microarchitectures—Sandy Bridge and P4—the µop/trace cache can improve the overall µop issue rate. On Sandy Bridge, if a 32-byte segment of code fits in a single µop cache line, its µop cache can deliver the equivalent of 32 bytes of code into the pipeline every cycle. In contrast, Sandy Bridge can only decode 16 bytes of instructions from the L1I per cycle. The P4 trace cache runs at half the clock rate, and can deliver a peak of 6 µops every 2 cycles, or 3 µops/cycle on average. The P4’s decoder can decode at most 1 instruction per cycle from L2, however. Most instructions require 1 to 4 µops. For instruction sequences that average fewer than 3 µops per instruction, the trace cache can deliver µops to the pipeline more quickly than the instruction decoder can. In modern high-core-count SMP systems, the trace cache has an additional intrinsic bottleneck that the more typical µop cache + L1I won’t have: instruction cache invalidation. Any sort of dynamic code generator such as a JIT compiler needs to ensure any instructions it writes get invalidated from instruction caches in all cores that might have it cached. That’s much easier to accomplish efficiently in the more traditional structure than it is in P4’s trace cache, since everything is indexed by address. This bottleneck wasn’t a factor when the trace cache debuted, but would be a noticeable burden in modern systems. In fact, this bottleneck is why ARM started making L1I caches inclusive in L2 in their Neoverse cores. Summary and Add’l Thoughts The P4 goes beyond most typical µop caches by caching µop sequences that cross branch boundaries. It captures decoded µops and sequencing information in its traces. A typical µop cache is simpler, capturing only the decoded µops. Both reduce fetch/decode power, and both can improve performance by increasing the µop issue rate. The P4 trace cache needs more overall space to get the same efficiency as a more typical µop cache + L1I combination. The same instruction can appear multiple times in the trace cache, and the trace cache completely replaces the L1I cache. In the example above, I compared P4 against Sandy Bridge, because I have pretty decent information on both thanks to Agner Fog’s microarchitecture document (linked below). The µop caches in Ivy Bridge, Haswell, Broadwell, Skylake, Ice Lake, Tiger Lake and their offshoots are all fairly similar to Sandy Bridge. I looked briefly at Agner’s descriptions of Zen 1 through Zen 4, and it wasn’t as complete as it was for Sandy Bridge. I didn’t dig deeply into the other microarchitectures in Agner’s doc, but I invite you to have a look if you’re curious. You can read more of what he’s written here:

Question: What happen if cache hit greater than cache miss?
Answer: That's the usual case, at least for L1 processor caches. As Jerry Coffin points out in the comments, L1s often have a hit rate >90%. There's nothing magical about a cache hit rate of 50%. The crossover point for where a cache improves performance may be above or below that threshold. Consider the following simple abstract model: Now, those of you who know cache design know this model is greatly simplified. That said, it's a good starting point. The average cost of a cached access is given by: C c a c h e = P h i t C h i t + ( 1 − P h i t ) C m i s s = P h i t C o v h d + ( 1 − P h i t ) ( C o v h d + C b a s e ) = C o v h d + ( 1 − P h i t ) C b a s e The cache reduces the cost of an access when: C b a s e > C o v h d + ( 1 − P h i t ) C b a s e Doing some algebra, we can that's true when: P h i t > C o v h d C b a s e The costs above could be cycles or nanoseconds or some other relevant metric. How about an example? Suppose the base cost is 100 units, and the overhead is 10 units. In that case, a cache hit costs 10 units and a cache miss costs 110 units. This cache will reduce costs when the hit rate P h i t > 0.1. That's a 10% hit rate. Different base and overhead costs will give different crossover points. The model above is a very simple model, but it can help you gain a quick estimate of potential performance improvement due to a cache. It's a useful starting point for building some intuition.

Question: Why is the assembly language dependent on a specific machine or computer?
Answer: Assembly language isn't one language. The exact assembly language details usually do not depend on the exact individual computer you're using. It's not as if each individual computer comes with its own unique assembly language, like a fingerprint. I mention that only because your question could be read that way. The details do depend on: For example, the 8086, 80286, 80386, 80486, Pentium, etc. are members of the x86 instruction set architecture family. Later family members introduced extensions to the architecture. The original 8086 is a 16-bit architecture. The 80386 added a 32-bit superset architecture sub-family. AMD™ introduced AMD64, a 64-bit superset that Intel® adapted into highly compatible Intel® 64. Assembly language meant for the 64-bit variant differs from the assembly language for the 32-bit variant. Both differ from the 16-bit variant. The later versions of x86 are (mostly) supersets of the earlier versions: And on top of that there's various extensions such as x87, MMX, multiple generations of SSE, multiple generations of AVX, etc. And that's just one instruction set architecture family. There are many, many others. I’ve personally programmed assembly code for TMS9900, 6502, 8085, 8086, 6805, 8051, TMS320C6000, CP1600, PIC24H, ARMv7, AArch64, and RISC-V (RV64G). I’m certain I have written at least a little code for some other instruction set architectures. Each of those is mutually incompatible with the others. Then there's the assembler tooling. For example, x86 has two major syntax variations: Individual assemblers provide variations on syntax and functionality beyond that, such as different directives and so on.

Question: How can you dynamically allocate memory for an array in C++ and what is the significance of the `delete [] ` operator when using dynamic arrays?
Answer: The delete[] operator pairs with new[]. Why? Because new[] makes a note of the number of elements in the array, and delete[] needs that information. Why? Because constructors and destructors (plural!), that's why. In modern code, I expect to see neither of those very often, if at all. My wish is that their existence fades way as obscure trivia. The 90s were fun, but they ended 24 years ago. I reach for std::vector by default when I need a dynamically allocated array. I might choose std::array if the size is known at compile time. In very specific circumstances, std::unique_ptr<T[]> / std::make_unique<T[]> can be useful; however, I have only seen a compelling use for it once, maybe twice.¹ And if you're using it to hold string data… My dear boy, have you considered using std::string?² Third party libraries offer more finely tuned options for flat arrays. Both the C++ standard library and third party libraries offer fancier containers. And once you're skilled with the language, you’ll have a better understanding of the tradeoffs and nuances. Most of the time, though, good ol’ std::vector is pretty solid for many uses. And old-school new[] and delete[]? Buh bye! ¹ Addendum As Kurt Guntheroth points out in the comments, std::make_unique<T[]> / std::unique_ptr<T[]> does give you the nice ownership management that you get from std::vector and lightweight array access you expect from std::array. It isn't a C++ container, however, and so it lacks certain niceties such as being able to ask its size(). It doesn't provide begin()/end() (and their cousins), so it's not as convenient to use with standard algorithms. Like std::array, it constructs all of its elements up front, and tears them all down at the end. Where I have personally seen them used effectively was as bulk storage. One use case I recall involved holding a firmware image blob that we wanted to extract string table data from. Another use-case mentioned in the comments involved a large frame buffer. In both of those cases, neither the initialization nor destruction have meaningful overhead. You can wrap a std::unique_ptr<T[]> in a class that exposes a container-like interface fairly easily. In fact, you could even use std::span in C++20 for that purpose, as long as the std::span’s lifetime is shorter than the std::unique_ptr<T[]>. The span won't manage ownership, as that's the smart pointer’s job. You could put both in the same class, so that their lifetimes are tied together: That does waste a pointer's worth of storage, however, inside std::span. You could slim it down like so: I’d prefer the latter, as constructing the span on the fly is cheap. If you want to get fancier, you could even add begin()/end()/size()/etc. directly to your class, along with the various type aliases expected of a container. Also, if T is a type such as int or std::byte, you might consider using C++20’s std::make_unique_for_overwrite if you don't need value initialization. In both of the examples I gave above (firmware image, frame buffer), the array immediately gets filled after allocation. std::make_unique<std::byte[]> would fill the array with zeros which then immediately get overwritten. Those examples don't benefit from the zero-fill. std::make_unique_for_overwrite<std::byte[]> will just leave the array filled with indeterminate values, saving that unnecessary overhead. ² Channeling Sir Laurence Olivier's comment to Dustin Hoffman on acting.
