Question: What is the difference between address space and memory location?
Answer: The difference between a memory address and a memory location is the same as the difference between a phone number and a phone. An address space is a coherent collection of related addresses which may or may not refer to memory locations. Addresses need not be purely numeric. For example, my mailing address has numeric and non-numeric components. The same is true for my driver’s license number. That’s right: My driver’s license number is a form of address. So’s my car’s license plate. Addressing and address spaces aren’t strictly computing topics. They’re a more general concept that computing makes use of. For example, driver’s license numbers, license plates, Social Security numbers, phone numbers, and mailing addresses are all typically distinct addressing spaces. Example: Phone Numbers For example, the 214 area code in the US that historically covered the Dallas, TX region.* You could call that a phone-number space which, if there were no other restrictions, could have 10 million phone numbers, from 214–000–0000 to 214–999–9999. (*Nowadays, phone numbers are less geographically constrained.) Many of those phone numbers are assigned to phones. Some don’t go anywhere. Some are assigned to other kinds of equipment, such as modems, FAXes, PBXes, and automated services. More than one phone number in that space may go to the same device. Computers: Physical Memory Address Spaces And so it is with physical memory address spaces. You might have RAM, ROM, peripherals, and whatnot allocated in that address space. There might be regions of that address space that nothing is assigned to. There might also be regions of address space that alias each other, so that multiple different addresses go to the same memory location. For example, on a 48K Apple ][+, physical memory addresses 0x0000 - 0xBFFF go to RAM, 0xC000 - 0xCFFF are assigned to various peripherals and internal controls, and 0xD000 - 0xFFFF are for ROM. On a 32K Apple ][+, the physical memory address space is similar, except that there’s nothing in the range 0x8000 - 0xBFFF. Computers: Virtual Memory Address Spaces Virtual memory address space is another kettle of fish. On a modern machine with MMUs and hardware address translation, each process in the system gets a private, virtual address space. The operating system sets up translations between the addresses your program uses—virtual memory addresses—and some portion of the physical memory address space. The operating system doesn’t usually expose the entire physical memory address space to your program. If a program accesses a virtual address within its virtual address space that doesn’t have a valid mapping, the program takes an address translation fault. Now this is the fun part. Modern virtual memory OSes keep two sets of books: they track the virtual memory address space they’ve promised to each process, as well as the actual virtual memory address space that’s available to the process at any given time. The OS might promise a range of virtual memory addresses to a process, but not actually map them. On an address translation fault, the OS has to scramble to make good on its promise—or, if it fails, terminate the process. That could involve swapping pages to and from disk, but it doesn’t have to. It could just mean the OS has to pony up a page full of zeros that you can write to, for example. Once the OS has patched things up, it can resume the faulting process. Virtual memory allows all sorts of interesting tricks. For example, the OS might map the same physical pages for a shared library into multiple process’ virtual address spaces, possibly at different virtual addresses! Computers: Other Kinds of Address Space Anywhere you have a coherent collection of addresses that identify items within an identifiable space, you have an address space. The phone number example I mentioned earlier really is an example of an address space. Within a computer, you’re usually interested in the memory address space. You could have other kinds of addresses, though. Even if you limit yourself to “addresses used directly by instructions,” you still can end up with multiple disjoint address spaces. On x86 processors, there’s an I/O address space that’s separate from the memory address space. It requires special instructions (IN, OUT, and friends) to access. On strict Harvard architecture computers, the instruction address space is orthogonal to the data address space. On ARM processors with TrustZone™, the Secure World address space is theoretically* orthogonal to the Normal World address space. (*Secure/Normal is treated as a physical address bit in cache tags. The intention is that the two worlds are completely isolated in the physical address map. However, many real-world systems will map non-cacheable registers into both Secure and Normal worlds at the same physical memory address.) Each of the different register sets that the processor can see constitutes an address space. That’s true for general purpose registers, control registers (sometimes called CSRs and MSRs), and so on. Depending on the processor and the address space, that address space might be exclusive to fields in the instruction word, or require specialized instructions to make use of. If you don’t limit yourself to addresses used directly by instructions, you now get into other kinds of address spaces. PCI and PCIe have a very non-flat Bus/Device/Function addressing scheme separate of how it might memory map portions of peripherals into the physical memory address space. Hard drives and SSDs have various block addressing schemes for their media. USB, network cards, etc. also have their own addressing schemes. Nested and Overlapping Address Spaces One address space might be a subset of another. For example, I live in an apartment. My mailing address is a member of multiple address spaces: These don’t necessarily perfectly nest. For instance, a city might overlap more than one county, with no county circumscribed entirely by the city. Houston overlaps Harris, Fort Bend, and Montgomery counties, but none of those three counties is contained entirely within Houston. When I lived in Farmer’s Branch, TX, I had a primarily-Dallas ZIP code. And so it is with computers as well. Consider that 48K Apple ][ example above. The early 48K Apple ][ systems had three banks of 16K DRAMs. Addresses 0x0000 - 0x3FFF went to the first bank, 0x4000 - 0x7FFF went to the second bank, and 0x8000 - 0xBFFF went to the third bank. Address 0x1234 is part of the overall physical memory address space as well as the first DRAM bank’s physical memory address space. The default address space for BASIC programs and variables overlaps all three memory banks, but the lower part of the first DRAM bank (0x0000 - 0x07FF) and upper part of the last DRAM bank (0x9600 - 0xBFFF) is outside of that address space. And, I mentioned 0xC000 - 0xCFFF is dedicated as an I/O address space. But, as you can imagine, it doesn’t stop there. You can break that down into a number of smaller address spaces: That’s around 20 to 30 distinct address spaces, depending on how you count, all within the “I/O address space.” Summary Got all that? A declaration introduces a name into a namespace, and tells the compiler that something exists, and what that something “looks like.” For example, the declarations for std::cin and std::cout may be resemble the following: This is from “Header <iostream> synopsis” here: https://eel.is/c++draft/iostream.syn When you declare objects and functions, that just tells the compiler to assume they exist, possibly somewhere else. A definition usually also acts as a declaration. (I can only think of one corner case offhand where it doesn’t, and it’s rather obscure.) If it does, then the header holds the complete definition. Otherwise, it just holds the declaration. For a variety of reasons, templates are often defined in headers as opposed to merely declared. By default, it assumes it needs to instantiate it. However, you can declare to the compiler that an instantiation lives elsewhere, with something like: Therefore, it’s possible that std::endl is declared and defined in <ostream>, but instantiated in the C++ standard library, at least for commonly used streams such as std::ostream. Or, if std::endl’s definition is small, the library implementor may have decided to let it be instantiated inline in your program. So where does namespace fit in? Namespaces aren’t tied to headers. Namespaces provide a way to organize identifiers for data types, classes, functions, objects, and so on into groups of names that share a common prefix. By default, any names you declare at file level go into the so-called global namespace. These names can be used without any prefix most of the time. In some cases, you might need a :: prefix if there’s a name conflict. You can wrap a set of declarations at this level in a namespace definition, such as: That declares the global variables x, foo::x and bar::x. Namespaces provide a way to organize larger programs so that names don’t conflict. In this example, I’ve declared three variables named x. They don’t conflict, because they’re in different namespaces. The C++ standard library puts most of its names in namespace std. For example, the C++ standard library declares the names cin, cout, and endl within namespace std. Thus, their full names are std::cin, std::cout, and std::endl. That means you could declare your own classes, variables, and functions with the names cin, cout, and endl if you like, and they won’t conflict with std::cin, std::cout, and std::endl.* You can read more about namespaces here: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/namespace *Unless you have something like using namespace std in your program. Question: What is the difficulty of learning C++? Is it easy to master it already knowing computer architecture and assembler?
Answer: Knowing computer architecture and assembler is as relevant to learning C++ as knowing the structure of an automobile and the physics of driving are to piloting an F1 race car. They can help you optimize so that you can reach higher performance plateaus once you know how to drive well, but they don’t get you off the starting line. Perhaps the biggest hurdle it might get you past in the short run is pointers, and their C++ cousin iterators. If you’re already comfortable with memory addressing and bulk memory as a big array of bytes, that’s useful. However, that’s mostly useful for low-level C++ code, much of which should be written, debugged, and placed in a library. It shouldn’t be the bulk of your code. C++ is a large language with many high level features. Neither computer architecture nor assembly language programming will teach you about the higher level concepts you need to use C++ effectively. For example, if I wanted to count how many times each whitespace separated word appears in a file provided on stdin, I could write something like: I don’t really see where my considerable knowledge of computer architecture or assembly helped me write that. But, if a piece of code like this became a performance bottleneck, then that knowledge might give me hints at possible reasons why. Knowledge of data structures and algorithms would also be rather useful in that situation. Now suppose I wanted to generalize the histogram code so that it could take a histogram of any input type, given a pair of iterators. Then I could call it like so in my original application: But I could also call it on a std::vector<int>: That’s just a quick example off the top of my head that still barely scratches the tip of the iceberg. And again, my knowledge of computer architecture and assembly didn’t come into play here. I can hear some folks at the back complaining that I started too far up a tower of abstractions, and then climbed higher. OK, fine. How about a beginner C++ problem such as finding the minimum and maximum integer values provided by the user on stdin, without using standard library algorithms? As a bonus, we won’t require input validation. There’s still a lot going on there that computer architecture and assembly language won’t prepare you for. Granted, I wrote that in a way most beginning students wouldn’t. I’ve been programming C++ long enough that I’m not sure I could write it as s beginner would. At least not easily. It also doesn’t help that most such assignments ask you to read the elements into an array and then scan the array, which honestly hurts my brain. While I did touch on templates, iterators, and a wee bit of generic programming above, I didn’t get anywhere near object oriented programming, classes and inheritance, dynamic memory allocation, ownership, etc. And then there’s the next level out, such as separate compilation, modularity, what does and doesn’t belong in a header, and so on. And even then we’re still traipsing around the tip of the iceberg, maybe dragging a toe in the water around it occasionally. Bjarne Stroustrup has said a design goal for C++ is to “Leave no room for a language below (except assembler).” When it comes time to write really low-level code that squeezes to most out of the machine, C++ lets you do that most of the time. That is where your knowledge of computer architecture and assembly language will become useful. Most C++ code shouldn’t be written at that level. Most C++ code should be written at a much higher level. C++’s standard library provides many useful abstractions to get you started. The language and its standard library also provide you many facilities for building abstractions of your own. The bulk of your application should rest on those high-level abstractions. C++ lets you dive to low-level code when needed, so that you can build efficient higher-level abstractions—if those abstractions don’t already exist. That really speaks to the crux of the issue. Having a solid command of computer architecture and assembly will help you take your C++ game to a higher level, once your C++ game is already strong. It won’t really help you understand how to climb the tower of abstractions C++’s standard library already offers, nor will it help you understand how to build high-level abstractions of your own. It won’t really help you understand how to build applications on those abstractions either. There is another place those skills might help: diagnosing and fixing bugs due to leaky abstractions. Abstractions hide low level details. But, that doesn’t mean they always do so successfully. When an abstraction fails to hide a low-level detail, we say that abstraction has leaked. For more details, I recommend reading Joel Spolsky’s The Law of Leaky Abstractions. Link: https://www.joelonsoftware.com/2002/11/11/the-law-of-leaky-abstractions/ And to be honest, as much as most of my answer above downplays it, there really is a lot of value there as well. Some of C++’s abstractions leak perhaps more than one would like. Heck, even some of the basic data types, common to C++ and several other languages, are leaky abstractions. You may have encountered that when programming assembly language. See: Welcome to C++! In case you’re wondering, I do love C++ in spite of its many quirks and flaws.

Question: Why is the triangle called a turtle on the logo computer program?
Answer: Seymour Papert added support to Logo drive a little robot that vaguely resembled a turtle. With Logo’s educational focus on young children, Papert felt the visceral aspect of making something move in the real world was important to the learning process. He wanted to enable what he called body-syntonic reasoning—reasoning about the robot’s motions by imagining oneself to be the robot, and using that intuition to understand and write programs that control it. Unfortunately, robots take up a lot of space, and are costly compared to computer graphics, especially nowadays. It wasn't long before the physical turtle—an invention of the late 70s/early 80s—became a small sprite on the screen.

It’s their space, their rules. It’s no different from comments: I can choose to delete any comments I like on an answer I write. I can choose to block whomever I like. These days, Quora’s focus is on increasing engagement, and turning that engagement in dollars. They need to make money to keep the lights on. Question: How do I use Gauss' Eatser algorithm in reverse? In our math class, we have a bonus homework question to calculate the year of easter given the date. Is this possible?
Answer: Yes, in a way. You need some additional constraints. The date of Easter varies over a 35 day range. That means any year range larger than 35 days will have at least one repeated date. You need to narrow the range of years under consideration to make the date unique, or allow for more than one correct year over a larger range of years. You also need to establish which church’s calendar you’re adhering to. The Eastern Orthodox church uses the Julian calendar, while Catholic and Protestant churches use the Gregorian calendar. AIUI, Gauss’ algorithm provides ways to calculate both. From Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_dates_for_Easter Can you run Gauss’ algorithm in reverse? Possibly. I looked at it only briefly, and it didn’t look exactly straightforward. The same is probably true for any other algorithm you might use to compute the date of Easter given the year. My instinct was to just brute-force it. If you’re using a computer for this, you could just run whatever algorithm you choose forward for the range of years under consideration, and compare dates. Otherwise, if you’re working this by hand, I would first work out the nearest year for which the given date is a Sunday. That should be a bit easier, given that you only need to account for leap years. That give you your first candidate year. Your other candidate years are typically steps of 5, 6, or 11 years away from that (depending on leap years).* Even if you’re asked to consider a 100 year range, that’s only a handful candidates to test against Gauss’ algorithm or any other algorithm you might use to determine Easter’s date for a given year. You might get multiple hits, though. If you’re asked to give the most recent year that held Easter on that date, then you’re probably only checking a few years. Yes, it’s “guess-and-check,” but it doesn’t require very many guesses IMHO. Good luck! *Corrected a brainfart here. I previously said multiples of 7. See conversation in the comments.

Question: Why was UNIX designed such that a parent process cannot directly call exec() without first having to call fork() and thereby copying (or using COW semantics for) all of the parent’s data structures which are seldom used by the child process anyway?
Answer: Who says you can’t directly call exec() without calling fork() first? Sure, it will replace the current process with the new process, but sometimes that’s exactly what you want. It happens often enough that the Bourne shell includes an exec command which does exactly that. That feature allows you to write programs that are wrappers around other programs. These wrappers can configure and/or edit the environment before exec’ing the target, such as: For example, suppose I have some fiddly proprietary software, let’s call it CrankySoft™, that requires its utility binaries to be in the $PATH. But, I have two versions of CrankySoft™ installed, one for legacy projects and one for new projects, and both have identically named utility binaries. Even worse, both also need to dynamically load shared libraries specific to the CrankySoft™ version that are also identically named. I can make wrapper shell scripts cranky-1.0 and cranky-2.0 to handle this. Perhaps something like this would do for cranky-1.0: And the script for cranky-2.0 might look similar, with v1.0 changed to v2.0 in the paths. Lest you think I’m making this scenario up out of whole cloth, I’ve had this sort of thing come up many times in my career. The exec statement at the end of the script calls exec() directly without fork(), replacing the shell interpreting the script with the executable. There’s no reason to keep the shell interpreter around once we’ve launched CrankySoft™. The wrapper might also be written in C, C++, or other language. They’ll rely on POSIX C APIs for this—or the system calls behind them—so I’ll focus on C. I’ve written security wrappers in C that wipe out all but the most essential UNIX™ environment variables, strip nearly all command line arguments, close all file descriptors, and then connect stdin/stdout/stderr to /dev/null or other explicit location before calling exec() on a security-sensitive executable. From C code, you can make all the environment modifications I mentioned above, as well as a few more,* such as: The UNIX™ nohup command is an example of that first bullet: It masks SIGHUP before exec()’ing the target program. The nice, chrt, and taskset commands are examples of the second bullet. I believe taskset is Linux-specific. The su and chgrp commands change user/group ID before exec()’ing a target command or shell. The chroot command uses the chroot() API to change the effective root directory before exec()’ing the target. (*It’s possible some shells can do some or all of these as well.) You might be thinking “OK, so? That still doesn’t answer why I should fork() then exec() for more typical applications.” Well, it kinda does, at least for one set of use cases. Often, you’ll want to redirect some combination of stdin, stdout, and stderr before launching a particular program. You might want to open or close other file descriptors*. You might also want to tweak an environment variable or three without duplicating the whole environment to use with execve(). You might want to setuid()/setgid() to a different user, particularly if you’re a daemon like sshd or httpd. (*Yes, I’m aware of close-on-exec, but that’s a recent flag in the history of UNIX™. It was added to POSIX in 2008.) And, of course, you can call fork() without calling exec(). The parent and child processes get separate virtual address spaces. But, they still share file descriptors, and so they can still communicate with each other. When fork() and exec() are separate steps, you can perform arbitrary amounts of work in the child before calling exec() without affecting the parent. That also lets you do other interesting things, such as setting up process and thread pools. Now let me preface this next example with the caveat that I haven’t dug into webserver technology and configuration in many years. The example may be out of date—I don’t know if it is!—but that doesn’t invalidate it. Some webservers such as Apache let you set up a worker pool, potentially with multiple child processes to manage all the workers. Apache can pre-fork() multiple child processes. Each child process manages some number of worker threads each. The parent process holds onto root permissions so it can bind ports 80 and 443, while dropping permissions in the child processes. The child processes each manage some number of worker threads. The child processes handle restarting worker threads if any worker dies. And the parent process can handle restarting a child process if any child dies. And, child processes can voluntarily terminate after some number of requests as a hedge against memory leaks and heap fragmentation. That encapsulation makes the webserver more robust against bugs in the server itself, as well as transient issues such as a brief out-of-memory situation that causes one of the workers to crash. OOM is less a big deal today, but it was a much bigger deal back in the day. And, back in the day, Common Gateway Interface (CGI) was all the rage. CGI gives you a way to invoke an external program to satisfy a request for a particular URL. The webserver heavily curates the environment seen by that program—like the wrapper example above—and passes details of the request on stdin. The CGI program then outputs the content to send to the client on stdout. Again, this is a case where the parent thread/process needs to curate the view of the world for the child after fork(), but before calling exec(). In Apache’s case, it could even launch a separate process to handle CGI requests, so that a fork() wouldn’t require cloning a bunch of worker threads. The CGI daemon communicates with the other worker threads through a socket. You also mentioned the cost of copying the parent and/or using COW. Copying the parent is indeed expensive! That’s what lead to the invention of vfork(). vfork() doesn’t split the child process’ virtual address space from the parent. Rather, it trusts that the only thing you’re going to do after vfork() is call exec() or _exit() (presumably when exec() fails). For the extremely common case of calling fork() and then immediately calling exec(), vfork() can speed things up on systems that actually need to copy some or all of the parent process context on a fork(). But, vfork() is a fragile hack. Thankfully, COW is now the norm, and modern OSes have optimized fork() quite a bit. For programs that call fork() followed immediately by exec(), very few writable data pages will get COW’d in the child. The main remaining cost involves copying the page tables for the child. If the OS can manage to COW those, that should reduce the cost of fork() in a process with a larger virtual address space. For some reason, I thought Linux already did this; however, I might just be remembering discussions from many years ago that don’t actually represent what Linux implements. This LWN link shows that the idea was under active discussion a year and a half ago: Link: https://lwn.net/ml/linux-kernel/20220519183127.3909598-1-shiyn.lin@gmail.com/ From one of the messages in the thread: The paper mentioned a list of benchmarks of the time cost for On-Demand fork. For example, on Redis, the meantime of fork when taking the snapshot. Default fork() got 7.40 ms; On-demand Fork (COW PTE table) got 0.12 ms. So, yes, there are still some optimizations we can perform. Circling back around to why: The UNIX™ philosophy is to provide many sharply focused tools that are effective at what they do, and can be composed with each other easily to create higher-order operations. fork() and exec() are no exceptions here. Hopefully my examples above show how that separation can be beneficial.

Question: How I can create a 4-bit adder/subtractor circuit? Using 74151 and 7483
Answer: The 7483 is already a 4-bit adder, with carry-in and carry-out. You can perform subtraction with an adder by negating—that is, taking the 2’s complement of—one of the inputs. That works because A - B = A + (-B). The 74151 is an 8-to-1 multiplexor. This isn’t really what I would reach for, as it’s not really what you need. It can be made to work, but you’ll need four of them. What you really want is a quad-XOR, such as the 7486. Good luck on your homework!

Question: Why is SYS_Write call 2x times slower than putchar when printing one character to stdout?
Answer: Only 2×? I would have hoped for a larger difference. The stdout output stream is buffered by default. The C standard library will buffer up a bunch of characters to write as a batch. Question: Does having "Smart Pointers" and the Standard Template Library make C++ count as having Garbage Collection, at least for those programs that use those two things exclusively (and not dumb pointers or hand made objects)?
Answer: C++ smart pointers implement reference counting. std::shared_ptr allows arbitrary non-negative reference counts, while std::unique_ptr allows exactly zero or one references. Reference counting is a limited form of garbage collection. It's not fully automatic in C++. You need to explicitly create smart pointers. In the case of std::unique_ptr, you also need to explicitly move pointers. Reference counting doesn't automatically handle cycles. C++ provides std::weak_ptr that allows you to create cycles without increasing the explicit reference count. You need to know exactly where to place them explicitly in your data structures, however. C++’s reference counting is tied to the lifetimes of the smart pointers themselves by default. You could consider that part automatic. Once you choose a smart pointer to manage an object, you're done. The destructor for the smart pointer will take care of things for you unless you explicitly tell the pointer to release the object earlier. Smart pointers track ownership. What ownership really means is “owns the responsibility for calling delete when they're the last to drop a reference to the object.” Normal C++ best practices would have you carefully design your system with clear owners for each object. Smart pointers simplify the implementation. You can still safely pass around non-owning raw pointers and references to objects managed by smart pointers, as long as you're make sure those pointers/references don't live beyond the smart pointer. Since most lifetimes nest, that's usually not too difficult. However, it feels distinctly different from working in a full-GC language. If you instead allocate every object whose address is taken on the heap, manage them all with std::shared_ptr, and use std::shared_ptr everywhere, you now pretty much have Perl 5’s GC model. Of course, you end up losing iterators in the process, as those are essentially pointers as well, either in fact or in spirit. The whole notion of iterator invalidation will quickly remind you you're in C++, not Perl, Java, or C#. Also, iterators cannot extend the life of an object or the container it's in. Now you might have noticed I said “every object whose address is taken” above. Why did I say that? In your question, you excluded “hand made objects.” I’m not really sure what you meant by that. But my guess was automatic, static, and thread-local storage duration objects—essentially anything not on the heap. In C++, you really, really want to keep automatic storage duration objects, beyond just the smart pointers themselves. That is, you really, really don’t want to relocate all automatic storage duration objects to the heap. Why? In C++, this declares an object: It's not an instance of a class, which is probably what you had in mind. It is an object, nonetheless. Its address can be taken just as easily as an instance of class Foo. All the same ownership issues still apply. You really don't want to make all your loop counters live on the heap, managed by std::shared_ptr<int>. The vast majority of your local variables should remain as such. For the most part, you only need smart pointers and heap allocation for objects whose address escapes the scope in which they are declared. That's the scope that would otherwise have determined the object’s lifetime. For automatic variables, it's the enclosing block. For class members, it's the lifetime of instances of the class itself. Reread that last line. If you pass a pointer or reference to a class data member outside the class, you might need to replace that member with a std::shared_ptr to a heap-allocated instance instead. This is starting to feel a bit awkward and not very C++ like, isn't it? For static and thread-local storage duration objects, you run into why I said “for the most part” above. Static and thread-local storage duration objects don't need smart pointers to manage their lifetime. Their lifetimes are tied to the process or thread they belong to. But you still might need to convert some of these to smart pointers and heap allocations if that's needed for interface compatibility. That is, if you replace all pointers with std::shared_ptr, then you're pretty much forced into using them anywhere you would have taken an object’s address. The smart pointers have “gone viral” and infected all your interfaces. So, yeah, you could make it work, sorta. You end up with something that feels distinctly non-C++-like. Its performance will suffer noticeably, and I doubt it would be much fun to program. You can get most of the benefits of GC if you follow the best practices I mentioned in the beginning. You still benefit from the reference-counted GC, but you don't add gratuitous overhead to your program. It requires a little more effort than a pure GC language, but it's usually worth it. Question: What is the purpose of keeping sections with a section header table inside an executable ELF file?
Answer: I’m going to read a little bit into this question. I’m going to interpret it as “Why do we have both a program header table and a section header table? That seems redundant.” Hopefully that will give better overall context and answer your question. If it doesn’t, please let me know in the comments. ELF Structure ELF files offer two different views of the executable: one via the program header table and the other via the section header table. Program Header Table (PHT) The program header table (PHT) describes segments of the executable, and where those segments go in memory—if they go in memory at all. This is the view a loader (part of which may be in the OS kernel) will use to load the executable into memory. The PHT is only needed in executable ELF files, such as program binaries and dynamic shared objects (aka. “shared libraries”). Non-executable ELF objects don’t need and likely won’t have a PHT. The PHT view is mostly memory oriented. A typical ELF file is organized into segments that align with the memory layout and attributes of the target system. There are some additional segments that aren’t specifically memory oriented, such as the INTERP segment, which tells the loader what “binary interpreter” to use. Typically, this is a pointer to the dynamic linker, which “interprets” the DYNAMIC segment when resolving dynamic link references. The PHT view is typically coarse grain, with few entries. This is particularly helpful on OSes that demand-page executables, as it gives them less to search through to determine what to load where. Section Header Table (SHT) The section header table (SHT) describes the executable in terms of named sections such as .text and .data. This structure isn't particularly interesting to the loader. On the other hand, linkers, debuggers, and other tooling rely heavily on this view. The SHT view is more semantically oriented. Different categories of segments play different roles, describing facets of the object file. For instance, .text sections hold executable code; .data sections hold data; .symtab sections hold symbol tables; and .debug sections hold debugging metadata. There are often way more sections than segments. For example, there may be separate sections for exception handling tables, string tables, and read-only variables. All of these might get grouped in a single read-only program segment. An ELF file may have numerous empty sections. Various tools may expect these sections exist, even if they hold nothing. These sections exist only as an entry in the SHT. The section count grows dramatically when you compile a program with GCC or Clang and use -ffunction-sections and -fdata-sections. These flags place each function and static-duration variable in its own section! This allows the linker to pull in only exactly what it needs when linking multiple ELF files together. Overall, the SHT view is rather rich and potentially very fine-grained. Why have both? By separating the two views, you reduce the tension between: As mentioned earlier, a given ELF file might not have both. It may only have an SHT, if the ELF object is meant to be linked with other ELF objects to form an executable. Real World Example So that I don’t get accused of using ChatGPT to write this answer,* how about a real world example? (*Yes, I’ve been accused of that, possibly due to length and my use of bulleted lists.) I compiled jzIntv as a shared binary on my x86-64 Linux box. If I use readelf -l on the binary to dump the PHT, I see the following: As you can see, the PHT has 9 segments, one of which is the program header table (PHDR) itself. The program segments overlap somewhat in the file: The first LOAD segment starts at file offset 0, and has length 0x207190. This overlaps the ELF header, PHDR, INTERP, and NOTE segments. The first 0x207190 bytes of the executable file will be brought into memory as a read-execute segment. That makes life more convenient for anything that needs to consult this ELF metadata at run time. The table at the end shows that segment 02 (the first LOAD segment) holds the contents of 17 separate ELF sections, if I counted correctly. The other program segments include read-write and read-only segments. Let’s walk through all of the remaining segments. Now if I dump the SHT with readelf -S, I see a total of 39 sections! Many of these sections are empty. This is a much richer view of the executable. I won’t walk through that long table. Hopefully you can see that it provides a much finer-grain, semantic view of the executable. So how about non-executable objects? I also ran readelf -l and readelf -S on locutus/locutus.o, one of the C++ compiled objects. Unsurprisingly, readelf -l returned: “There are no program headers in this file.” In stark contrast, readelf -S tells me there are 230 ELF sections in this object’s SHT! Because I build jzIntv with -ffunction-sections and -fdata-sections, I end up with a lot of fine-grained sections, as you can see in this excerpt: The (truncated) suffix _ZNSt6vecto is part of a mangled C++ identifier. Sections 200 through 204 all likely correspond to functions and data from a specialization of std::vector, if I had to guess. And sections 205 and 206 are likely data associated with my internal class t_locutus. Hopefully, the summary above makes it clear why we have both the PHT and SHT, and what the SHT actually contains.

Question: How is it possible to reach points higher than 255 in an 8-bit game?
Answer: Three words: Multiple precision arithmetic. You might also hear this called arbitrary precision arithmetic. They're closely related; however I would say arbitrary precision arithmetic includes numbers that vary in length and can get arbitrarily large. Multiple precision arithmetic typically focuses on numbers that are fixed in length. They just happen to be longer than the machine word size. Both use the same techniques to compute values larger than the machine word size. The short version: You use multiple bytes to store the value. When you add or subtract multiple precision numbers, you need to handle carries/borrows from lower bytes to upper bytes. I cover the concept in this answer: Really, it's not fundamentally any different from how you perform arithmetic by hand with carries and borrows. But instead of digits that go 0 to 9, you can think of bytes as digits that go 0 to 255.

Question: How do I invent completely new central processing units that support data types larger than 64 bits?
Answer: I’m going to be charitable and assume you mean numeric data types. String is a data type, for example, and strings longer than 64 bits are quite common. For instance, the processor that rendered this answer for display so that you could read it routinely works with strings—including the string containing this answer—that are much longer than 64 bits. With that out of the way… There isn’t any invention required. You can work with arbitrarily large numeric data types on a 6502 from nearly 50 years ago, not to mention most of the processors that preceded it. Now, perhaps you meant implement native hardware support for numeric data types larger than 64 bits as instructions. Those already exist as well. Any machine with SIMD or vector instructions that natively operates on >64-bit vectors supports the numeric data type “vector of numbers whose total length is larger than 64 bits.” Perhaps you meant implement hardware support for integers and/or floating point numbers that are larger than 64 bits. That’s less common, but still exists. For example, multiple processors have support for 128-bit quadruple-precision floating point. Quoting Wikipedia: IEEE quadruple precision was added to the IBM System/390 G5 in 1998, and is supported in hardware in subsequent z/Architecture processors. The IBM POWER9 CPU (Power ISA 3.0) has native 128-bit hardware support. Native support of IEEE 128-bit floats is defined in PA-RISC 1.0, and in SPARC V8 and V9 architectures (e.g. there are 16 quad-precision registers %q0, %q4, ...), but no SPARC CPU implements quad-precision operations in hardware as of 2004. Non-IEEE extended-precision (128 bits of storage, 1 sign bit, 7 exponent bits, 112 fraction bits, 8 bits unused) was added to the IBM System/370 series (1970s–1980s) and was available on some System/360 models in the 1960s (System/360-85, -195, and others by special request or simulated by OS software). The Siemens 7.700 and 7.500 series mainframes and their successors support the same floating-point formats and instructions as the IBM System/360 and System/370. The VAX processor implemented non-IEEE quadruple-precision floating point as its "H Floating-point" format. It had one sign bit, a 15-bit exponent and 112-fraction bits, however the layout in memory was significantly different from IEEE quadruple precision and the exponent bias also differed. Only a few of the earliest VAX processors implemented H Floating-point instructions in hardware, all the others emulated H Floating-point in software. The NEC Vector Engine architecture supports adding, subtracting, multiplying and comparing 128-bit binary IEEE 754 quadruple-precision numbers. Two neighboring 64-bit registers are used. Question: What mechanism did the DEC TOPS-20 system use for parsing the arguments to system commands? I think that there may have been a JSYS that was given a description of the arguments that a command could accept and it parsed the command's argument list.
Answer: I know very little about DEC TOPS-20, but I did manage to find a suitable set of manuals. I found the text below in JSYS_REFERENCE.MEM.txt here: It looks like COMND (JSYS 544) does something similar to what you describe: 3.26 COMND JSYS 544 Parses one field of a command that is either typed by a user or contained in a file. When this monitor call is used to read a command from a terminal, it provides the following features: The COMND call allows comments in the command line. A command line can contain a comment if the field before the comment has been terminated and the comment is preceded by an exclamation point or a semicolon. If the comment starts with an exclamation point, COMND ignores all text between the exclamation point and either the end of the line or the next exclamation point. If the comment starts with a semicolon, COMND ignores all text on the remainder of the line. A command line can contain the name of an indirect command file so long as the file name comes at the beginning of a field. It must, however, be the last item on the line, and its contents must complete the command. The user must follow the name of the indirect command file (after any recognition is performed) with a carriage return. If a carriage return does not end the command line immediately after the name of the indirect command file, the system outputs the message ?INDIRECT FILE NOT CONFIRMED. Also, if the user types a question mark (instead of the file specification of the indirect file) after he types the at-sign (@) character, the message FILESPEC OF INDIRECT FILE is output. If the indirect file itself contains an ESC or a carriage return, COMND treats them as spaces. COMND places the contents of the indirect file in the text buffer, but does not display them on the user's terminal. As the user types his command, the characters are placed in a command text buffer. This buffer can also include the command line prompt. Several byte pointers and counts reflect the current state of the parsing of the command. These pointers and counts are as follows: The following illustration is a logical arrangement of the byte pointers and counts. Remember that the prompting text buffer need not be adjacent to the text buffer. These byte pointers and other information are contained in a command state block whose address is given as an argument to the COMND monitor call. The .CMINI function initializes these pointers. COMND Parses a command line field by field. COMND substitutes default values for missing fields in the command line when the user types a carriage return, ESC, CTRL/F, or question mark. These characters are called action characters because they cause the system to act on the command as typed so far. Other characters that terminate a field are space, tab, slash, comma, and any other nonalphanumeric character. Normally, parsing does not begin, and the COMND call does not return control to the program, until an action character is typed. But if B8(CM%WKF) is on in word .CMFLG when the COMND call executes, parsing begins after each field is terminated. A program parses a command line by repeated COMND calls. Each call specifies the type of field the program expects to be parsed. The program supplies this information, placing a function code and any data needed for the function in a function descriptor block. On successful completion of each call, the byte pointers and counts are updated in the command state block, and any data obtained for the field is returned. The program executing the COMND call should not reset the byte pointers in the command state block after it completes parsing a command line. It should set up the command state block before it begins to parse any commands, and then use the .CMINI function to initialize the command state block before parsing each command line. This allows the .CMINI function to use the CTRL/H error-recovery feature. If the program resets the pointers and counts in the command state block, instead of using the .CMINI function to do so, use of the CTRL/H feature is not possible. When a CTRL/H is typed, the .CMINI function allows recovery from an error in the last command only if the following are both true: The COMND call allows the user to delete his typed input with the DELETE, CTRL/W, and CTRL/U keys without regard to field boundaries. When the user deletes part of a field that has already been parsed, the COMND call returns to the program with B3(CM%RPT) set in word .CMFLG, or the program resumes execution at the reparse address contained in word .CMFLG of the command state block. This address should be the place in the program at which parsing of the command line begins. If this address is zero, the program must test AC1 for this bit, and reparse the command line from the beginning, if necessary. (See the description of word .CMFLG of the command state block.) Question: Is this code dangerous, this code was written in C++ int n = 100; for (int I = 0; I < n; I++) {int array [I+1];} Am I creating multiple array with the same name or am I just replacing the old array with the new bigger one?
Answer: Here’s the code, reformatted for readability, and undoing autocorrect’s obnoxious capitalization: This is not valid standard C++ code, but it is valid C99 code. C++ is not exactly a superset of C. In C99, this creates and destroys a variable length array (VLA) on each iteration of the loop. Some C++ compilers offer VLAs as a language extension. In either language, this code isn’t dangerous. Semantically, it’s just creating and destroying 100 arrays, sized 1 to 100 elements. You can turn this into valid standard C++ code by fixing the size of the array at compile time: That would work just as well for whatever you intended to use the array for. Now, the loop in your question doesn’t do anything, and so any reasonable compiler will simply delete it if you turn on any sort of optimization. Presumably your actual code does something with the array. Let’s modify the examples above slightly to see what some popular compilers (GCC and Clang++/LLVM) generate for both loops. Here, dummy() is a function that presumably exists elsewhere. I’ve only provided a declaration so that the compiler can’t make any assumptions about what dummy() contains. This will force it to create the array. Here’s GCC 13.2’s output for each, using the flags -O3 -std=gnu++17. (gnu++17 is GNU’s name for their extended C++ dialect): Note: I’m using Godbolt’s Compiler Explorer, and it demangles C++ function names. That’s why dummy(int*, int) shows up above rather than _Z5dummyPii. It also defaults to Intel syntax, so the instructions above are in INST  dst, src order. You might notice that your original version does a lot of extra work to set up and tear down the VLA as compared to the modified version. In the modified version, the compiler reserves storage for the array once at the start of the function. Clang++ 17.0.1, invoked with the same flags, produces similar code. (Clang++ supports the GNU extensions.) While there’s some superficial differences, they’re pretty similar in character. The punchline is that your original code does extra work that isn’t particularly useful. That extra work isn’t the artifact of a specific compiler. Both GCC and Clang++/LLVM do extra work for the VLA that doesn’t really benefit you. Your array is what’s known as an automatic variable. Colloquially, we say it “lives on the stack.” Technically speaking neither C nor C++ actually specifies the existence of a stack. Stacks are just an incredibly popular way to implement automatic variables and track nested function calls. Automatic variables are called that as they are automatically created at the start of their lifetime and automatically destroyed at the end of their lifetime. For automatic variables in an inner block like this, you can think of them being created where their declaration is reached in the program, and destroyed when you exit the block that contains them.* In C and C++, a block controlled by a for-loop is entered and exited once per iteration. (* I’m handwaving some arcane details here, such as when exactly certain steps happen, as those details don’t affect this answer.) Is it reasonable to allocate an array like this as an automatic variable? In this particular example, you have at most 100 elements in your array and the elements are small. This is perfectly fine to allocate on the stack in most environments. For larger arrays, you’ll want to dynamically allocate an array instead. Colloquially, we say dynamically allocated objects are “on the heap.” Dynamic allocation is usually more expensive than automatic allocation. I say usually, as sometimes the compiler is able to optimize it away. If you really do need a potentially large array that changes size on each iteration, and doesn’t carry forward elements from iteration to iteration, I recommend the following idiom: The type T represents whatever data type you’re making an array of. In the original example, it was int. It could be some more complex type, such as std::string or a class you’ve defined. The array.reserve() step allocates memory once, outside of the loop. By reserving the maximum size up front, you ensure std::vector won’t have to reallocate its storage during the loop. If you don’t know the maximum size up front, or the maximum size is very large and unlikely to occur in practice, you might pick a different size as a reasonable starting point. Or, you could omit this step entirely. However, keep in mind that when std::vector does resize, any pointers, references, or iterators that point to one of its elements will become invalid. The array.resize() step sets the array size to whatever size you desire this loop iteration. It doesn’t need to be at the top, necessarily. It can appear at any point you know what the size needs to be. And obviously, it needs to be before any reference to an element in the array. Alternatively, you could use array.push_back() to grow the array element by element if you don’t know the array’s size a priori, or if you don’t want to default-construct all of the elements before overwriting them with other details. The array.clear() step resets the array size to 0, destroying the elements in the array. This ensures the elements don’t carry forward from iteration to iteration, as in your original example. You could omit this step if carrying them forward is harmless. The advantage of this approach is that std::vector knows its own size. It works well with C++ standard algorithms that take pairs of iterators or ranges (C++20) as well as range-based for-loops. The downside, of course, is that it performs dynamic allocation. I honestly wouldn’t worry about it unless profiling measurements spike it out as a performance issue. For example, if this function gets called many times, those dynamic allocations could add up. You can address that a number of different ways. Perhaps the cleanest that comes to mind is to wrap the function in a class that holds onto the std::vector. Then you only perform the dynamic allocation when you instantiate the class. You could also simply declare the array as static. That’s simpler, but it gives you much less control over the lifetime. Static objects get destroyed when the process ends. In a multithreaded program, you could have race conditions between that destruction and threads exiting. In this particular example, where we clear() the array every time we’re done with it, I don’t think we have an issue. I would avoid this pattern outside toy programs nonetheless. The punchline: It’s not dangerous code, but it is non-standard C++ and not the best way to accomplish what you’re trying to do.

Question: Why did C++ choose the keyword "virtual" to mean a function that is meant to be overridden? Why not "weak" or "lesser" or some other keyword?
Answer: Well, for one thing, it's neither weak nor lesser. In fact, virtual dispatch is a more powerful facility than ordinary function invocation. In the case of C++ virtual member functions, the real concept here is that the virtual member function name represents a virtual interface. There's a level of indirection behind the interface—virtual dispatch—that isolates the caller from the details of which actual implementation needs to be invoked based on the concrete object type you have an instance of. This isn't the only computer construct that uses virtual in this manner. For example, virtual memory addressing* adds a layer of indirection between the addresses your program uses and the actual physical addresses the hardware uses—if any. Virtualization in general adds a layer of indirection between the interface you interact with and the concrete entity that is on the other end of that interaction. C++’s virtual member functions aim to provide a similar sort of virtualization for interfaces that related classes might implement. As long as you obey Liskov’s Substitution Principle, instances of any classes that implement a particular virtual interface should be interchangeable with each other at run time, with respect to code that uses that interface. And that feature is neither weak nor lesser. It's actually quite powerful. * Virtual memory addressing has nothing to do with hard disks. Rich virtual memory operating systems usually support paging to disk when software asks for more RAM than what's installed. Virtual memory addressing is only one piece of that puzzle in environments that support paging.

Answer: It should be possible, if not for FORTH specifically.* The main issue is that stack based machines favor serial computation. In a stack machine, the operands to most instructions are implicit. They come from the top of the stack, with the result(s) going to the stack. The main exceptions would be: And both of those may source operands from the stack as well. A practical stack machine will have some operations that rearrange the top N items of the stack. For instance, a stack rotation moves deeper entries in the stack toward the top and elements at the top deeper into the stack. And you’ll have a few other operations that duplicate or drop entries from the stack. Techniques such as register renaming can be modified to work on a stack machine. Register renaming is a staple of superscalar out-of-order processors. The implicit operands to a stack operation map to stack slots. A register renaming engine could map the top N slots of the stack (for suitable N) to rename registers in a relatively straightforward manner. So what’s the issue then? Code generators for stack machines typically minimize stack depth and minimize operations that rearrange the stack. From an algorithm perspective, this is like the difference between DFS and BFS. A stack machine prefers something more like DFS, and if you can rearrange the computation tree to maximize depth over breadth, you minimize stack depth and the number of stack manipulations required. For example, suppose I’m adding four integer values together: e = a + b + c + d. Integer addition is commutative and associative. You could group these operations as ((a + b) + (c + d)) or (((a + b) + c) + d). A code generator for a register based superscalar machine might prefer ((a + b) + (c + d)), because the first two additions can occur in parallel. A code generator for a stack machine might prefer (((a + b) + c) + d), because it minimizes the stack depth and stack rearrangement you need to perform during the computation. In a stack-based machine, the first realization might look like: In that realization, the stack depth grows to 3. The second realization might look like: The second realization saves a stack slot, but it misses the opportunity to parallelize two additions. This might sound theoretical, but I assure you it isn’t. At a previous $DAYJOB, I know our code generator actually had a target configuration option that selected one of the two strategies for code generation. (Or at least it did at one time. That infrastructure evolved quite a bit over my tenure there.) It might also sound minor. In many cases it is. But for something like an accumulation, where the result feeds into the next computation in a loop, this serial approach directly slows that accumulation with a large serial computation in your critically recurrent path. Therefore, to be effective, a superscalar stack machine would need to be able to examine a large enough window of operations to discover instruction-level parallelism among multiple serial computation chains. And, in order to effectively extract that instruction-level parallelism, I believe it would need to be a superscalar out-of-order (OoO) machine in order to allow those serial chains to execute concurrently. With a strict in-order pipeline, the main parallelism you’re likely to get would be between operand fetches from memory, and result storage to memory. The renaming engine might squash the cost of rotating the stack, duplicating top of stack, and dropping elements from the top of stack. Once you shift to OoO, you can start parallelizing largely-independent computations. You just need a large enough instruction window to discover them. Modern OoO processors have a fairly deep reordering buffer, so the odds are good you can find those opportunities. Will it perform as well as a register-based architecture on a similar microarchitecture? Probably not unless you tweak the code generator to prefer parallelism despite the additional stack depth and/or stack manipulations it requires. The delta may not be huge for many workloads. It will, however, be a headwind to performance overall. But it is possible to implement. * And why did I say “for FORTH specifically”? FORTH itself is a high level language that has some powerful facilities for defining and redefining verbs in the language. I’m not a FORTH expert, and I’m not familiar with existing FORTH machines and whatever bytecode they might execute. From that standpoint, I felt it was safest to not make any claims specific to FORTH, and instead just focus on stack machines more generally.

Question: How would something like a Pentium III ported to 7 or 5nm process perform today? Would it be even semi competitive with any sort of semi-recent CPU (like Intel 2nd gen or 1st gen Ryzen)?
Answer: Well, the first thing to point out is that it would be tiny by today’s standards. Based on a quick search, the 1.133GHz Pentium III on 130nm was 80mm² with a 256KiB L2 cache. Scaled to 5nm, that would probably be less than 0.2mm² if everything scaled more or less linearly. I’m skeptical it would be quite that tiny. SRAMs, logic, and wires all scale differently. And there’s an additional caveat I mention below. From a clock rate perspective, it would probably scale up to the 2.5GHz - 3GHz range, given its relatively deep pipeline and small size. At first blush, it seems like you’d get more process clock entitlement. However, the original likely used significant amounts of custom logic. I’m assuming any port to a modern process would require conversion to standard cell logic. Conversion to standard cell will also increase its size. From an instructions per clock (IPC) perspective, it’s behind the pack in a big way. According to a table I found at Wikipedia, Pentium III pulls about 3.4 Dhrystone MIPS/MHz, whereas modern cores are more like 10 to 12 Dhrystone MIPS/MHz. That makes it about 1/3 of the IPC of a modern CPU. Honestly, the Pentium III number sounds a little high to me, while the modern processor number sounds a little low. The IPC ratio might be more like 1/4th or 1/5th on Dhrystone in practice. Add to that the fact that Dhrystone fits entirely in L1 cache. For workloads that need to go to external memory, the Pentium III will be severely hampered by its limited reorder buffer (40 µops). To put it in perspective, Intel®’s current efficiency cores (Gracemont) have a 256 µop reorder buffer. I don’t know how many cache misses the Pentium III can get in flight, but it certainly doesn’t hold a candle to modern processors that can get many dozens of cache misses outstanding. Gracemont can have 80 outstanding loads and 50 outstanding stores—and that’s an efficiency core. Pentium III’s 40 µop reorder buffer can’t get that many instructions in flight. On the Pentium III, each instruction with memory accesses takes 1µop per memory access in addition to the µop(s) for the instruction itself. Therefore, on the Pentium III you’re probably topping out at about 20 memory accesses in flight, maybe 25 if you’re really lucky. The Pentium III has an ancient SSE implementation—the very first SSE implementation, in fact! It’s a double-pumped 64-bit implementation. With any workload that benefits from SIMD instructions on modern cores—which most do, with modern compilers and auto-vectorization—the spread grows further. As a result, even if you get the clock rate up to 3GHz, I expect it to be at least an order of magnitude slower than a modern desktop processor at the same clock rate on many meaningful workloads. But hey, they’re tiny. You could plop down a gazillion of them! Addendum In the analysis above, I assumed we'd just move the Pentium III core forward, and put modern uncore (memory controller, bus interface, etc) logic around it. Back in the Pentium III era, most of that was in the motherboard chipset. Now it's all integrated. So, I totally expect many channels of DDR5, etc. in this imagined system with a time traveling core from over two decades ago. In other words, I approached this from the standpoint of porting the Pentium III CPU core into a modern system-on-a-chip (SoC) infrastructure. Wrap some logic around the Pentium III to translate its FSB protocol to whatever interconnect protocol you have, and put a modern interconnect, memory controller, and other infrastructure around it. The Pentium III itself shrinks down so small that it seems highly unlikely you’d put just one on a chip by itself. Rather, you’d plop down many of them, or plop down one or more of them next to some other beefy IP that’s large enough to justify building an entire chip. Disclaimer: The above is all very rough finger-in-the-wind estimates without particularly deep research, and therefore has large error bars. Your mileage may vary. Discontinue use if you experience side effects such as dizziness, excessive sweating, or unexplained rashes. Par value 0.02¢.

Question: Why were CGA and EGA digital, but VGA analogue?
Answer: It comes down to a combination of color gamut and video bandwidth. As Phillip Remaker’s answer rightly points out, bandwidth is a major issue. I do have a quibble with his answer, however. CGA, EGA, and VGA all place limits on the number of colors you can display simultaneously. However, that doesn’t affect what goes over the cable. Rather, the gamut of possible colors affects what goes over the cable. And as Phillip rightly pointed out, the pixel clock kept increasing as well. The real story emerges when you multiply the bits per pixel by the pixel clock. When you go from CGA to EGA, the bandwidth nearly doubles: ~58Mbps to ~98Mbps. That’s not to bad to absorb at that time. When you go from EGA to VGA, the bandwidth increases by a factor of 4.5 to ~453Mbps. Yowzers! That’s maybe a bit much for 1987 technology. To send that data digitally would require a firehose of a cable and a correspondingly chonky connector also, since it would likely be sent as parallel data rather than serial. Going to analog also enabled third parties to push the pixel clock and resolution further more easily. And by easily, I primarily mean cost effectively. Analog remained the most cost effective way to send high bandwidth video in PCs until digital technology caught up at a price point that enabled wide-scale deployment. Echoing CGA’s origins, that happened around the time television went digital. PC displays and TVs started out joined at the hip, and have ended up joined at the hip once again.

Question: How does RAM differ from a computer operating system?
Answer: Let’s start with the most obvious distinction: RAM is hardware, whereas computer operating systems are software. It’s like the difference between an office building and the management team of a company that uses that building. RAM consists of physical hardware that holds data when the computer is powered up. That’s pretty much all it does. Operating systems are programs that run on the CPU and manage both the hardware as well as application programs that run on the machine.

Question: Is it true that VLIW instruction set architectures never attained mainstream popularity? If so, why? Does it simply not provide enough of a performance boost over alternative technologies to be worth implementing?
Answer: VLIW stands for Very Long Instruction Word. Traditional VLIW architectures start with the 1980s RISC model of exposing machine resources, including exposing pipeline delays, and go a step further adding instruction level parallelism, deep instruction pipelines, and the resulting pipeline resource hazards into the mix. As with early RISC processors, traditional VLIW processors have exposed delay slots and large register files. Like RISC, they emphasize pipelined functional units that can take a new instruction every cycle. VLIW adds multiple functional units that operate in parallel. The long instruction word specifies which instructions to launch in parallel each cycle. The idea is to move the cost of hardware resource management and uncovering opportunities for instruction level parallelism from hardware to software—namely, the compiler. That way you spend more transistors on computation and less on finding computations to run in parallel at run time. The goal is high performance with minimal hardware overhead. The hardware can just issue instructions into the parallel pipelines, trusting that the compiler has resolved all the dependencies and resource conflicts. The instruction stream is statically scheduled in advance by the compiler, so that the hardware doesn’t need to spend transistors on scheduling the instructions. When the VLIW strategy works, it’s very effective. And when it doesn’t, it’s a huge liability. I spent nearly 20 years supporting a successful line of VLIW DSPs in a wide variety of roles, ranging from applications engineer to CPU and memory system architect. I am intimately familiar with VLIW’s strengths and weaknesses. Codesize First, let’s put aside one of the early criticisms of VLIW: codesize. Traditional VLIWs such as Multiflow and Cydra used a fixed-length instruction word—up to 1024 bits!—with dedicated slots for each functional unit. This simplified instruction decode and dispatch by keeping each functional unit’s instruction stream in a dedicated lane whose size and format was tailored to that unit. That model works well when most of the functional units are active every cycle. When there’s little inherent parallelism, however, most of the slots are empty and contain NOPs. That’s a huge waste. The VLIW DSPs I supported dispensed with that model. They fall into what might be called a compressed VLIW model, where you only spend opcode slots for the instructions you actually issue. The NOPs for idle units get compressed away. On the plus side, idle units don’t need an explicit NOP. On the minus side, instructions take on more uniform widths and spend opcode bits to specify which unit to dispatch to and which instructions issue in parallel. The compressed VLIW instruction set encoding looks more RISC-like with fairly uniform instruction sizes. The TMS320C6000 family—the main DSP family I supported—has 32-bit instructions, spending 1 bit on a p-bit to specify parallelism, and a few more to specify which of its 8 units to dispatch to. Later family members introduced a compact instruction encoding that has a 32-bit header per every 256-bit fetch packet, and offers a mix of 16-bit and 32-bit slots in the remaining 7 words in the fetch packet. This diagram from the TMS320C62x DSP CPU and Instruction Set Reference Guide (SPRU731A) shows how p-bits express which instructions issue in parallel on that architecture: The upshot is that compressed VLIW codesize might be somewhat larger than its RISC counterparts, but the increase isn’t as dramatic as the traditional VLIWs of the 80s. So, while VLIW codesize is often somewhat larger, it’s not a show-stopper. That’s my point. Big Performance Wins The biggest performance wins for this sort of architecture come from compute loops and other compute-heavy functions that have high degrees of inherent parallelism. Compiler techniques such as software pipelining and multi-block scheduling extract instruction-level parallelism from the source code. The compiler is able to schedule many instructions in parallel, and the hardware delivers. For digital signal processing workloads, as well as many high end scientific compute and linear algebra workloads, this works quite well. Back in 2011 or thereabouts, we compared one of our high-end DSP solutions to both x86 and GPU based solutions on certain workloads. IIRC, we saw that we had a 5× energy efficiency advantage over a GPU, and beat the general purpose CPU at wall clock runtime and overall energy efficiency. That’s quite a win! However, there are many real-life workloads don’t fit this model very well. Big Performance Losers, Part 1: The Memory System In the traditional exposed-pipeline VLIW model, instructions have an architecturally defined latency, and they need to stick to that latency. In the text below I’ll call this architectural latency for short. I’m aware of two major traditional VLIW latency models: Equals and Less-than or Equals. In the Equals model, the apparent run time instruction latency always equals the architectural latency. In the Less-than or Equals model, the apparent run time instruction latency may be less than or equal to the architectural latency, but is never larger. The TMS320C6000 DSPs were a bit of a hybrid here. When interrupts are disabled, the C6000 is an Equals architecture. When interrupts are enabled, it’s a Less-than or Equals architecture. That introduces one hiccup up-front: You always have to schedule instructions for the maximum latency, but you can’t take advantage of when results appear to arrive “early.” And to make the most use of your register file, you have to disable interrupts to guarantee no results arrive early. Ick. If that weren’t bad enough, neither model tolerates late results. Where that hurts you most is in the memory system. If you have a flat memory system with fixed latency, there isn’t a problem. If you have caches or any other non-deterministic factors, you’re in trouble: Any memory system stall needs to stall the entire CPU to ensure no architectural latency is exceeded. If your workload mostly fits in cache, and only takes a moderate number of compulsory cache misses, then the VLIW approach performs decently. If you can keep your memory system stalls to, say, 10% of your cycles, then you extract 90% of the peak performance offered by the CPU. Some tricks such as prefetching and pipelining multiple misses that occur in parallel or close proximity can help you achieve that goal. If your workload has many cache misses, however, your performance tanks. The VLIW approach doesn’t let you advance instructions unrelated to the cache miss. If any instruction stalls, all instructions stall. Because VLIW relies on the compiler to schedule everything up-front, it has no capacity to adapt to random stalls that happen at run time. Some of this can be ameliorated by adding a scoreboard. The scoreboard keeps track of which results are ready when they’re expected to be. When you don’t have a scoreboard, any stall that might cause a result to arrive late must stall the entire pipeline. With a scoreboard, you can delay stalling until an instruction tries to read a result that should have already arrived, but is tardy. A basic scoreboard helps a little, if you can schedule instructions far enough apart to hide memory system stalls. It’s no panacea, though. You end up transforming an Equals architecture into a sort-of Less-than-or-Equals architecture with respect to load instructions that might miss the cache. Big Performance Losers, Part 2: Exposed Pipelines and Branching Traditional VLIWs expose delay slots for everything, including branches. On the C6000 DSP, branches have 5 exposed delay slots. That means every function call and return takes a minimum of 6 cycles. Calling an empty function requires 12 cycles. There isn’t any scope for a branch predictor to help you out there. Furthermore, it becomes difficult to deal with instruction delay slots across branch boundaries. Within a function, you can use multi-block scheduling and software pipelining to account for most of those cases. Hardware features such as predication enable if-conversion to replace short forward branches associated with if-then-else constructs. With these features, we were usually able to schedule instructions effectively for the pipeline within most functions. Across function-call and function-return boundaries, however, you typically need everything to land before the branch is taken. You hit similar problems with branch-table based switch-case dispatch. That call/return overhead—and in some benchmarks, switch-case—quickly becomes a performance bottleneck in real world code. A Case Study: Dhrystone Let me start by saying I’m no cheerleader for Dhrystone. I find its continued relevance at this level frustrating, given how tiny it is. But, I ignore it at my own peril. Side note: I last explored Dhrystone deeply a bit over 8 years ago. Any cycle counts I quote in this answer are meant to be representative, but may not be completely accurate. We compared the DSP we were developing (the C71x DSP) against an in-order issue superscalar general purpose processor with a shallow pipeline and an out-of-order issue superscalar general purpose processor with a deeper pipeline. From what I remember, the in-order processor was able to complete an iteration of Dhrystone in around 235 cycles. The out-of-order processor was able to complete an iteration of Dhrystone in around 168 cycles. OK, that doesn’t seem too surprising, right? Well, with the deeper pipeline, a single isolated iteration of Dhrystone on the out-of-order processor actually took longer than it did on the in-order processor—closer to 270 cycles, if I remember correctly. The OoO processor was able to overlap iterations of Dhrystone to get a better score. A new iteration of Dhrystone starts while over a third of the previous iteration’s work is still in flight. What that meant was that our statically scheduled VLIW DSP had no chance of catching up to the OoO processor, unless it somehow managed to reduce the critical path through Dhrystone to less than what the short-pipeline in-order processor was able to achieve. The OoO processor extracted parallelism at a much higher level than a loop or a function. It extracted parallelism across iterations of the entire benchmark! The next iteration of Dhrystone started long before the previous iteration completed! And that’s at a mere 3.5 DMIPS/MHz. Modern processors are much faster than that. In our C71x DSP architecture, we employed some clever microarchitectural techniques in order to approach the performance of the in-order processor. We could turn pipeline protection on or off. Specialized scoreboarding logic handled both early and late results in both modes. And we hid all branch delays, relying on a branch predictor to help us out there. Ultimately, it was clear we would never be able to break into the territory the out-of-order processor was able to achieve. And that was for an embedded out-of-order processor from over a decade ago. Sure, a really smart compiler could try to inline the entire Dhrystone benchmark and try to software pipeline it. That misses the point. The reality is that real-world workloads don’t have an outer benchmark loop wrapped around them that a compiler has access to. Modern OoO pipelines extract instruction-level parallelism across unrelated stretches of code that the compiler may be completely unaware of. In-order pipelines eventually hit a wall. The Punchline VLIW architectures offer nice benefits for certain workloads, such as heavy compute workloads where much of the time is spent in heavy compute loops. This makes VLIW attractive for DSP and high-performance compute workloads that are dominated by such compute loops. They don’t do so well with general purpose workloads. They’re not able to effectively hide random memory system stalls, and they’re not able to extract instruction level parallelism across unrelated bits of code. In the already-lengthy answer above, I didn’t cover every issue VLIW faces, or all the potential approaches for addressing those issues. I’ve tried to give a taste. I will say that we did address some of these issues with a novel approach in the last DSP family I worked on (the TMS320C71x); however, my conclusions in the Dhrystone anecdote take those into account. I’ve also written a few other answers on VLIW that may flesh out some of additional details and answer follow-up questions: … … … … … … … … … … … … … … … … … … …
