Question: In programming, how many nested loops are too many? Is it always, 'it depends' or do ya just get to a point where it's just silly now'?
Answer: As Mark Harrison mentions, it depends on the dimensionality of the data. But, that’s not the only thing that matters. It also matters how you’re operating on the data. For instance, exhaustive motion search in tile-based video encoding can be thought of as a 6-level loop nest, despite working with 2-D images: Now, you usually don’t write that directly as 6 levels of loop nest. You might put the outermost 2 levels in one function that steps over tiles. The innermost block of that loop nest calls another function to loop over the search window. In that function, you might manually unroll the innermost tile-summing loops to apply SIMD/vectorization and to take advantage of overlaps between successive offsets of the tile. You might end up with a 2-level loop nest in one function that invokes another function with a 2-level loop nest containing a bunch of unrolled SIMD/vector computation. But logically, that’s still a 6-level loop nest. Other sorts of 2-D convolution and correlation algorithms also end up with four or more logical levels of loop nest. More generally, some data traversal patterns look like a deeply-nested loop even if the code itself isn’t deeply nested. For example, a 1-D Cooley-Tukey FFT has 3 levels of loop nest, but the data access pattern for the butterflies might be expressed with a 4th level. For those reasons, we developed address generators and vector fetching hardware with 6 levels of loop nest on the last DSP I worked on. I’ve ended up with deep loop nests in other places outside signal processing. For instance, quick-and-dirty exhaustive search implementations can end up with a loop level for each parameter I’m searching over. That fits in line with Mark’s observation; however, in this case the number of parameters determines the dimensionality. Exhaustive searches are rare in practice, as a k -deep loop nest has roughly O ( n k ) time complexity, assuming all parameters have a similar number of alternatives. On occasion, I’ve also used deep loop nests to generate permutations. That was before I learned about better algorithms to generate permutations with simpler loop structures. In C++, you can just use std::next_permutation and avoid any explicit loop—it’s hidden in the library call! Given all that, let’s talk practicalities. Suppose you’re faced with a problem that’s most naturally addressed by a deep loop nest. To keep your code readable, you probably want to avoid more than about 2 to 4 levels of loop nest in your actual implementation. If you need more than that, consider breaking it up into multiple functions. The outer loops can call a function that implements the inner loops, as I suggested in my motion search example above. For the motion search that might look something like: You could also collapse loops by combining logically connected levels into a single level that encapsulates them. Consider the motion search example again. Instead of using separate x and y loops for the tile location, I could have a single loop that iterated over “tile location” encapsulated in a coordinate object. Now I just need an iterator object that iterates over the tile grid, as in this example for C++11 and later: Now you can do something like this: That could be worth doing if the same pattern arises repeatedly.

Question: Why is it that the C programming language can be used across multiple different devices but Assembly cannot?
Answer: I assume you mean “multiple different architectures” as opposed to “multiple different devices.” We're long past the days when each computer was unique by about 75 years, give or take. Assembly language isn't one language. Rather, it's the human readable form of the machine code for a particular processor architecture family. Each family has its own instruction set. There may be many different mutually incompatible dialects of assembly code for the same instruction set. For example, look up MASM and AT&T syntax for x86 assembly code. The Z80 is largely backward compatible with the 8080; however, because Intel® copyrighted* their instruction set, Zilog developed their own mnemonics and syntax. (*It’s unclear whether that copyright claim was meaningful.) In fact, you can even have incompatibility within the same assembly language dialect for the same processor family. Newer family members may support instructions and registers that aren't present on older family members, for instance. Instructions for newer processors won't work on older processors that lack those extensions. Now, there have been some assembly translators. It works best when the architectures involved are related, and the newer one takes translation into account. 8080 → 8086 is a famous example. These translators are rare. C code, on the other hand, can be compiled for whatever target architectures the compiler supports. As long as you stick to certain rules and build the right abstractions, it's not that difficult to write portable C code. All you need is a compiler for whatever target architecture you're interested in, and in many cases you are in good shape. It does take effort and care. It's orders of magnitude more approachable than porting large piles of assembly language though. Addendum Since it came up in discussion on a different answer, I figured I would mention it here. If you run the assembled code in a simulator or interpreter, then you can run your assembly language wherever you’ve ported the simulator/interpreter. That assembly language can even target a virtual machine, rather than a real CPU. That particular thread brought up EFI byte code specifically. My answer focuses on assembly code for the native instruction set in its native form. That's what I believe most people think of when they see that phrase without further qualifications. You can develop other kinds of assembly language with different properties. For example, you could create an assembly language that provides a common subset of core operations and abstract “registers,” and use macros or a specialized tool to generate the actual machine code for different machines. Or you could create an assembly language that targets various sorts of virtual machines, such as JVM byte code, CPython byte code, EFI byte code, UCSD pCode, Microsoft’s pCode, etc. When describing it to others, you should call out the fact that it's not traditional native assembly language, otherwise you're likely to cause confusion.

Question: In the MSP430 assembly language, what is the underlying logic of the JGE instruction?
Answer: I’m not sure what you mean by underlying logic. That suggests you're asking about implementation details that most Quorans won't have access to. If you're asking what it does from a programmer's model perspective, that's a different question. It's a conditional jump: Jump if Greater-than or Equal. It takes the jump only if the Negative and oVerflow status flags are both zero, or both one. That condition is consistent with a signed comparison where the first value is greater than or equal to the second value. Consider this code sequence: The jump will be taken if the value in R1 is greater than or equal to the value in R0. That might seem backward. The CMP instruction works by subtracting the first operand from the second, which is why you need to read it right to left. I wrote a much longer article on conditional branches here: That article covers the CP1610 rather than the MSP430; however, the two are very similar. They both draw heavily on the PDP-11, and therefore work similarly. The CP1610’s BGE (Branch on Greater-than or Equal) is roughly equivalent to MSP430’s JGE. The CP1610’s S and OV flags are equivalent to the MSP430’s N and V flags, respectively. Addendum Now that I’m at a real computer rather than my phone, I figured it would be worthwhile to excerpt the relevant portion from the link above. The following excerpts from the link above may be useful. Remember, BGE on the CP1610 is equivalent to JGE in MSP430. I wrote this several years ago, and I can see my writing style has improved in the meantime. At least, that’s what I tell myself. :-) How Signed Arithmetic Works With Conditional Branches The next couple of paragraphs describe how these branches work with compares. Most of the time, you do not need to think about these details when writing programs, so feel free to skim it for now and come back to it later. The compare instruction compares two numbers by subtracting them, and then setting the flags based on the result. Question: Is learning specifically *assembly* language - as opposed to machine/object code - still useful? Wouldn’t one obtain the same pedagogical benefits from studying how a high-level language (e.g. C) is compiled to object code without learning assembly?
Answer: Each teaches different things, and has different scope of relevance. Machine Language I sincerely doubt anyone teaches machine language as a programming language. If you’re studying machine language in a course, it’s most likely a computer architecture course of some form. You’re studying how a particular machine encodes its operations into bit-patterns. Machine language is primarily relevant to: Some aspects of machine language may be relevant above that level. At that point, they’re mostly interested in bigger-picture details such as code size tradeoffs. Assembly Language Assembly language is the human readable form of machine language. When you learn assembly language, you’re effectively learning a lightly abstracted form of machine language. Assembly language abstracts away details of the encoding and focuses on the operations and resources the machine exposes to software. It’s useful to learn how to break down complex operations into much simpler machine operations. You can gain an appreciation of what’s involved in seemingly simple operations, such as passing arguments to a function, computing arithmetic expressions, or implementing control constructs. You probably won’t develop much software in assembly language. These days, you might use assembly language to write relatively focused bits of code, such as: These examples all share a common property: Once they’re written, they typically fade into the background. With possible exception to the tiny embedded systems, they become part of the furniture the rest of your applications rest on. The tiny embedded systems might actually become part of some appliance or other device where the processor is invisible, such as a dishwasher or lightbulb. When you port to a new architecture—or a newer revision of the same architecture—most of these need to be reworked to take advantage of the new architecture. Once they’re reworked, they can be forgotten again. I say “most” above, as there are many cases where you have a high level language fallback that you can start with. Or, in the case of a newer revision of the same architecture, the existing assembly may still run just fine. You might not get the full entitlement of new processor features until you have time for a rewrite. For many of these, you can skip writing assembly directly and instead use compiler intrinsics in a high level language. However, you still need to understand the instructions you’re targeting with those intrinsics. You just let the compiler worry about managing registers and memory accesses and so on. The more you know about the instruction set, the more effective you’ll be at using these intrinsics for a speedup. More commonly, you’ll end up reading assembly rather than writing it. Most compilers can be talked into outputting assembly code for something they’ve compiled. And, most debuggers let you see an assembly representation of the code in an object file or in RAM. It’s much easier to read and understand assembly code if you’ve written it before. In these cases, if you can read assembly language, you can determine exactly what the compiler has asked the hardware to do. That may provide insight into performance anomalies or subtle bugs that weren’t apparent in the higher level language. Maybe the compiler performed some optimization you didn’t realize was legal, and that broke things. Or maybe it did a terrible job optimizing some algorithm. Or maybe there’s a hardware bug that’s only tickled by a specific instruction sequence. Whatever the issue, you have a powerful tool in your toolkit if you can read assembly. High Level Language At this level, you could ignore most of the details of the machine. In fact, Java’s bold claim on introduction was “write once, run everywhere.” More jaded folks restated it as “write once, debug everywhere;” however, the issues they allude to reside at levels other than the instruction set. This is the level you’ll spend the vast majority of your time at. This is where you’ll learn how to be a programmer. These days, most folks learn data structures, algorithms, and software abstractions at this level. There is a lot more flexibility to scale your programming efforts up in a high level language. And, you can learn different programming paradigms that aren’t tied so closely to the way processors function. A low level procedural language such as C is still within arm’s reach of the processor. C, in fact, defines an abstract machine as part of its language semantics that is, in some sense, a lowest common denominator among all the machines C runs on. Other paradigms, such as functional programming, use an entirely different semantic model and require you to think differently about how to structure your program. It’s still useful to understand assembly language in this context. If you know what the underlying machine supports natively, you have some sense of the relative cost of different approaches. However, unless you’re looking at compiler output to see what it really generates for some particular input, that value is going to remain somewhat vague. With today’s highly optimizing compilers, the connection between code and instructions could be far less direct than you imagine. Add to that the fact that other facets of the system—caches, branch predictors, I/O—are also all rather important as well. They may be the dominant hardware factors affecting your application. Pulling it Together You asked: Wouldn’t one obtain the same pedagogical benefits from studying how a high-level language (e.g. C) is compiled to object code without learning assembly? I don’t think you would in a modern curriculum. The focus and scope at each level should be different. As your question hints at, the audience for machine language is quite specialized. The focus at that level is very different, and shouldn’t really be on programming at all. While some aspects of programming and code generation are relevant to processor architects, for instance, it’s not the focus. And yes, there are low-level hackers that love to twiddle everything right down to the bare metal, but that’s beyond the scope of coursework. The vast majority of developers can ignore machine language the vast majority of the time. For assembly vs. high level language, you do have more potential overlap. In my opinion, the pedagogical focus should be more complementary than anything. Assembly language opens the door to working with the machine as it is, on its terms. A modern curriculum shouldn’t focus on developing applications at this level. Rather, you want to learn how complex operations decompose into simple machine operations. You want to understand how many things you take for granted—system calls, function calls, basic arithmetic, variable accesses, virtual dispatch, etc.—map to machine primitives. You might also want to learn how to build primitives in assembly language that you expose to high level languages so they can use the machine effectively. High level languages allow you to abstract away the very same details assembly helps you understand. Once you get past the basics of programming, turn your attention upward towards building ever larger abstractions, and building applications on those abstractions. Learn and apply data structures and algorithms. Learn how to apply design patterns to structure libraries and application software so that they can be extended and maintained. Assembly language serves a foundation for that stack of abstraction. You won’t think about it most of the time. But, when you need to work with the processor directly, or drill down through that stack of abstraction to understand a performance issue or a particularly tricky bug, you’ll have some tools in your toolbox to tackle it. A Special Case: Compiler Developers If you happen to end up developing compilers, now you’re on the other side of both the high level language and assembly language. You get to be one of the people behind the curtain that connects the two, lowering high level code into machine instructions. You’ll need to understand both the high level language and assembly language.* That’s a whole different ball of yarn. In my experience, most compiler developers have a different focus on and understanding of assembly from those who develop in assembly directly. The compiler has its own abstractions wrapped around the various machine operations and resources. Those abstractions are geared toward automatic code transformation, optimization, and object code generation. Compiler theory has its own set of courses that teach how to do that. (*You’ll also need to understand the machine language if your compiler outputs it directly, and you’re working on the part that does that step. That only affects a small piece of the compiler that isn’t touched nearly as often as the rest.)

Question: Why do we write delete than new in copy assignment operator overload, if our class has a member that is a pointer to another object in C++?
Answer: Let’s forget new and delete for a moment. What is the actual principle involved here? Resource ownership. And what does it mean for an object to own a resource? It means that object is responsible for ensuring that resource is released when it’s no longer needed. Ownership of Non-static Data Members A class may have static and non-static data members. For the purposes of this answer, I am only going to focus on non-static data members. Where I say “data member” below, I mean “non-static data member.” When you construct an object of that class, each data member gets constructed as well, in order of declaration. When you destruct an object of that class, each data member get destructed as well, in reverse order of construction. For example, if you have a data member that represents a file, such as an instance of std::fstream, constructing that data member may open a file. Or maybe you open the file later using some member function. It doesn’t matter, though. Destructing that member will close any file associated with it, if one is open. That releases the file resource. Instances of a class clearly own their non-static data members. But what does that mean for pointer data members? Ordinary Pointers are Oblivious to Ownership Ordinary pointers are a primitive data type in C++, like int or double. By default, constructing and destructing an ordinary pointer does nothing—a default-constructed ordinary pointer holds an indeterminate value, and destructing an ordinary pointer always does nothing. You can construct an ordinary pointer with an initializer value such as nullptr or a pointer to an object. But, that won’t change how it’s destructed. Destructing an ordinary pointer always does nothing. Ordinary pointers don’t manage ownership. They’re completely oblivious to the concept. The language expects you to keep track of that. Owning vs. Non-owning Pointers Under normal circumstances, pointers can hold one of the following: A given class may have one or more pointer data members. If they point to valid objects, those data members may or may not point to a resource that a given object owns. For example, consider this class: You could use this class to represent a span of characters in a string: If you follow the half-open interval policy of the C++ standard library, the Span named span now represents the span of characters "lo" currently held in the array hello[]. If I print that Span with the following loop, I’ll see “lo” on the output: Does the object span own those characters? No! They’re owned by the array hello[]. When span is deconstructed, it shouldn’t do anything with respect to those pointers. And if you look at my implementation above, I don’t define a destructor. I just use the default destructor, which does nothing for the pointer members begin_ and end_. This is exactly correct. Neither begin_ nor end_ are owning pointers. Destruction must do nothing for these pointers. But what if I have some fancier class that holds a pointer to an instance of some other class that it allocates? This is most probably an owning pointer. In that snippet above, though, I didn’t take care of my full set of ownership duties. At a bare minimum, I probably need a destructor: But, as you probably guessed, that isn’t enough. The Big Five (Formerly The Big Three) What are the Big Five? Before C++11, #3 and #4 didn’t exist, which is why you might hear of the Big Three. C++11 introduced move semantics, which I’ll get to in a minute. Move semantics expanded the Big Three to the Big Five. The Big Five are directly involved with ownership. Let’s take a closer look. Destructor I’ll cover the destructor first, even though I listed it last. The destructor is responsible for destructing any resource owned by the object that the default destructor for any data member wouldn’t release. If your object owns another object through an ordinary pointer, then your object’s destructor has the responsibility of destructing that owned object, most likely by calling delete (or delete[]) on it. Copy Construction Copy construction creates a new object as a copy of an existing object. Copy assignment replaces the value of an existing object with a copy of an existing object. If you copy-construct an object, then in principle you should copy everything the source object currently holds. But what if that object has an owning pointer to some other object? Well, there are two options: Option #1 is the simpler of the two. Each object retains unique ownership of everything it owns. Copying an object with an owning pointer requires you to create copies of all objects owned through pointers, so that the original and the copy each uniquely own the objects they own through pointers. This is probably the only model you’ve encountered in your coursework so far. Option #2 is more complicated. When multiple objects share ownership of some shared object, you need additional bookkeeping to keep track of whether any object is still interested in owning that shared object. You probably haven’t encountered that yet, so I will focus primarily on option #1 in this answer. Copy Assignment Copy assignment is closely related to copy construction. However, you’re assigning to an existing object that may already own some resources. So, just like copy construction, you need to copy all of the resources that the source object currently owns. But, before you can make the destination object the owner of those copied resources, you need to release (destruct) any resources the destination object currently owns. For most data members, that just means copy-assigning to those data members in the destination from their corresponding members in the source. But for owning pointers, you have some additional work to do, because ordinary pointers are oblivious to ownership. You need to construct copies of any objects that the source currently owns through pointers, and you need to destruct any objects that the destination currently owns through pointers. Then, you can make the destination object the owner of the copies you just created. That’s the process that gets at the crux of your question. You might notice, though, that I didn’t state the steps in the same order. In your question, you had: I put these in the opposite order, because new can throw an exception if you’re out of memory. Likewise, copying an object can throw an exception if something else goes wrong. If you want a strong exception guarantee—that is, either the copy-assignment succeeds, or it fails with an exception leaving the original unmodified—then you want to make the copies first and only then release the resources associated with the target. That is: Why this process? As I mentioned before, allocating memory or constructing a copy of owned objects could throw an exception. You don’t want to modify the object you’re assigning to until you know you won’t encounter an exception. The construction step may need to be wrapped in a try / catch block to unwind a partially constructed copy of the source object’s resources, to avoid a leak in case of an exception. Move Construction and Move Assignment Move semantics are a nice addition to C++ that arrived with C++11. They allow one object to “steal” the resources of another object. Move construction takes ownership of resources held by the moved-from object. For objects owned through pointers, the newly constructed object doesn’t need to do much. It just initializes its pointers to point to the objects it now owns. The moved-from object needs to update its pointers to point to nothing (e.g. nullptr), so that its destructor doesn’t try to release resources it no longer owns. Move assignment is similar; however, the moved-to object needs to end ownership of any objects it owns through pointers. For ordinary pointers, that means calling delete (or delete[]) on those resources before replacing those pointers with the values owned by the moved-from object. I’m glossing over a bit here in the sake of brevity and keeping this answer somewhat focused. Smart Pointers Part of the reason I said ordinary pointers above is that C++11 provides some smart pointer classes that manage ownership tracking for you: std::unique_ptr and std::shared_ptr. These manage unique ownership and shared ownership, respectively. If nothing else, they will cause the compiler to complain when you don’t manage the pointers properly. In particular, std::unique_ptr prevents you from copying the pointer it wraps. Rather, you need to make a copy of the pointed-to object when copy constructing or copy assigning, and initialize the std::unique_ptr in the destination to a pointer to that copy. Also, the destructors for both std::unique_ptr and std::shared_ptr understand ownership. When you destruct a std::unique_ptr, it will also destruct the object it points to, if it points to an object. And when you destruct a std::shared_ptr, it will also destruct the object it points to if you destruct the last std::shared_ptr that points to that object.* (*There are some curlicues around std::weak_ptr, control blocks, and std::make_shared that I won’t get into here.) The upshot is that if you’re able to replace your ordinary pointers with C++11 smart pointers, and otherwise keep your data members well behaved, you may be able to replace your hand-written Big 5 with a compiler-supplied Big 5. If you make appropriate use of the modern C++ standard library, you could completely avoid calling new and delete directly in most programs. Conclusion So why do you write delete then new, in your copy assignment member function? Because you’re managing ownership for an object held by an owning pointer using a pre-C++11 style that didn’t offer strong exception guarantees. To get strong exception guarantees in a pre-C++11 environment, you would perform these steps in a different order. You might need try {} catch blocks to handle cases with more than one object owned via pointers in a way that won’t leak resources in the presence of exceptions and would still offer a strong exception guarantee. In C++11 onwards, you would probably use smart pointers to manage ownership, and end up with a cleaner result. You may even be able to use the compiler-supplied default versions of the Big 5 with most classes.

Question: Let's say I declare a valid opcode instruction with db in-between other *actual* instructions, like mov, will the processor treat the expression defined with db as an instruction, or just as byte variables? How does the processor know the difference?
Answer: Let me get this straight. You want to do something like this, correct? Here, DB stands for Define Byte or Data Byte. It directly injects the byte 0x2C into the code stream in the example above. Directives such as DB or .byte or similar don't define variables. They just inject bytes into the assembled output. Likewise for their cousins DW and .word. The exact names of the directives will vary by assembler, but in my experience they all follow a similar model. Can the processor tell the difference between this byte and any other 0x2C in memory? No. How would it? The above sequence assembles to the following 5 bytes. Notice there aren't any flags or markers that distinguish opcode bytes from argument bytes from bytes inserted by the DB directive. Bytes are bytes. So what happens when the processor tries to execute this byte I inserted? It treats it as an instruction, just like any other. Invalid Opcodes If I inserted an invalid opcode into code stream here, then what happens next depends on the CPU. The original NMOS 6502 didn't check for invalid opcodes. As a result, it has a number of “undocumented instructions.” I put that in quotes, as their existence is unintentional. These aren’t instructions that were deliberately added but left undocumented.* Some of these invalid opcodes behave like a combination of officially defined instructions. Several are so-called KIL opcodes that hang the chip until the next reset. Links: (*Unlike the 8085’s undocumented V and K flags and associated instructions, which appear to be deliberate, but incompatible with Intel’s 8080 to 8086 forward compatibility story. Link in the comments.) The 6502’s CMOS upgrade—the 65C02—treats invalid opcodes to NOPs. Modern CPUs typically throw invalid opcode exceptions. Older CPUs displayed a mix of behaviors, either ignoring invalid opcodes, or running random operations that just happened to fall out of the implementation. Valid Opcodes If it's a valid opcode, then the processor will execute it just like any other instruction. Now those of you that really know their 6502 may have noticed I’m up to something with my example. And those of you who aren't 6502 experts may have suspected something anyway, if you’ve read enough of my other answers. This is our original assembly code: It assembled to: A disassembler will take object code and display the instruction sequence associated with it. It decodes the instructions in much the same way that the processor would, at least on straight-line code. What do you suppose a disassembler will show us for the 5 bytes of object code above? I suggest you try disassembling this code yourself. I’ll wait while you work it by hand. It's only 5 bytes. There's a nice opcode summary here: Link: http://www.6502.org/tutorials/6502opcodes.html  This image may also help, by mapping bytes to mnemonics: . . . . . . Ready? It disassembles to: Wait, what? What happened to the other LDA? It became part of the BIT instruction! If we start at the first LDA instruction, we’ll end up executing the two instructions you see above—LDA #$42 followed by BIT $47A9. The second LDA is gone! The Liksee (LXI) and Movie (MVI) Tricks What I just showed you is a 6502 version of what's also been called the LXI (“liksee") trick, named for the 8080 LXI instruction. There's a related MVI (“movie”) trick, named for the 8080 MVI instruction. I’ll let Tim Paterson (of MS-DOS fame) explain: Link: https://archive.org/details/dr_dobbs_journal_vol_15/page/215/mode/1up And that's exactly what's happening in my example. I just happened to use BIT, because it only modifies flags and only needs 4 cycles. A relative branch takes 3 cycles, but requires two bytes. This is a size/speed tradeoff. So let's see what's really going on here: If you jump to a, you’ll reach point c with A = $42, because the BIT instruction “swallows” the second LDA. If you jump to b, you’ll reach point c with A = $47. Nifty, eh? The Punchline Bytes are bytes. If you try to execute some bytes you inserted into the code, the processor won't treat those bytes differently from other instructions. With that knowledge in hand, you can do some clever—if somewhat sleazy—tricks. Addendum Note that my answer assumes the OP is injecting one or more bytes between two instructions in otherwise executable code. If you are using a machine with an MMU that can treat some memory regions as executable, and others as non-executable, that doesn't really affect my answer. The instructions involved should already be in an executable region. The data byte will be right in there with them. As I stated: bytes are bytes. They don't have flags or markers on them to flag them individually as data or code. Some MMUs may treat separate regions of memory as executable vs. non-executable, but that's unrelated to the question at hand.

Question: In assembler compiler and interpreter, which one is used very much and why? Whereas, why are the remaining both are not used very much?
Answer: All three are used quite regularly. Interpreters If you’ve ever written a formula in a spreadsheet, you’ve used an interpreted language. Likewise if you’ve ever written a batch file or shell script. Languages such as Python and Lua are typically interpreted by default. Javascript was initially implemented as an interpreted language. Modern implementations of Javascript may still interpret short bits of Javascript, as that’s less expensive than doing something fancier. Compilers Languages such as C and C++ are typically compiled by default. These are quite popular as well. Some compilers still emit assembly language, however, and use an assembler to make the final object code. GCC is one such compiler. LLVM-based compilers can also be configured this way if the target requires it. The Continuum Between Compilers and Interpreters Some languages, such as Java and C#, specify a language that’s meant to be compiled down to an intermediate bytecode. That bytecode can then either be interpreted by a virtual machine, or just-in-time compiled to native code. And, of course, there are C and C++ interpreters, as well as Python and Javascript compilers. Assemblers There aren't as many folks directly writing assembly language today as there were 30+ years ago. But, that doesn’t mean that assemblers don’t get used on a regular basis. As I mentioned above, there are still compilers that output assembly language and rely on an assembler to put together the actual object code. Also, major codebases often have a bit of assembly language in there somewhere, whether it be in a system library, OS interface, or something else. Operating system kernels typically have some assembly language source files, as do typical standard library implementations. Also, if you use a modern 64-bit ARM-based device,* there’s a good chance you’re running low-level software such as ARM’s TF-A that includes several assembly helper files in the codebase. (*I don’t know whether this is true for Apple’s ARM based devices. I haven’t checked.) Punchline The takeaway is that assemblers, interpreters, and compilers are all still regularly used. Assemblers are low-level plumbing that continue to find work in modern codebases, mostly indirectly, but also directly for the few critical bits that need it. Interpreted languages show up many places, including places where the folks writing interpreted code don’t necessarily realize they’re writing interpreted code. If you browse the web or use a spreadsheet or fiddle with macros, scripts, or batch files, you’re using an interpreter most likely. If you browse the web, your computer is likely interpreting some fraction of the Javascript embedded in the pages you visit. Compiled languages get a lot of oxygen, but they’re not the only game out there. And compiled languages may compile down to something that’s interpreted or assembled. Historically interpreted languages might also have a just-in-time compiler implementation. That said, traditionally compiled languages might also have an interpreted implementation that provides better diagnostic or debugging insight. Your teacher probably wants you to pick one of those three as “the way we do things now,” with the claim that the other two are obsolete or little used. Your teacher has fallen into the intellectual trap H. L. Mencken described in the quote above.

Question: As a programmer, what things would I have to learn and master very well if I wanted to make graphical interfaces in C++ completely from scratch without having to use any library?
Answer: No libraries? None at all? I think you're toast. The core language is designed to have at least a couple headers to encapsulate implementation defined details that are sometimes exposed through compiler magic. If you reject the C++ standard library, you don't get those. You're only slightly better off if you allow yourself the C++ standard library. If you target a bare metal system with a simple frame buffer display and straightforward input mechanisms, you stand a chance. But, you will need to learn how to write low level hardware interface code and drivers in order to do so. A skilled embedded developer could actually put together a pretty decent GUI framework. I watched Arnauld Chevallier put together IntyOS entirely in assembly language, so I know it's possible: Given that you're asking this question on Quora, I doubt you qualify as a skilled embedded developer at this point in your career. Realistically, you're going to want to use some of the basic interface libraries that come with whatever operating system you're using. At a minimum, you’ll want to use OS interface libraries that give you access to the display, human interface devices (keyboard, mouse, neural probes, etc), time keeping, file systems, etc. Now you can focus on reinventing the wheel, without the distraction of reinventing the rest of the vehicle it will be attached to. You should probably get a good idea of what wheels look like first. I would say the first step would be to use some existing GUI frameworks to see what the design space looks like. There's the current crop of desktop GUIs, all of which are pretty heavy duty. You might spend some time with older, simpler GUI frameworks to see how to scale down. I think you may conclude you have better uses of your time than boiling the ocean.

Question: Is it true that C allows one to pass by value an entire struct - even a large struct - as a function argument but does not allow one to pass by value an array - even a small array - as a function argument (instead requiring pointers)? If so, why?
Answer: Yep! The same goes for return values as well. This passes a large structure by value to and from a function: C doesn’t permit passing even a tiny array such as char a[1] by value, either as an argument or a return value, however. Why? To make it easier to catch errors while porting B code to C. In B, arrays didn’t have names—at least the contiguous storage associated with the array didn’t. B didn’t have types, either. You operated on machine words. A given word would behave as a pointer or an integer or a character or a function address based on how you used it. Word-sized locations in memory were referred to as cells. If you declared an array variable in B, what you really got was a variable consisting of a single cell. In turn, that cell was initialized the starting address of an unnamed, contiguous collection of cells elsewhere. You could even assign different addresses to that variable. Function arguments and return values were always just words as well. You didn’t pass arrays to and from functions, you passed addresses to the elements. C was derived from B and shared much of the syntax. But, C also added a bunch of new functionality, including a type system. With that type system came structures (struct). That forced Dennis Ritchie to reconsider how arrays were handled. He’s already told the story, so I’ll just quote it here: Embryonic C NB existed so briefly that no full description of it was written. It supplied the types int and char, arrays of them, and pointers to them, declared in a style typified by The semantics of arrays remained exactly as in B and BCPL: the declarations of iarray and carray create cells dynamically initialized with a value pointing to the first of a sequence of 10 integers and characters respectively. The declarations for ipointer and cpointer omit the size, to assert that no storage should be allocated automatically. Within procedures, the language's interpretation of the pointers was identical to that of the array variables: a pointer declaration created a cell differing from an array declaration only in that the programmer was expected to assign a referent, instead of letting the compiler allocate the space and initialize the cell. Values stored in the cells bound to array and pointer names were the machine addresses, measured in bytes, of the corresponding storage area. Therefore, indirection through a pointer implied no run-time overhead to scale the pointer from word to byte offset. On the other hand, the machine code for array subscripting and pointer arithmetic now depended on the type of the array or the pointer: to compute iarray[i] or ipointer+i implied scaling the addend i by the size of the object referred to. These semantics represented an easy transition from B, and I experimented with them for some months. Problems became evident when I tried to extend the type notation, especially to add structured (record) types. Structures, it seemed, should map in an intuitive way onto memory in the machine, but in a structure containing an array, there was no good place to stash the pointer containing the base of the array, nor any convenient way to arrange that it be initialized. For example, the directory entries of early Unix systems might be described in C as I wanted the structure not merely to characterize an abstract object but also to describe a collection of bits that might be read from a directory. Where could the compiler hide the pointer to name that the semantics demanded? Even if structures were thought of more abstractly, and the space for pointers could be hidden somehow, how could I handle the technical problem of properly initializing these pointers when allocating a complicated object, perhaps one that specified structures containing arrays containing structures to arbitrary depth? The solution constituted the crucial jump in the evolutionary chain between typeless BCPL and typed C. It eliminated the materialization of the pointer in storage, and instead caused the creation of the pointer when the array name is mentioned in an expression. The rule, which survives in today's C, is that values of array type are converted, when they appear in expressions, into pointers to the first of the objects making up the array. This invention enabled most existing B code to continue to work, despite the underlying shift in the language's semantics. The few programs that assigned new values to an array name to adjust its origin—possible in B and BCPL, meaningless in C—were easily repaired. More important, the new language retained a coherent and workable (if unusual) explanation of the semantics of arrays, while opening the way to a more comprehensive type structure. Link: https://www.bell-labs.com/usr/dmr/www/chist.html Because C did away with the separate pointer to the array, the old B practice of reassigning that pointer no longer works. That is, in B you could do this: That replaces the pointer in the cell named a with the pointer value from the cell named b. (And, in this example, if you didn’t save a’s original value somewhere, it’s now lost forever.) In C, that no longer works. You need separate pointer variables, like this: If arrays were first class types that permitted whole-array assignment, the original program would change meaning dramatically. So, instead array assignment is forbidden, forcing a hard break. Meanwhile, C allowed you to continue using the old B syntax for pointer parameters in K&R style function declarations: When ANSI C came along, this practice was carried forward into ANSI C prototypes, unfortunately. In the linked page, Dennis points out the consequence: On the other hand, C's treatment of arrays in general (not just strings) has unfortunate implications both for optimization and for future extensions. […] More fundamentally, the definition of C so specifically describes the semantics of arrays that changes or extensions treating arrays as more primitive objects, and permitting operations on them as wholes, become hard to fit into the existing language. So what about struct? The B language didn’t have data types, including struct. That came into existence later in C’s history. Therefore, free of the backward-compatibility burden, struct could become a first-class type. C allowed copying structures by assignment and passing structures as function arguments¹ and return values fairly early in the language’s history.² This inconsistency between arrays and structures has nothing to do with the cost of copying arguments passed by value. It has everything to do with C’s relationship to B, and the way Dennis designed the language to provide a smoother transition from B to C. For folks interested in reading more about the relationship between arrays and pointers in various contexts, these answers might be helpful: … … … … … … … … ¹ Some early implementations didn’t do a great job. Some had problems with reentrancy and what-not. ² Dennis points out that while AT&T’s implementations picked this up quickly, not all 3rd party implementations did right away. From the C History page linked above: While it foreshadowed the newer approach to structures, only after it was published did the language support assigning them, passing them to and from functions, and associating the names of members firmly with the structure or union containing them. Although compilers distributed by AT&T incorporated these changes, and most of the purveyors of compilers not based on pcc quickly picked up them up, there remained no complete, authoritative description of the language.

The Most Obscure Language I've Used Professionally And perhaps the most obscure language is one that's proprietary to my previous employer: VTG. I implemented a version of it. I didn't invent the language, though. A couple other people developed it about 15 years before it was handed to me. I wrote a completely new implementation in C++14. I started with the existing language syntax and extended it in several interesting ways. VTG’s language looks like a funky assembly language. Its source code consists primarily of constraint strings that specify what types of instructions to select and how they need to be connected. VTG then generates random assembly language programs that meet the constraints. The constraints can be extremely tight, resolving to a specific instruction, or completely flexible, resolving to anything other than a branch. Among my extensions were a macro facility, support for labels and braches, aggressive deferred evaluation for constraints, richer control of the register allocator, and selective eager evaluation for specific arithmetic constructs. I also developed a library of helper macros for validating floating instructions. VTG’s entire user base—in terms of people writing in VTG’s source language—over its 25+ year lifespan is probably fewer than 50 people. The user base for my implementation was probably on the order of a dozen people. But, it was a key piece of infrastructure in our team. Runner Up A runner up is Swipe, the VLIW instruction scheduler I inherited and extended a variety of interesting ways, at the same job. You feed a basic block to Swipe, and it will schedule the instructions and allocate registers. It could software pipeline loops or list-schedule straight-line code. I consider Swipe as less obscure, as it has a lot in common with the linear assembly optimizer my employer released. They even share a common ancestor for parts of their implementation. I also consider it less of an actual language. Swipe is really just a tool to assist with assembly language programming. VTG, OTOH, would generate runnable programs.

Question: What was the most unusual dialect of the BASIC programming language you have seen or used, and what made it so?
Answer: That's easy: Intellivision ECS BASIC. (Levitation unit sold separately.) History ECS stands for Entertainment Computer System. This system was put together in a relative hurry because Mattel’s original plan—the Keyboard Component—wasn't coming together quickly enough. The Keyboard Component was a fancy 6502-based device that had a computer controlled block addressable 4-track cassette drive, a full sized keyboard, 16K × 10-bit RAM, all running in tandem with the Intellivision’s 16-bit CP-1610 CPU, plus sound and graphics hardware. The Keyboard Component even included a separate 40×24 character generator that could superimpose white text over the Intellivision's graphics. It was truly a technical marvel, but too unreliable to release. Jay Leno was hired to entertain at one of Mattel's Christmas parties. He joked: You know what the three big lies are, don't you? “The check is in the mail,” “I’ll still respect you in the morning,” and “the Keyboard will be out in the spring.” It's too bad. The Keyboard Component ran a modified version of Microsoft’s 6502 BASIC (available as a cartridge), and had some genuinely interesting features. Customers were getting rightly upset that the computer upgrade they were promised hadn't materialized. The FTC threatened to find Mattel—supposedly $10K/month—and so it needed something, quickly. Management set up a parallel development project, in a different part of the organization, at least somewhat away from the eyes of the Keyboard Component folks: the Low User Cost Keyboard Interface, aka. LUCKI. That’s what Mattel released as the Entertainment Computer System (ECS). The ECS doesn't include a second processor or second video chip. It has a very simple half-duplex modem-like cassette interface like other early 80s computers. But, it includes a simplified keyboard (48-key chicklet), and it includes its own home-grown, hastily written BASIC. It ticks enough of the boxes (at least superficially) that the FTC stopped fining Mattel. And lastly, it killed the Keyboard Component for good. ECS BASIC: Simplified and Slow ECS BASIC was a very simplified BASIC. All of its keywords were at most four letters long. For example, instead of INPUT and PRINT, you got INPU and PRIN. You only had three string variables (A$, B$, and C$), and three 1-D array variables (AA, AB, and AC). You couldn’t even use INPU and PRIN with string variables; rather, you had to use GET and PUT. Mattel positioned its computer as an educational product, rather than just a toy. In line with that, they developed the first syntax-highlighted BASIC that I know of. They even patented it: US Patent 4,617,643: Syntax error correction method and apparatus. Here’s an example I just whipped up: You can see that the color scheme described in the patent differs somewhat from what they actually productized. This is what they actually went with: It also has a weird feature related to this: An empty line gets color-coded black-on-grey to indicate a syntax error. However, it still gets added to the program! In other line-number BASICs, an empty line usually just deletes the line from the program. In ECS BASIC, you need to use the DEL command for that. When you LIST your program, the interpreter prints that number in white on the screen. When you RUN it, it scans and prints all of these white lines as well before proceeding. Let’s add a line to my program to show it in action: What happens when I run it? This behavior seems to be part of its more general handling for invalid input lines: ECS BASIC was also dog slow. Some of that had to do with inefficient implementation. In particular, the math routines look like they were hand translated from the 6502 BASIC’s floating point package, poorly, based on what I saw when I disassembled it. Did I mention this was a rush job? The biggest speed limiter, however, came from a deliberate design decision: the interpreter loop periodically sync’d with the vertical retrace interrupt. Or, more correctly, with the console’s built-in EXEC and its retrace interrupt handler. It only let the the interpreter loop make progress for 1 out of 3 display frames, typically. The interpreter loop could be as slow as 1 token interpreted every 50ms (20Hz). Why? ECS BASIC EXEC Integration The Intellivision includes a fairly rich, event-driven built-in execution environment known as the EXEC. The EXEC manages moving objects on the screen—what we now call sprites—as well as reading the hand controllers and playing sounds and music. Early Mattel games relied heavily on the EXEC to load graphics into the video hardware and to manage graphics and sound. ECS BASIC integrates with the EXEC to provide access to its functionality. It provides a set of subroutines for calling into the EXEC: In addition to the variables that acted as implicit arguments to the various subroutines above, ECS BASIC included a set of “functions” that manipulate objects once they were on the screen. Syntactically, many of these look more like magic variables, because they can be assigned to. There were a few other special purpose functions that it provided: ECS BASIC’s EXEC integration makes it a fairly interesting BASIC, in that it has support for movable objects (sprites), including animation and automatic motion right out of the box. So why does that kill the interpreter’s speed so badly? The EXEC itself was written more for size than speed. It only updates its notion of the world at 20Hz, phasing updates across three display frames.* If I recall, two of the phases update objects 0–3 and 4–7, and the third handles interactions between objects (collision dispatches). (*Or 16.7Hz if you have a PAL/SECAM system running at 50Hz refresh rate.) ECS BASIC doesn’t make use of the EXEC’s collision detection features, but it does manage picture sequencing and object motion. That means both the EXEC and the ECS need to manipulate the same variables. That could be a race-condition nightmare. Now, ordinarily you might use a mutex; however, that’s tricky in an interrupt driven environment. You could mask interrupts and implement a critical section; however, the interpreter is so slow that you could end up missing interrupts entirely, which will blank the display. So what did they do? They did the simplest, most conservative thing possible: They completely pause the interpreter loop for the 2 phases where the EXEC updates the moving objects. That means it’s completely paused, doing nothing, for 2 out of 3 display frames. *d’oh*! Other ECS BASIC Oddities ECS BASIC was designed to be extended. The parsing logic and main interpreter loop both probe for an expansion ROM at a particular address, and will vector there if it sees the correct signature. Mattel advertised an extended BASIC along with a 16K memory expansion (to complement the anemic 2K in the ECS unit). It’s unclear how much development work went into it. In the product brochure is a picture of a convincing mock up; however, it’s just a block of carved wood, painted to match the Intellivision. They did, however, release a game that integrates with ECS BASIC: Mr. BASIC Meets Bits ’n Bytes. This is an interesting blend of a game framework and BASIC: You get three partial games that you can program the remaining logic for in BASIC! So, that about wraps up the most unusual BASIC implementation I’ve spent time with. ECS BASIC is a relatively unique oddity of the early days of video game systems that played at being computers.

Question: What's the difference between System V and System V AMD64 in context of ABI?
Answer: UNIX™ System V is a family of commercial UNIX™ versions. System V has undergone four major revisions, with variants of System V Revision 4 (aka. SVR4) being the most commercially successful. System V defines an Application Binary Interface. This interface defines file formats, the contents and locations of various libraries, linking conventions, system interface functions etc. This is also called the gABI, for Generic ABI, as none of the information contained within it is processor-specific. It remains constant across all hardware platforms. “System V AMD64” isn’t quite a thing. You’re probably thinking of the SysV AMD64 Processor Specific ABI Supplement. These days, it goes by x86-64 psABI for short. This is a separate document that gives details of how to implement System V on x86-64 platforms. That includes calling conventions, register usage, the sizes and alignments of various data types, the behavior of the floating point unit, how to implement position-independent libraries and executables, how registers map to debug information, and so on. Question: Why does the number of processor cycles required to process a single array element grow with the working set (array) size? Measurements from "What every programmer should know about memory" (page 20-21).
Answer: I would replace the term process with access. Access means a read and/or write of a value in memory. Also, I would emphasize working set size over array size. The working set size is the total amount address space accessed over a particular measurement period. This applies to all data, whether or not it's in an array. In a modern computer, the cost of a single memory access can vary over a wide range. If all data is in physical RAM—as opposed to a swap file or memory-mapped data file on disk—you can still see 4+ orders of magnitude difference between best-case and worst-case access time. The actual processing (arithmetic, comparisons, etc.) doesn't usually vary so much by comparison, once you factor out the memory accesses. Ulrich Drepper gives a very detailed explanation in his article, with diagrams and everything. I won't attempt to repeat all of his excellent analysis here. I’ll just try to summarize the themes. The high level takeaway is that in terms of latency, processors are much faster than main memory. We do what we can in hardware to hide it, but the more memory you touch, the less effective the hardware is at hiding this gap. Unloaded main memory access latency on a typical personal computer has been in the 40ns to 160ns range since some time in the 1980s, and is unlikely to improve. Loaded memory system latency can be several times larger. Bandwidth and CPU clock rate have both increased dramatically, but latency hit a wall. Imagine a 4GHz CPU with an unloaded latency of 40ns and a loaded latency of 400ns. That's 160 to 1600 CPU cycles for a single memory access. Caches help hide the latency; however, they only help when you access the same value multiple times, or a collection of values that are located together—i.e. your memory access pattern has reuse and locality—while the data you need is still in cache. As you increase your working set beyond the sizes of your caches, you decrease the likelihood that the data your program wants to access is in cache when your program needs it. Virtual memory addressing adds another unwelcome twist: The processor must translate the virtual address to a physical address. A single memory access could trigger 3 or more accesses to translation tables. If you're running a virtual machine, it can be dramatically worse—up to about two dozen additional accesses on one processor In know of. Worse, these are tree traversals, so you can't overlap the accesses. A parallel set of address translation caches (μTLB, L1 & L2 MMUs / TLBs) try to accelerate that process. However, they rely on the same reuse and locality properties as the data cache, just at a different granularity. I recommend you reread Ulrich Drepper’s fine article, and maybe work through some simplified examples by hand with a very small cache. It's instructive and it may help your intuition.

Answer: C and C++ are different languages. But, where they share operators, their relative precedence and associativity are the same. I’ll focus on C, although it’s not difficult to extrapolate to C++. C does have some oddities in its precedence structure, but the difference between left-to-right and right-to-left is not one of those. C makes sensible choices here. Let’s turn to page 53 of K&R 2nd Ed: The first thing you’ll notice is that nearly all the operators are left-to-right. There are three categories that are right-to-left: Let’s take a closer look. Unary Operators The expression -a means “negate a”. The unary negation operator negates its only operand. It’s considered right-to-left because its operand appears to its right. To reclassify it as left-to-right, you’d need to write a-, which is just weird. If you see the expression a-*b, what does that mean? I wrote it without spaces on purpose. If you told me that unary - and unary * were left-to-right associative just like their binary counterparts, then that would parse as (a-) * b. I don’t know about you, but I find that seriously weird. But, by making the unary operators right-to-left, this parses as a - (*b). Assuming b is a pointer or an array, then this dereferences the pointer associated with b, and subtracts the value it points to from a. Assignment Operators C treats assignment as an operator that results in a value, rather than as a statement. If it were a statement, its associativity wouldn’t even enter the discussion. For example, in Pascal, assignment is a specific type of statement. When you write… …it’s pretty clear you’re going to evaluate the expression b + 42, and then assign the result to a. Superficially, the C expression a = b + 42 does the same thing. But, because assignment is an operator in C, the expression has a value. Its effective value is the value that’s in the assigned lvalue. C allows you to write stuff like the following, unlike Pascal: The right-to-left associativity ensures this parses as a = (b = 0). The expression assigns 0 to b, and then assigns the effective value of b to a. Why did I say “the effective value of b”? If you do something like this… …then a ends up with 255, not -1. Yes, it’s weird, but such situations tend to be rare. In general, I don’t see many chained assignments like this these days. They were more common 30 years ago. The ?: Operator This is where it gets fun. As far as I know, the ?: operator is a C innovation. If nothing else, C popularized it. What does right-to-left associativity bring to the table here? It effectively allows you to write a compact if-else stack in an expression: In C, that’s equivalent to: They map pretty closely. When used properly, I feel the compact form aids readability. The right-to-left associativity ensures that everything after the colon is taken as a single expression. The example above parses as: But, I don’t think I needed to tell you that. It just reads naturally, doesn’t it? PHP decided to borrow ?: from C, but made it left-to-right associative. I… I can’t even begin to parse that mentally. Instead, I’ll borrow an example from PHP: A Fractal Of Bad Design. (Link: https://eev.ee/blog/2012/04/09/php-a-fractal-of-bad-design/) prints horse. I’ll let you puzzle that one out on your own. It’s an enlightening journey. More General C Precedence Oddities Most of C’s precedence hierarchy makes sense, IMO. If you understand PEMDAS/BODMAS, most arithmetic expressions make sense. Operators for array indexing, pointer dereferencing, structure member access, etc. have an appropriately high precedence. For example, when you write str.member + arr[index], you know that the addition operator isn’t going to interfere with the member access or the array indexing. Operators which are meant to separate expressions—e.g. &&, ||, assignment (=), and comma (,)—have appropriately low precedence. That said, there are a few places that aren’t so obvious. For example, the following correctly prints which values of i are even and odd: This very similar looking piece of code does not: That second version tells us every value of i is odd! Why? Because it parses like this: Oops! You need extra parentheses: Dennis Ritchie himself lamented this situation: Rapid changes continued after the language had been named, for example the introduction of the && and || operators. In BCPL and B, the evaluation of expressions depends on context: within if and other conditional statements that compare an expression's value with zero, these languages place a special interpretation on the and (&) and or (|) operators. In ordinary contexts, they operate bitwise, but in the B statement the compiler must evaluate e1 and if it is non-zero, evaluate e2, and if it too is non-zero, elaborate the statement dependent on the if. The requirement descends recursively on & and | operators within e1 and e2. The short-circuit semantics of the Boolean operators in such ‘truth-value’ context seemed desirable, but the overloading of the operators was difficult to explain and use. At the suggestion of Alan Snyder, I introduced the && and || operators to make the mechanism more explicit. Their tardy introduction explains an infelicity of C's precedence rules. In B one writes to check whether a equals b and c is non-zero; in such a conditional expression it is better that & have lower precedence than ==. In converting from B to C, one wants to replace & by && in such a statement; to make the conversion less painful, we decided to keep the precedence of the & operator the same relative to ==, and merely split the precedence of && slightly from &. Today, it seems that it would have been preferable to move the relative precedences of & and ==, and thereby simplify a common C idiom: to test a masked value against another value, one must write where the inner parentheses are required but easily forgotten. (Link: https://www.bell-labs.com/usr/dmr/www/chist.html) There are other places where we don’t have natural intuition about precedence for C’s operators. These arise for operators that aren’t part of the PEMDAS/BODMAS we grew up with. For example, does a << b + 1 mean (a << b) + 1 or a << (b + 1)? Even experienced C programmers will add parentheses to make the meaning clear. And in case you were wondering, it means a << (b + 1). Summary C’s precedence hierarchy has a couple of non-obvious choices in it. These choices result in extra parentheses in many complex expressions, in order to make their meanings clear. The selection of which operators are left-to-right vs. right-to-left associative, however, isn’t a meaningful factor here. C++’s situation is similar. It adds more operators relative to C, but the overall dynamic remains the same.
